The full title of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment is The Great, Vast Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Sutra of Definitive Meaning. It has twelve chapters. In it Śākyamuni Buddha, through dialogues with twelve great bodhisattvas, proclaims the wondrous principle of the Tathagata's perfect enlightenment (the perfect enlightenment of the self-nature) and the methods of cultivation.
Master Hanshan said:

"Where one seeks what is most simple yet refined, most urgent yet essential, nothing surpasses the supreme Dharma-gate of Perfect Enlightenment. Its text runs to no more than thirteen thousand words, yet it gathers in the boundless ocean of teachings, encompasses the perfect doctrine of the Dharma-realm, penetrates to the source of the one mind, and traverses the purport of the three contemplations. Partial and perfect interchange; single and double are cultivated to completion; it searches out the false master and strips away the maladies of Chan, so that the wondrous gate of mind-awakening is entered directly in a single leap. This is what is called the true sutra of the Dharma-realm and the wondrous practice that accomplishes Buddhahood. Sudden awakening and sudden realization are as clear as a fruit held in the palm. The purport of the Patriarch's coming from the West and its secret, wondrous meaning have nothing left beyond this. No student of the Buddha but takes this as a guide."
(Postscript to the Engraved Commentary on the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment)

[The Three Contemplations] refers to the three contemplations of the Tiantai school: the contemplation of emptiness, the contemplation of the provisional, and the contemplation of the middle. The contemplation of emptiness sees that all dharmas, being produced by conditions, have no own-nature and are empty just as they are; the contemplation of the provisional sees that although all dharmas are equally illusory, they nonetheless possess provisional marks and functions; the contemplation of the middle sees that all dharmas are neither empty nor provisional, being the true principle of the Middle Way that is both empty and provisional. [Partial and perfect interchange; single and double cultivated to completion] see Chapter Eight, "The Twenty-Five Rounds." [The false master] the false master, namely the illusory self of the five aggregates of body and mind. [Searching out the false master] see Chapter Nine, "Dispelling the Four Marks." [Stripping away the maladies of Chan] see Chapter Ten, "Keeping Far from the Maladies of Chan." [As clear as a fruit held in the palm] as one sees a fruit in the palm of the hand. [The purport of the coming from the West] the essential purport of Bodhidharma's coming from the West.
"The Great, Vast Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Sutra of Definitive Meaning"
Great, Square, and Vast"

, these three characters are the essence, mark, and function of this sutra. "Great" means greatness of essence: this sutra gathers in the boundless ocean of teachings and encompasses the perfect doctrine of the Dharma-realm. "Square" means the squareness (uprightness) of mark: this sutra is the norm and rule of all dharmas. "Vast" means vastness of function: this sutra, according with its essence, pervades everywhere, with wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without end.
[Perfect doctrine] the school whose purport is the true and perfectly complete teaching of the Mahayana. [Square] upright; norm, rule.
Perfect Enlightenment"

, the core of this sutra is perfect enlightenment, which means both the perfect enlightenment of the self-nature that accomplishes Buddhahood and the Dharma-gate of perfect enlightenment that is cultivated in reliance upon it. The Buddha said:
"The unsurpassed Dharma-king
(the Tathagata)
has a great dharani-gate
(a great gate of total retention)
, which is named Perfect Enlightenment."

[Perfect Enlightenment] the perfect enlightenment of the self-nature, waking completely from the dream of ignorance. The self-nature has two states: the intrinsic nature and the consciousness nature. The intrinsic nature is the state of the self-nature's perfect enlightenment; the consciousness nature is the state in which the self-nature is deluded. The intrinsic nature is Buddha; the consciousness nature is sentient being. Therefore, cultivating to Buddhahood means bringing the self-nature to perfect enlightenment (perfect enlightenment). (On the intrinsic nature and the consciousness nature, see in detail
The Mind, the Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha

.) [Sentient beings] also called beings with feeling, that is, all creatures that possess feeling and consciousness. In the ten dharma-realms, apart from the Buddha, the beings of the nine realms are all called sentient beings. [The ten dharma-realms] hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, Buddhas. The first six are the six mundane realms; the last four are the four noble realms. [The dream of ignorance] In this sutra the World-Honored One teaches that all beings are within the dream of ignorance and that all dharmas are matters within the dream of ignorance:
"Good sons, this ignorance has no real substance. It is like a person in a dream: while dreaming, the dream is not nothing; but upon waking, nothing whatsoever is obtained."
The Mahayana Ghanavyuha Sutra says:

"Forms seen in a dream are only false views of the mind; once awake they do not exist. In the dream of ignorance one sees men and women and all manner of forms; when perfect enlightenment is attained, nothing is seen."
[Form] here "form" is the general term for material existence. (On the dream of ignorance, see in detail
The True Nature of All Dharmas
sutra"

, translated into Chinese as "conforming scripture," is the general name for all Buddha-Dharma. "Conforming" means that above it conforms to the wondrous principle of all Buddhas and below it conforms to the capacities of sentient beings. "Sutra" means a thread: it threads the meanings of the Dharma together so that they are not scattered; it also means a scripture.
Sutra of Definitive Meaning"
, the most thorough, ultimate, and perfectly complete of scriptures.

[Definitive meaning and provisional meaning] The Buddha taught the provisional-meaning teachings for humans, gods, and the two vehicles, because their vessels were small and could not bear the great Dharma; he taught the definitive-meaning teaching for the bodhisattva vehicle, because their faculties were great and could bear the great Dharma.
Translated in the Tang Dynasty by
Buddhatrata
Translated by Buddhatrata of the Tang Dynasty.
Buddhatrata, rendered in Chinese as "Juejiu" (Awakening Rescue), was a man of Jibin (
ji
), and he translated the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment at the White Horse Temple in Luoyang. The Kaiyuan Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings,

chapter nine, says: "The sramana Buddhatrata, called in Tang times 'Juejiu,' a man of Jibin in northern India, translated at the White Horse Temple in the Eastern Capital one fascicle of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment of Definitive Meaning."

[Jibin] a country of the Western Regions. Xuanzang of the Tang, in his Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, calls it "Kashmir," that is, present-day Kashmir. [Kaiyuan] the reign title of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang (Li Longji) (CE
). [Eastern Capital] in Tang times this meant Luoyang; the capital was then at Chang'an.
The essential tenet of this sutra is:
forever transcending all illusions and realizing entry into perfect enlightenment
(bringing the self-nature to perfect enlightenment)
More specifically: all dharmas are illusory; in transcending illusion there is enlightenment; when there is nothing further to transcend, one enters perfect enlightenment.
The method of cultivation is:
perfectly illumine the mark of enlightenment and keep far from all illusions.
This sutra says:

"All Tathagatas, in the causal ground of their original arising, rely upon the perfectly illuminating pure enlightened mark, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the path of Buddhahood."
It also says:

"Good sons! Those bodhisattvas newly learning and the beings of the degenerate age who wish to seek the Tathagata's pure and perfect enlightened mind should with right mindfulness keep far from all illusions." "Knowing illusion, one at once transcends it, without resorting to expedient means; transcending illusion, one is enlightened, and there are no gradual stages. All bodhisattvas and the beings of the degenerate age who cultivate in accordance with this will thus be able forever to transcend all illusions."

[Perfectly illumining the mark of enlightenment] In the causal ground, all Buddhas rely upon the light of the perfect-enlightenment self-nature to illumine in return the quiescent, pure enlightened mark of the self-nature, forever cut off ignorance, and accomplish the path of Buddhahood. [Ignorance] taking the illusory as real. This sutra says:

"What is ignorance? Good sons! All beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversions, like a deluded person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy reflections of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in space and a second moon. Good sons! Space truly has no flowers; the diseased one falsely clings to them, and because of this false clinging he is not only confused about the nature of space itself but also deluded about the place where the flowers truly arise. Because of these false existences, he revolves in birth and death; this is called ignorance."

For the bodhisattva of initial resolve, the method is to turn the light back and illumine the self-nature, like a pearl that emits light which then illumines the pearl itself. The wisdom that illumines is prajñā; the object illumined is ignorance. Prajñā permeating ignorance is like the summer sun melting ice. Toward objects and conditions one neither clings, nor stalls, nor is stained; gradually the illusions subside and the true essence is gradually revealed. At first it is like a new moon, then it increases stage by stage until the moon's disk is full. When all illusions have ceased, quiescent illumination stands before one.
[Keeping far from all illusions] In this sutra the Buddha says:

"Good sons! All bodhisattvas and the beings of the degenerate age should keep far from all illusory and false realms. Because of firmly holding to the mind of keeping far, that mind, being like an illusion, should also be kept far from. Keeping far is itself illusion, so this too should be kept far from. Being free of the illusion of keeping far, this too should be kept far from. When there is nothing left to keep far from, all illusions are removed."

(Paraphrase: Good sons! All bodhisattvas and the beings of the degenerate age should keep far from all illusory and false realms. Because they firmly hold to the thought of keeping far from illusory realms, this thought is itself illusory and must therefore also be kept far from; keeping far from this mind of keeping far is itself illusory and must therefore also be kept far from; keeping far from this keeping far is itself illusory and must also be kept far from; when one reaches the point of having nothing to keep far from, all illusions are removed.)

Dividing a sutra into three parts began with Master Dao'an of the Jin dynasty, though most scholars of his time did not follow it. Later the Bodhisattva Bandhusri's Treatise on the Buddha Ground circulated in this land and also contained three parts: first, the section on the causes and conditions for the teaching's arising; second, the section of what the sage's teaching sets forth; third, the section of practicing in accordance with the teaching. Only then did people believe in Master Dao'an's brilliance; ancients and moderns alike follow it.

This sutra consists of three great parts: the introductory part, the main part, and the transmission part. "The Assembly of Sages" is the introductory part; the final chapter, "Twelve: Receiving and Preserving, Transmitting and Spreading," together with "Guarding Day and Night," is the transmission part; the eleven chapters in between are the main part (the body of the text). These eleven chapters are: 1. The Causal Ground and the Practice of Dharma; 2. The Illusion-like Samādhi; 3. The Stages of Cultivation; 4. Three Questions on Ignorance; 5. Forever Cutting Off Rebirth; 6. The Differences in What Is Realized; 7. The Three Great Wondrous Gates; 8. The Twenty-Five Rounds; 9. Dispelling the Four Marks; 10. The Need to Keep Far from the Four Maladies; 11. Dwelling in Quiescence and Devoting Oneself to Practice.
Note: The above division into chapters and the chapter titles are provided for ease of understanding and reference, much like a textual outline; they are not original to the sutra.

The Assembly of Sages" chapter describes how the World-Honored One, in the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light, entered the samādhi of the Treasury of Great Radiant Light, and within that samādhi manifested the reward body in a Pure Land (the Land of Real Reward and Adornment), teaching the Dharma to the great bodhisattvas and their retinues.

"Thus have I heard. At one time the Bhagavan entered the samādhi of the treasury of great radiant light, the true reception wherein all Tathagatas abide in the adornment of light, which is the pure enlightened ground of all beings: body and mind quiescent, the fundamental limit of equality, complete throughout the ten directions, non-dual and compliant; and in that non-dual realm he manifested pure lands."

This is what I (Ānanda) personally saw and heard. At that time the World-Honored One entered the samādhi of the Treasury of Great Radiant Light. This is the realm of radiant adornment in which all Buddhas dwell (the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light), and it is also the ultimate enlightened ground of all beings, pure and undeluded. The World-Honored One's body and mind were quiescent, the fundamental limit of equality, complete throughout the ten directions, compliant in non-duality; within that non-dual realm he manifested the reward body in a Pure Land (the Land of Real Reward and Adornment), teaching the Dharma to the great bodhisattvas and their retinues.

[Bhagavan] one of the common epithets of the Buddhas, also rendered Bhagavat; here it refers to Śākyamuni Buddha. [Supernatural powers] the ability to do as one wishes without any obstruction. [Treasury of Great Radiant Light] that is, the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light. In the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light there is no other dharma at all, only great radiant light, and so it is called the Treasury of Great Radiant Light. [Samādhi] rendered in Chinese as "concentration" or "true reception." [True reception in samādhi] samādhi is also translated "true reception"; "samādhi true reception" juxtaposes the Sanskrit and the Chinese. [Body and mind quiescent, the equal fundamental limit, complete throughout the ten directions, non-dual and compliant] this describes the true realm of quiescent light. [Fundamental limit] the ultimate and final boundary; that is, the absolutely equal principle-essence, most often referring to nirvāṇa. Also called the true limit, suchness, the actual. [Non-dual and compliant] without discrimination or grasping (non-dual), yet following conditions and according with affairs (compliant). [Manifested pure lands] manifested in pure lands (manifested his body in pure lands). Here "lands" renders the fusion of "zhi" (of) with "yu" (in). For example, in The Foolish Old Man Removes the Mountains: "cast them to the tail of the Bohai Sea." The pure land here refers to the Land of Real Reward and Adornment.

[The three bodies] the dharmakaya, the reward body, and the response body. The dharmakaya is the intrinsic nature possessed by all beings, but beings are deluded and do not manifest it, while the Buddha is awakened and has realized it; the reward body is produced by the Buddha's wisdom and merit and is distinguished into the reward body for his own enjoyment, which is the body in which the Buddha himself enjoys the Dharma-bliss of inner realization, and the reward body for others' enjoyment, which is the body manifested by the Buddha to teach the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds; the response body, also called the transformation body, is the Buddha body manifested in response to the capacities and conditions of beings. [The four lands] the Land of Coexistence of Ordinary and Noble Beings, the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder, the Land of Real Reward and Adornment, and the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light. The Land of Coexistence of Ordinary and Noble Beings is the land where ordinary beings and the noble ones who manifest bodies to teach them dwell together; the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder is the land inhabited by the two vehicles and by bodhisattvas before the grounds; the Land of Real Reward and Adornment is the land inhabited by the Buddha's reward body and by bodhisattvas on the grounds; the Land of Eternally Quiescent Light is the land inhabited by the Buddha's dharmakaya. [Before the grounds] before the first ground. Those before the grounds are ordinary bodhisattvas; only on the grounds are they dharmakaya bodhisattvas.

"Together with a hundred thousand great bodhisattvas and mahasattvas, whose names were: Mañjusri Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Universal Vision Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Pure Wisdom Bodhisattva, Majestic Virtue and Freedom Bodhisattva, Voice of Discernment Bodhisattva, Purifier of All Karmic Hindrances Bodhisattva, Universal Enlightenment Bodhisattva, Perfect Enlightenment Bodhisattva, and Excellent and Worthy Leader Bodhisattva, these being the leaders. Together with their retinues they all entered samādhi and dwelt together in the Tathagata's assembly of equality."

Those who took part in this assembly included a hundred thousand great bodhisattvas, among them: Mañjusri Bodhisattva, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Universal Vision Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Pure Wisdom Bodhisattva, Majestic Virtue and Freedom Bodhisattva, Voice of Discernment Bodhisattva, Purifier of All Karmic Hindrances Bodhisattva, Universal Enlightenment Bodhisattva, Perfect Enlightenment Bodhisattva, and Excellent and Worthy Leader Bodhisattva, these being the leaders. All the great bodhisattvas and their retinues entered concentration (samādhi) and dwelt together in the Tathagata's assembly of equality.

[Great bodhisattvas and mahasattvas] here refers to bodhisattvas of the ten grounds and of equal enlightenment. [The ten grounds] In the fifty-two stages of bodhisattva practice, the fifth set of ten is called the ten grounds; on these grounds the Buddha-realm is gradually opened, all-knowing wisdom is attained, and one belongs to the noble rank, hence they are also called "the ten noble ones." [Equal enlightenment] the fifty-first of the fifty-two Mahayana stages, namely the bodhisattva who has completed the ten grounds and is about to realize the Buddha-fruit, whose merit and wisdom are nearly equal to the Buddha's, hence the name "equal enlightenment." [Leaders] the chief positions among the assembly are called leaders; there may be one leader or many. [Retinues] disciples and followers.

blocks.text: 1. The Causal Ground and the Practice of Dharma

inline.s: This chapter is the dialogue between Mañjusri Bodhisattva and the Buddha on the core question of "the Tathagata's causal ground and practice of Dharma" (how the World-Honored One practiced when he was in the causal ground), and it is the general outline of the entire sutra.

"Thereupon Mañjusri Bodhisattva rose from his seat in the midst of the assembly, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, walked around him three times to the right, knelt with joined hands and said to the Buddha: Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, may you for the sake of all the Dharma multitudes who have come to this assembly proclaim the Tathagata's original pure causal ground and practice of Dharma, and tell how bodhisattvas in the Mahayana should bring forth a pure mind, keep far from all maladies, and enable the beings of the future degenerate age who seek the Mahayana not to fall into false views. Having said this, he prostrated himself with all five limbs to the ground. Thus he entreated three times, again and again."

Thereupon Mañjusri Bodhisattva rose from his seat in the great assembly, bowed his head at the Buddha's feet, walked around him three times to the right, knelt with joined hands, and reverently said to the Buddha: "Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, may you proclaim for the Dharma multitudes who have come from every direction to this Dharma assembly how the Tathagata practiced when he was in the causal ground, and how bodhisattvas in the Mahayana should bring forth the pure mind and how they should keep far from all maladies, so that the beings of the future degenerate age who seek the Mahayana may not fall into false views." When Mañjusri Bodhisattva had finished these words, he prostrated himself with all five limbs to the ground. Thus he made his request three times, again and again.

[Bowing the head at the Buddha's feet, walking around three times to the right, kneeling with joined hands] this is the protocol for requesting the Dharma. [Bowing the head at the Buddha's feet] both knees, both elbows, and the head touch the ground, worshipping with the crown of the head and receiving the Buddha's feet; this is the highest form of reverence. [Joined hands] an Indian gesture of respect, also called the vajra clasp, in which the fingers of the two palms are interlocked. [Original arising in the causal ground] when he was first in the causal ground. [Causal ground] the whole period from the first resolve to learn Buddhism as an ordinary being until the perfection of Buddhahood is called the "causal ground." [Prostrating with all five limbs to the ground] the two hands, two knees, and the crown of the head touching the ground; the highest form of reverence.

The Dharma-gate of perfect enlightenment: perfectly illumine the pure enlightened mark of the self-nature (like a pearl emitting light that illumines the pearl itself) and forever cut off ignorance. This is the path of cultivating perfect enlightenment (bringing the self-nature to perfect enlightenment) and attaining Buddhahood; it is the core of the entire sutra.

"Then the World-Honored One said to Mañjusri Bodhisattva: Excellent! Excellent! Good son. You are able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, to inquire about the Tathagata's causal ground and practice of Dharma, and to enable all beings of the degenerate age who seek the Mahayana to dwell in and uphold the right Dharma and not fall into false views. Now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Then Mañjusri Bodhisattva, rejoicing as he received the teaching, and the whole great assembly listened in silence."

Then the World-Honored One said to Mañjusri Bodhisattva: "Excellent! Excellent! Good son. You are able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas, to inquire about the Tathagata's causal ground and practice of Dharma, and to enable all beings of the degenerate age who seek the Mahayana to dwell in and uphold the right Dharma and not fall into false views. Now gather your mind and listen attentively; I shall explain it for you." Then Mañjusri Bodhisattva, rejoicing as he received the teaching, and the whole great assembly listened in silence.

The World-Honored One praised Mañjusri Bodhisattva's question and consented to proclaim for them how he himself had practiced in the causal ground (the causal ground and practice of Dharma); the great assembly rejoiced and listened.
[Dwell in and uphold the right Dharma] to be able to dwell in and uphold the right Dharma. [Listen attentively] to listen with one mind and reflect on the meaning.

"Good sons! The unsurpassed Dharma-king has a great dharani-gate named Perfect Enlightenment. From it flow all purity, suchness, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and paramita, teaching the bodhisattvas. All Tathagatas, in the causal ground of their original arising, rely upon the perfectly illuminating pure enlightened mark, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the path of Buddhahood."

Good sons! The Tathagata (the unsurpassed Dharma-king) has a great gate of total retention named Perfect Enlightenment. From it ceaselessly flow purity, suchness, bodhi, nirvāṇa, and paramita to teach the bodhisattvas. All Tathagatas, when first in the causal ground, likewise relied upon this Dharma-gate of perfect enlightenment, perfectly illumined the pure enlightened mark of the self-nature (like a pearl emitting light that illumines the pearl itself), forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplished the path of Buddhahood (perfectly realizing the Buddha-fruit).

purity (undefiled), suchness (neither false nor changing), bodhi, nirvāṇa, and paramita", these describe the intrinsic enlightened mind-essence, the tathagatagarbha (also called the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment). The "wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment" in this sutra is the intrinsic nature spoken of in many sutras and treatises (for example, The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch). (See in detail
The Mind, the Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha

Here the World-Honored One answered the two questions Mañjusri Bodhisattva had raised: first, how did the Buddha practice when he was in the causal ground? Second, how should bodhisattvas of the present and future practice? The answer to both questions is:
"All rely upon the perfectly illuminating pure enlightened mark, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the path of Buddhahood."
This is the general outline of the entire sutra.

This passage says: all Tathagatas, when first in the causal ground, had no other dharma, but all relied upon the light of this perfect-enlightenment self-nature to illumine in return the quiescent, pure essence of enlightenment. When that illumination becomes perfectly complete with nothing left unpenetrated, ignorance is forever cut off and the path of Buddhahood is accomplished.

[Dharani] rendered in Chinese as "total retention." "Total" means gathering in all dharmas; "retention" means the ability to hold boundless meanings. [Perfect enlightenment] the perfect enlightenment of the self-nature. [Suchness] neither false nor changing. "True" means real and not deceptive; "such" means unchanging as it is; the two meanings of real-and-not-deceptive and unchanging-as-it-is together are called "suchness." [Bodhi] rendered in Chinese as "enlightenment"; it is the great wisdom able to cut off all afflictions. [Nirvāṇa] rendered in Chinese as "perfect quiescence": "perfect" is the perfection of all wisdom and virtue, "quiescence" is the stilling of all delusion and karma. It is also translated "extinction and deliverance": "extinction" is the elimination of the three delusions, namely view-and-thought delusion, the delusion of dust-like subtlety, and ignorance; "deliverance" is deliverance from the two kinds of birth and death, fragmentary and transformational. Taken together, when wisdom and virtue have both reached the ultimate and perfect state, and even birth-and-death and affliction have been transcended, this is called nirvāṇa. It is the suchness-realm beyond birth and death and beyond space and time realized by the noble ones, and it is the most ideal and most beautiful destination of all beings. [Paramita] rendered in Chinese as "reaching the other shore." The practitioner, riding the great ship of Dharma, crosses from this shore of birth-and-death and affliction to the other shore of nirvāṇa's peace and bliss; this is called "reaching the other shore."

[Perfect illumination] illuminating completely, with nothing left out. [The pure enlightened mark] the quiescent mark of the self-nature's intrinsic enlightenment. Master Hanshan's Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

"Therefore all Tathagatas, in the causal ground of their original accomplishment of Buddhahood, have no other dharma, but all rely upon the light of this perfect-enlightenment self-nature to illumine in return the quiescent, pure essence-mark of enlightenment, which is the nature-essence itself. When this illumination is perfectly complete with nothing left unpenetrated, ignorance is forever cut off and the dharmakaya is perfectly realized. Since there is only this one dharma, it is said that 'all rely upon the perfectly illuminating pure enlightened mark, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the path of Buddhahood.'"
It also says:
"Yet the method of cultivating the cutting off
(that is, cultivating the cutting off of ignorance)

relies in every case upon the light of wisdom of the perfect-enlightenment self-nature to illumine in return the quiescent, pure mind-essence; hence it is said, 'perfectly illumine the pure enlightened mark.'"

[Intrinsic enlightenment] The mind-essence (self-nature) of beings is by nature pure, free from all false marks, luminously aware, and endowed with the virtue of knowing awareness. This is the inherent virtue of the mind-essence, and so it is called intrinsic enlightenment. Yet this intrinsically enlightened mind-essence has from beginningless time been covered by ignorance and affliction and hidden until today; once, through the work of cultivation, its inherent virtue first becomes manifest, this is called initial enlightenment. The Awakening of Faith says:

"The mind-essence is free from thoughts. The mark of being free from thoughts is equal to the realm of space and pervades everywhere. The one mark of the Dharma-realm is the Tathagata's equal dharmakaya; relying upon this dharmakaya, it is called intrinsic enlightenment."
Question: How does one perfectly illumine the pure enlightened mark?

Answer: The pure enlightened mark is the quiescent mark of the self-nature's intrinsic enlightenment; that is, the self-nature's state of no-thought. Thoughts are of three kinds: coarse thoughts, subtle thoughts, and extremely subtle thoughts. For example, for one who recites the Buddha's name, deluded thoughts are coarse thoughts and the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is a subtle thought. Extremely subtle thoughts are the subtle arising and ceasing, the flowing on, of the consciousness-mind; they are the mark of the alaya-consciousness. Ordinarily, when coarse and subtle thoughts have both ceased, this is called no-thought, which is no-thought in the common sense. Further, if extremely subtle thoughts also cease, this is ultimate no-thought.
The way to begin the work of perfectly illumining the pure enlightened mark is:
no-thought, turning the light back to illumine the self-nature's state of no-thought.
The self-nature
's

state of no-thought is the pure enlightened mark; turning the light back to illumine that state of no-thought is to be enlightenedly aware of that pure enlightened mark. At first, "no-thought" means the no-thought in which coarse and subtle thoughts have both ceased, and there is still an illuminator and something illumined. As the work deepens, until illuminator and illumined both vanish and the extremely subtle flowing on is utterly stilled, this is perfectly illumining the pure enlightened mark, forever cutting off ignorance, and accomplishing the path of Buddhahood.
On how to pass from enlightened awareness into perfect illumination, Mr. Xu Hengzhi, in
How to Practice the Buddha-Dharma
, gives a most penetrating discussion:

Broadly speaking, the elimination of habitual tendencies proceeds as follows. Ordinary people are troubled by affliction and deluded thoughts all day long, taking the false as real, and always fall into the maze of subjectivity without knowing it. Only when suffering makes them feel something, and they realize that deluded thoughts and habitual tendencies do no small harm, are they willing to cultivate the Buddha-Dharma as an antidote. But in the early stages of practice their mental state is sure to be half-believing and half-doubting, now clear and now dim, with mere understanding and no actual proof. When they speak of precepts they lean toward external forms; when they speak of concentration they cling to dead stillness; when they speak of wisdom they fall back on the jargon of Chan. When habitual tendencies arise, they still have no strength to resist them. This is exactly '
(precepts, concentration, and wisdom)
present when spoken of
, absent when needed.'

After devoted and single-minded cultivation of the Buddha-Dharma, after hundreds and thousands of trials and resistances, the mental state gradually opens, strength gradually becomes sufficient, and one can awaken to and see one's own original essence.

At this point one knows that all judgments of right and wrong, favorable and unfavorable, beautiful and ugly, love and hate, and so on, are nothing but the false discriminating activity of one's own mind; one can refrain from following their flow and gradually eliminate one's habitual tendencies.

Thus habitual tendencies turn from coarse and heavy to light and fine, from long-lasting to brief, from intense to mild, from great matters to small matters, from forced to natural, from powerless to powerful, from deliberate to unnoticed. In short, the root of habitual tendency has been loosened and is no longer as solidly clung to as before. Continuing in this way to sweep away habitual tendencies with prajñā, the power of concentration and wisdom grows stronger day by day, with a momentum that nothing can resist. One can perfectly illumine one's own habitual tendencies everywhere and become enlightened at every moment; the self-nature gradually becomes a single, wholly luminous whole, utterly still with not a single thought, yet vividly alive and inconceivable. Without deliberately gathering the mind, the mind is naturally undistracted. When habitual tendencies arise, a single turn and they are ungraspable, impossible to lay hold of. Delusion cannot be grasped, and enlightenment cannot be touched either. Neither moving nor still, neither ordinary nor noble, beyond all thought and discussion; this is precisely what is meant by "perfect enlightenment."
The cultivation of any Dharma-gate is inseparable from enlightened awareness. For when mind and object meet,
without awareness there is no turning

; without turning there is no emptiness; without emptiness there is no concentration; without concentration there is no wisdom. In the course of sweeping away habitual tendencies, the progress of the power of enlightened awareness may be divided into the following levels
(in the levels below, note the two elements, "the arising of mind" and "enlightened awareness")
[Enlightened awareness] to contemplate with an awakened mind.
The arising of mind
(ignorance)
comes first, and
enlightened awareness
(prajñā)
comes after, and must be summoned with the utmost effort;
2. Though enlightened awareness comes after the arising of mind, summoning it requires little effort;
3. Awareness arises as soon as mind arises, though there is still a slight sequence;
4. When mind arises, enlightened awareness arises at the same instant;
5. Enlightened awareness comes first and the arising of mind after, though at times awareness is forgotten;
6. Enlightened awareness can always be ahead, though one still has to attend to the awareness; (the above are stages of exertion)
7. One does not know there is awareness, yet is never apart from it; one clearly knows objects are present, yet they are no obstruction;
8. One enters the state of constant quiescence and constant illumination.
We may examine ourselves: which state have we actually reached
Master Dayu said:
Illumining stillness, still illumination; above all, refrain from strain.
To become a Buddha or a patriarch, there is no other secret to gain.

"What is ignorance? Good sons! All beings, from beginningless time, have had all manner of inversions, like a deluded person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy reflections of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye that sees flowers in space and a second moon."

What is ignorance? Good sons! All beings, from beginningless time, have had their self-nature deluded and perverse, giving rise to all manner of inversions and taking the false as real; this is ignorance. It is like a person who has lost his bearings, taking north for south and east for west: he falsely takes the body of flesh formed by the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind as the mark of his own body, and the illusory shadows arising when the six sense-faculties contact the six dusts (the shadowy reflections of the six dusts) as the mark of his own mind. It is like an eye affected by spots that falsely sees flowers in the sky and a second moon.

This means that the self-nature, "falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of its own body and the shadowy reflections of the six dusts as the mark of its own mind," thus loses the originally possessed dharmakaya and the knowing mind, and falsely takes the five aggregates of body and mind as "I."
[Deluded and perverse (
bei

)] confusion and perversity. [Perversity] opposing the right path. [The self-nature deluded and perverse] When the self-nature is deluded and perverse, it falsely takes the five aggregates of body and mind as itself, and thereupon pursues objects and creates karma, revolving in birth and death. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: "When the self-nature is deluded, one is a sentient being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha." (See in detail
The Mind, the Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha

.) [The five aggregates] the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. Because these five are gathered and produced, they are called the "five aggregates"; and because they can cover over a person's true nature, causing confusion and inversion and the creation of all karma, they are also called the "five shadows." Among them, the aggregate of form refers to matter and is called "form-dharma"; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness belong to mind and are called "mind-dharma." These are the five great elements that constitute body and mind. The aggregate of form is the physical body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness) are mind. [The four great elements] All tangible matter in the world is composed of the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, and so they are called "great": the great element earth, the great element water, the great element fire, and the great element wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. [The shadowy reflections of the six dusts] The thoughts, feelings, and emotions produced when the six sense-faculties contact the six dusts; these are the illusory shadows manifested when the six faculties take the six dusts as conditions, and so they are called the shadowy reflections of the six dusts, also named the conditioning mind. [Flowers in space] flowers in the sky. "Hua" in ancient usage is the same as "flower."

“Good man! The sky is not really filled with flowers; it is the false grasping of one with diseased eyes. Because of this false grasping, not only do they mistake this empty self-nature, they also delude themselves about the place where the flowers truly arise. From this false existence they revolve in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

Good man! In truth there are no flowers in the sky; this is the illusion falsely grasped by the diseased eye. Because of false grasping, not only do they falsely grasp the sky as substantially existing, they also think there truly are flowers that arise from it. Because sentient beings, through inverted confusion, falsely take the illusion-manifested body and mind to be real and cling to them as self, they revolve in birth and death without end; therefore it is called ignorance.
[Not only mistaking this self-nature of emptiness] wrongly thinking that emptiness has a self-nature. In truth all dharmas are without self-nature (see
The Real Nature of All Dharmas

), so emptiness too has no self-nature. [Without self-nature] means that all dharmas have no real substance of their own; it is also called no nature. [Not only mistaking this self-nature of emptiness, they also delude themselves about the place where the real flowers arise] Not only do they falsely grasp emptiness as really existing (as substance), they also think there truly are flowers arising from it.
Q: If all dharmas are without self-nature, why is it said that sentient beings have self-nature?

A: The word self-nature has two meanings in Buddhist learning: first, the wondrous, luminous, all-virtuous spiritual capacity, which is the self-nature of sentient beings; second, a real substance. The meaning of “all dharmas are without self-nature” is that all dharmas have no real substance, being all illusions, like the matters of a dream. Without self-nature is also called no nature. The Treatise on Consciousness-only says: “All dharmas are without self-nature.” The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are ever without nature.” The Surangama Sutra says: “All illusions become without nature.”
Q: Why is it that when one falsely grasps the four great elements as one’s own body and the shadow of the six objects as one’s own mind, one revolves in birth and death?
A: Because we sentient beings are all within the dream of transmigration (about the dream of transmigration, see
The Real Nature of All Dharmas

, the chapter on “the dream of ignorance”). If one takes this body (the four elements) and this mind (the shadow of the six objects) as self, then feelings of love and aversion arise. Following the feelings one creates karma, and through karma one receives retribution, so birth and death revolve without rest. If one wishes to escape this dream of birth-after-birth and death-after-death, one must accomplish it through cultivation. The common path is to cut off all afflictions, and at the moment of death be able to be master; then one can end birth and death and escape transmigration. The founder Huangbo’s Essential of Mind Transmission says:

“Whenever a man approaches the end, he should contemplate the five aggregates as empty, the four elements as without self, the true mind as without mark, neither going nor coming. At birth the nature does not come; at death the nature does not go. Serenely extinct, mind and realm as one. If one can thus directly, in an instant, understand, and not be bound by the three times, this is a man who has gone beyond the world.”
If one cultivates the Pure Land gate, one needs only the ten recollections at death to be continuous (see
The Conditions for Rebirth
), and one will sense Amitābha Buddha coming to receive and guide, escaping this dream of transmigration and being reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

“Good man! This ignorance has no real substance. Like a man in a dream - while he dreams, the dream is not nothing, but when he wakes he gains nothing at all. Like the many flowers in the sky, which vanish in the sky - one cannot say there is a fixed place where they vanish. Why? Because there is no place from which they arise. All sentient beings, within the unborn, falsely see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called revolving in birth and death.”

Good man! This ignorance is not really existent. Like a man in a dream - while he dreams, the matters of the dream are not nothing, but when he wakes, all is gone. If the eye-disease is cured (the metaphor of awaking from the dream of ignorance), the many sky-flowers vanish in the sky, and one cannot say there is a definite place of extinction. Why? Because the sky-flowers never arose to begin with - how could there be a place of extinction? All sentient beings, within the original state where not a single thing exists, falsely see arising and ceasing; this falsely-seen arising and ceasing is what is called revolving in birth and death (the divided birth-and-death and the transformation birth-and-death).

This means: the revolving of birth and death is like the matters of a dream - it is the illusion that sentient beings, from beginningless time, falsely grasping the five aggregates’ body and mind, have set up.

[Revolving in birth and death] revolving in the divided birth-and-death and the transformation birth-and-death. [Divided birth-and-death] For sentient beings within the three realms and six destinies, because they are sensed by good and evil karma, each has a limited lifespan and a delimited body, so their birth and death is called “divided birth-and-death.” One who ends divided birth-and-death has escaped transmigration. [Transformation birth-and-death] For the sages of the three vehicles, having already cut off the delusions of views and thought and ended divided birth-and-death, during the process of cultivation their deluded thoughts gradually pass away and their realization gradually grows; this movement of delusion and awakening is different in each stage, and the passing from one stage to the next is like a single birth-and-death; its changes are so wondrous, subtle and inconceivable that it is called “transformation birth-and-death.” One who ends transformation birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit.

“Good man! Those Tathagatas who, on the stage of cause, cultivate complete enlightenment, knowing that these are sky-flowers, have no revolving, and have no body and mind to undergo that birth and death. It is not by contrivance that it is non-existent; it is because the fundamental nature is non-existent.”

Good man! Those Tathagatas who, on the stage of cause, cultivate the complete-enlightenment gate, knowing that all this arising and ceasing is illusion (this sutra uses the metaphor of sky-flowers for illusion), have no revolving in birth and death; and knowing body and mind to be illusory, they have no body or mind to undergo birth and death. This is not a non-existence after contrivance, because body, mind, birth and death never existed to begin with. (This speaks of the real nature of all dharmas: all dharmas are ultimately empty, all non-existent. See
The Real Nature of All Dharmas

“Those who know this consciousness are like empty space. Those who know emptiness are the mark of sky-flowers. Nor can it be said: there is no knowing nature. Both existence and non-existence are dispatched; this is called pure awareness in accordance. Why? Because of the nature of emptiness, because of ever being unmoving, because in the Tathagata-store there is no arising or ceasing, because there is no knowing or seeing, like the nature of the Dharma-realm, ultimately complete and perfect, pervading the ten directions. This is called the dharma-practice of the stage of cause. Bodhisattvas, by this, in the Great Vehicle give rise to the pure mind; sentient beings of the last age, cultivating in accord with this, do not fall into wrong views.”

That person who knows the sky-flowers are illusory is like empty space, equally unmoving (equally regarding everything, neither bewildered nor drawn by illusions). Knowing that the myriads of forms are like empty space, with not a single thing, they empty away the mark of the sky-flowers. But it also cannot be said that there is no mark of the sky-flowers. Both existence (falsely grasping dharmas as real) and non-existence (denying that dharmas have marks) are dispatched; this is called pure awareness in accordance (neither attached to existence nor falling into emptiness). Why? Because of the reason that empty space has not a single thing, because of the reason of being serene and unmoving, because of the reason that in the Tathagata-store there is no arising or ceasing, because of the reason of no knowing or seeing, because of the reason that the Dharma-realm is ultimately complete and pervading the ten directions. This is called the Tathagata’s dharma-practice of the stage of cause. Bodhisattvas, by this, give rise to the pure mind in the Great Vehicle; sentient beings of the last age, cultivating by this, do not fall into wrong views.

[Those who know this consciousness are like empty space] That person who knows the sky-flowers are illusory is like empty space, equally unmoving (equally regarding everything, neither bewildered nor drawn by illusions). The verse later says: “The awakened are like empty space, equally unmoving.” [That is the mark of sky-flowers] That is, empty away this illusory mark of the sky-flowers. Here “empty” is a verb. [Pure awareness] The mind-substance without defilement is called pure; not deluded toward the objects is called awareness. [In accordance] according with conditions and circumstances. [Pure awareness in accordance] pure awareness and in accordance. Neither attached to existence nor falling into emptiness. This is the Great Vehicle’s orthodox teaching that the Buddha revealed in the Diamond Sutra: universally ferrying sentient beings to Buddhahood, yet not attached to the mark of ferrying them. Compassion and emptiness working together, compassionately ferrying beings yet not attached to the mark. The Diamond Sutra says:

“All the many kinds of living beings - whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation, whether with form or without form, whether with perception or without perception, whether neither with perception nor without perception - I cause them all to enter the nirvāṇa of no remainder and cross them over; thus crossing over innumerable, countless, boundless living beings, in truth no living being is crossed over.”
(see
The Diamond Sutra Explained

) [Because there is no knowing or seeing] Here “knowing and seeing” refers to the views established by way of deliberation and discrimination. This differs from wisdom; wisdom is the non-discriminating prajñā.

[Dharma-realm] In terms of phenomenal marks, dharma means the various dharmas and realm means boundaries: all the things of the phenomenal world each have their distinct, different marks and cannot be confused, called the “phenomenal Dharma-realm.” In terms of the principle-substance, though the various dharmas are endlessly different in outer marks, they share one nature (ultimately empty, all non-existent), called the “principle Dharma-realm.”

Then the World-Honored One, wishing to re-declare this meaning, spoke in verse: Manjushri, you should know: all Tathagatas, having fully penetrated ignorance and known it to be like sky-flowers, are able to escape the flow. Again, like a man in a dream, when he wakes nothing can be obtained.”

Then the World-Honored One, wishing to re-declare the meaning of the above instruction, spoke in verse: Manjushri, you should know: all Buddhas, fully awakened to ignorance and knowing all dharmas to be like sky-flowers, illusory and unreal, are able to escape the flow (referring to escaping the divided birth-and-death and the transformation birth-and-death). Again, like a man in a dream - after the great dream wakes, where is the man in the dream?
[Again, like a man in a dream, when he wakes nothing can be obtained] This is what Mazu called “not mind, not Buddha.” The Exposition of the Five Lamps records:
“A monk asked: ‘Why does the Master say, “Mind is Buddha”?’ The Master
(Mazu)
said: ‘To stop the infant’s crying’
(this is the expedient saying for those new to the study)
.’ He asked: ‘When the crying stops, then what?’ The Master said: ‘Not mind, not Buddha.’ He said: ‘For those who come beyond these two kinds, how do you indicate?’ The Master said: ‘Tell him
(him)
it is not a thing.’”
The Exposition of the Five Lamps further says:
“The Chan master Zizai of Funiu Mountain at Yique, of the Li family of Wuxing, first followed the master Guoyi, and after full ordination studied under Mazu and awakened the mind-ground
(enlightenment)
. Mazu had him deliver a letter to the National Master Zhong
(the National Master Huizhong)
. The National Master asked: ‘What Dharma does the great master Ma use to show his disciples?’ He said: ‘Mind is Buddha.’ The National Master said: ‘What sort of words are those’
(he greatly disapproved)
!’ After a long while
(a long time passed)

he asked again: ‘Besides this, is there any further teaching?’ The Master said: ‘Not mind, not Buddha. Or it is said: not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.’ The National Master said: ‘That is a little better’
(that is about right)

[To stop the infant’s crying] a metaphor for the expedient teaching (not the ultimate teaching). When a child cries, an adult gives him a yellow poplar leaf, saying: “This is a piece of gold; you may take it and buy sweets.” The child holds it and stops crying. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says: “As when an infant cries, the parents give it a yellow poplar leaf and say: ‘Do not cry! Do not cry! I shall give you gold.’ The infant, seeing it, gives rise to the thought of real gold and stops crying; yet this poplar leaf is not really gold.”

In the above kōan, three levels are spoken of: “mind is Buddha,” “not mind, not Buddha,” and “not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.” The mind spoken of here refers to the self-nature. “Mind is Buddha” means that Buddha is nothing else; the perfectly awakened self-nature is the Buddha. “Not mind, not Buddha” means that self-nature and Buddha are both illusions - matters in the dream of ignorance. “Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing” speaks of the “that” which is dreaming the dream of ignorance.

“The awakened are like empty space, equally unmoving; awareness pervading the ten directions is to accomplish the Buddha-way. The many illusions have no place of extinction; accomplishing the way is also no attainment, because the fundamental nature is complete. Bodhisattvas within this can give rise to the bodhi mind; sentient beings of the last age, cultivating this, avoid wrong views.”

The awakened, like the serene stillness of empty space, equally regard all dharmas (because they are equally all illusions), unmoved and unturned by them; thus awareness pervading the ten directions, they accomplish the Buddha-way. When the many illusions pass away there is no place of extinction; having accomplished the Buddha-way there is also no attainment, because the fundamental nature is complete. Bodhisattvas within this can give rise to the bodhi mind; sentient beings of the last age, cultivating thus, do not fall into wrong views.

[The many illusions have no place of extinction] When the many illusions pass away there is no place of extinction; because the many illusions never arose to begin with, so when they pass away, where could there be a place of extinction? [Accomplishing the way also no attainment] Accomplishing the way is also a matter in the dream of ignorance, hence it is said to be no attainment. [Giving rise to the bodhi mind] Giving rise to the bodhi mind, in full, is giving rise to the anuttara-samyak-sambodhi mind, also abbreviated as giving rise to the mind. Mr. Liu Zhuyuan says: “The bodhi mind is the pure self-nature mind. This pure self-nature mind is equal in beings and Buddhas, possessed by everyone, neither increasing nor decreasing. To give rise means to set it going, to develop it. Giving rise to the bodhi mind is to set going and develop the pure self-nature mind. At the beginning it is only setting it going; seeing the nature is the developing.” (see
The Essentials of Baiyun

) The master Guifeng says: “To see the four elements as broken illusions, to penetrate the six objects as sky-flowers, to awaken that one’s own mind is the Buddha mind, and to see the fundamental nature as the Dharma nature - this is giving rise to the mind.” (The Transmission of the Lamp)

blocks.text: 1. How to be free of the illusory

inline.s: “Then Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, circled him three times to the right, knelt with palms together, and said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, I pray that for the bodhisattvas of this assembly and for all the sentient beings of the last age who cultivate the Great Vehicle, having heard this realm of pure complete enlightenment, you will tell how they should cultivate.”

Then Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, circled him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, I pray that you will preach for the bodhisattvas of this assembly and for all the sentient beings of the last age who cultivate the Great Vehicle, how, having heard this realm of pure complete enlightenment, they are to cultivate in order to reach it.

“World-Honored One, if these sentient beings know that things are illusory, then body and mind are also illusory; why do they, with illusion, still cultivate within illusion? If the nature of all illusions entirely ceases, then there is no mind; who is it that cultivates? How again can one speak of cultivating as illusory? If these sentient beings originally do not cultivate, abiding long among the transformations of birth and death, and never comprehend the illusory realm, how can the deluded mind be liberated? I pray that for all sentient beings of the last age you will show what expedient means, progressively cultivated, cause them to be forever free of all illusions. Having spoken, he fell prostrate on the ground. Thus three times he begged, ending and beginning again.”

World-Honored One, if they know that all dharmas are illusory, then body and mind are also illusory; since it is so, why do they still use illusion to cultivate within illusion? If the nature of all illusions entirely ceases, then there is no mind - then for whom is this cultivation? Why again is it said that cultivation is like illusion? If these sentient beings do not cultivate at all, then abiding long among the transformations of birth and death, they will never comprehend that this whole realm is an illusory realm; how then can the deluded mind be liberated? I pray that for all sentient beings of the last age you will reveal what good, skilful means, progressively cultivated, will cause them to be forever free of all illusions. When Samantabhadra Bodhisattva had finished this speech, he fell prostrate on the ground. Thus three times he begged, ending and beginning again.

[If these sentient beings] if those sentient beings. Here “sentient beings” includes the bodhisattvas of this assembly and all the sentient beings of the last age who cultivate the Great Vehicle. Within the ten Dharma-realms, apart from the Buddha, the nine realms of sentient beings (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, heavens, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas) are all called sentient beings. [Who is it that cultivates] that is, for whom is the cultivation. The “for whom” is inverted to “who is it for” to strengthen the tone. For example: who does it for whom. [Expedient means] the skilful, accommodating means, methods or speech used to transform sentient beings. “Expedient” is relative to “real” and “ultimate”; it means setting up the teaching according to capacity.

blocks.text: 2. Knowing the illusory is to be free of it

inline.s: “Then the World-Honored One said to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You have been able, for the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask about practicing the bodhisattvas’ samādhi of the illusory, and the progressive expedient means, causing sentient beings to be free of all illusions. Listen attentively now; I shall speak it for you. At that time Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, receiving the instruction with joy, and all the assembly, listened in silence.”

Then the World-Honored One said to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You have been able, for the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask about the method of practicing the samādhi of the illusory and the progressive sequence of cultivation, causing sentient beings to be free of all illusions. Now still your minds and listen attentively; I shall preach it for you. At that time Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, receiving the instruction with joy, and all the assembly, listened in silence.

“Good man! All the various illusory transformations of sentient beings all arise within the Tathagata’s wondrous mind of complete enlightenment, like sky-flowers arising from the sky. Though the illusory flowers pass away, the empty nature is not destroyed. The illusory mind of sentient beings still passes away in dependence on the illusory; when all illusions are entirely extinguished, the mind of awareness does not move. To speak of awareness in dependence on illusion, this too is called illusion. If one says there is awareness, one has not yet left illusion. For one who says there is no awareness, it is likewise. Therefore when illusion is extinguished, this is called unmoving.”

Good man! The various illusory realms felt by all sentient beings all arise within the Tathagata’s wondrous mind of complete enlightenment. These illusory realms are like sky-flowers arising from the sky. Though the illusory flowers (the metaphor for the various illusory realms) pass away, the empty nature (the metaphor for the wondrous mind of complete enlightenment) is not destroyed. The illusory minds of sentient beings (feeling, thought, volition, consciousness) pass away along with the passing of the illusory realms; when both the illusory realm and the illusory mind are completely extinguished, the wondrous mind of complete enlightenment is unmoving (the self-nature returns from the consciousness-state to its fundamental state). To speak of awareness in dependence on the illusory realm and illusory mind - this awareness too is illusion. If one says there is awareness, one has not yet left illusion. For one who says there is no awareness, it is likewise, still not leaving illusion. Therefore when all these illusions are completely stilled, this is called the wondrous mind of complete enlightenment unmoving.

[The illusory mind] That is, the perceptual mind of feeling, thought, volition and consciousness within the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness); that is, the shadow of the six objects spoken of in the sutra text above.
This passage speaks of two minds: the illusory mind (the shadow of the six objects) and the Tathagata’s wondrous mind of complete enlightenment.
Q: What is “borrowing the false to cultivate the true”?
A: Using the falsely-combined body and mind of the five aggregates to cultivate and realize the true-tathata Dharma-body: break one portion of ignorance, realize one portion of Dharma-body.

“Good man! All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age should be far from all illusory, empty, false realms. Because they firmly hold a mind of distance, they also distance the mind that sees things as illusory. Distance being illusory, they also distance it. The distance from the distance being illusory, they also distance it. Reaching what there is nothing to distance, then all illusions are removed. For example, making fire by friction, the two sticks depending on one another: when the fire appears the sticks are consumed, the ashes fly and the smoke vanishes; to use illusion to cultivate within illusion is likewise. When all illusions are entirely extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation.”

Good man! All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age should be far from all illusory, empty, false realms. Because they firmly hold a thought of distance, this thought is also illusory and should likewise be distanced; distancing this mind of distance, this too is illusory and should also be distanced; distancing this distance, this too is illusory and should also be distanced; when one reaches what there is nothing to distance, then all illusions are removed. For example, making fire by friction: a stick quickly rubbed on a block; when the fire comes out, the stick and the block are consumed by the fire, and the ashes fly and the smoke vanishes. To use illusion to cultivate within illusion is likewise (this says: by the illusory mind to still the illusory realm; when the illusory realm is stilled, the illusory mind too is stilled). When all illusions (the illusory realm and the illusory mind) are extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation (because the wondrous mind of complete enlightenment remains; the verse below says:
“Empty space is originally unmoving; illusion arises from awareness; when illusion is extinguished awareness is complete, because the mind of awareness is unmoving.”

“Good man! To know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means; to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages. All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, cultivating by this, are thus able to be forever free of all illusions.”

Good man! To know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means (without borrowing other methods or devices - freely, freely!); to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages. All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, cultivating by this, are thus able to be forever free of all illusions.

To know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means; to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages” - this is the World-Honored One’s instruction on how to cultivate the samādhi of the illusory.
The Awakening of Faith says:
Be confident in your own nature, know the mind’s deluded agitation and that there is no previous realm; cultivate the method of distance
to know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means; to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages”
Because of truly knowing that there is no previous realm, by various means give rise to the practice of accordance,
without taking and without thinking
Through the power of long, distant cultivation, ignorance is then extinguished
Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind does not arise
Because of no arising
(because the mind does not arise)
, the realm accordingly passes away
Because both cause and condition entirely pass away, the marks of the mind are all exhausted; this is called attaining nirvāṇa, accomplishing the spontaneous karma.

[Be confident in your own nature] deeply believe that one’s own nature is the Buddha. [Know the mind’s deluded agitation] know that because one’s own mind deludedly agitates, the fundamental nature transforms into the consciousness-nature and one falls to the level of a sentient being (see
Mind, Self-nature, and the Tathagata-store

). Therefore the present cultivation is to stop this agitation: without taking and without thinking. Through the power of long cultivation, one returns the consciousness-nature to its fundamental-state nature. [There is no previous realm] there is no present realm. The appearance of a realm is an illusion that appears because the mind deludedly agitates. [Both cause and condition entirely pass away] The mind’s deluded agitation is the cause for the appearing of the realm; and the appearing of the realm in turn becomes the aiding condition for the mind’s agitation, causing the mind to agitate all the more. Cause and result each support the other, growing ever stronger. “Both cause and condition entirely pass away” means the mind does not deludedly agitate, and the realm passes away as well.
Q: How, concretely, does one become free of illusion?

A: Be aware at once, see through the illusory marks, withstand the allure and the coercion of the illusory marks, extinguish the feelings of love and aversion, do not take up the marks, and remain unmoved. Master Guifeng’s Chart of the Teacher-student Succession of the Chan School of the Mind says:

“Realize that the various dharmas are like a dream; originally there is nothing at all. Mind and realm are originally still; it is not that they are now first empty. Deluded into existence, one sees the matters of flourishing and decay, noble and base. Since the marks of things exist, they contradict or accord with one another, and feelings of love and aversion arise. When feelings arise, one is bound by all the sufferings. Yet it is all dream-doing and dream-receiving - what loss or gain is there? With this wisdom that can realize, even the dream-mind too is like a dream; even suppose there were a single dharma surpassing nirvāṇa, it too is like a dream, like an illusion. Having reached the original nothingness, it is fitting to lose the self and forsake feeling. When feeling is forsaken, the cause of suffering is cut off, and only then does one pass beyond all suffering and distress. This is to take the forsaking of feeling as the cultivation.”

(Translation: realizing that the various dharmas are like a dream, originally these do not exist; mind and realm are originally empty and still, it is not that only today they are emptied. Deluded into existence, one sees the matters of flourishing and decay, noble and base. Since the marks of things exist, realm and mind accord or contradict, and feelings of love and aversion arise. When feeling arises, one is bound by all the sufferings. Yet all this is dream-doing and dream-receiving - what loss or gain? With this wisdom that can realize, even the dream-mind too is illusion; even suppose there were a dharma surpassing nirvāṇa, this too is illusion. Since one already penetrates the original nothingness, it is fitting to lose self (no-self) and forsake feeling. When feeling is forsaken, the cause of suffering is cut off, and only then does one pass beyond all suffering and distress. This is to take the forsaking of feeling as the cultivation.)

[Forsake feeling] to do away with feeling. In ancient texts, “forget” is used for “lose,” meaning “extinguish.” So “lose self and forsake feeling” means: lose self and destroy feeling. “This is to take the forsaking of feeling as the cultivation” means: this takes the destruction of feeling (extinguishing the feelings of love and aversion) as the cultivation.
“Then the World-Honored One, wishing to re-declare this meaning, spoke in verse:”
Then the World-Honored One, wishing to re-declare the meaning of the above instruction, spoke in verse:

“Samantabhadra, you should know: all sentient beings, from beginningless time, deludedly entering ignorance, are all established from the Tathagatas’ mind of complete enlightenment; like sky-flowers, depending on the sky they have marks. If the sky-flowers then pass away, the empty space is originally unmoving. Illusion arises from awareness; when illusion is extinguished awareness is complete, because the mind of awareness is unmoving.”

Samantabhadra, you should know: all sentient beings, from beginningless time, deludedly entering the realm of ignorance, are all established from the Tathagatas’ mind of complete enlightenment; like sky-flowers, depending on the sky they have marks. If the sky-flowers (the metaphor for the illusory realm and the illusory mind) then pass away, the empty space (the metaphor for the mind of complete enlightenment) is originally unmoving. Both the illusory realm and the illusory mind arise from the mind of complete enlightenment; when all illusions are entirely extinguished, the mind of complete enlightenment is then fully aware and complete, because the mind of awareness is unmoving (the self-nature returns from the consciousness-state to its fundamental state).

[The Tathagatas] the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times. The Buddhas of the three times are: past Buddhas, present Buddhas, future Buddhas. Here the future Buddhas mean the present sentient beings. [The mind of awareness is unmoving] no thought or reflection arises; the subtle flow is forever stilled. [Subtle flow] the subtle arising and ceasing, flowing and migrating of the consciousness-mind; the mark of the alaya consciousness.

“If those bodhisattvas, and the sentient beings of the last age, always should be free of illusion, and all illusions be entirely distanced. Like fire born in wood: when the wood is exhausted the fire passes away; awareness then has no stages, and the expedient means is likewise.”

The bodhisattvas of this assembly, and the sentient beings of the last age, should always be free of illusion (“to know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means; to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages”); all illusions are to be entirely distanced. Like fire born in wood: the wood (the metaphor for the illusory realm) is burnt up, and the fire (the metaphor for the illusory mind) also passes away. Awareness then has no stages (to be free of the illusory is awareness); the expedient means that causes all sentient beings to be forever free of all illusions is likewise.

[The expedient means is likewise] This answers the question that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva raised at the very start of this chapter: “What expedient means, progressively cultivated, cause all sentient beings to be forever free of all illusions?”

“Then Universal Eye Bodhisattva, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, circled him three times to the right, knelt with palms together, and said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, I pray that for the bodhisattvas of this assembly, and for all the sentient beings of the last age, you will expound the progressive stages of the bodhisattvas’ cultivation - how to contemplate? how to maintain? Sentient beings, not yet awakened - what expedient means can universally awaken them?”

Then Universal Eye Bodhisattva, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, circled him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, I pray that you will expound for the bodhisattvas of this assembly, and for all the sentient beings of the last age, the progressive stages of the bodhisattvas’ cultivation - how to contemplate? how to maintain? And for sentient beings, not yet awakened, what expedient means will universally awaken them?

“World-Honored One, if these sentient beings lack the right expedient means and the right contemplation, and hear the Tathagata speak of this samādhi, their minds grow deluded and downcast, and they cannot enter into complete enlightenment. I pray you will set forth compassion, and for our sake and that of the sentient beings of the last age, provisionally speak the expedient means. Having spoken, he fell prostrate on the ground. Thus three times he begged, ending and beginning again.”

World-Honored One, if they lack the right expedient means and the right contemplation, and hear the World-Honored One speak of this samādhi of the illusory, their minds will grow deluded and downcast, and they will not be able to enter complete enlightenment. I pray the World-Honored One will greatly set forth compassion, and for our sake and that of the sentient beings of the last age, provisionally speak the expedient means. When Universal Eye Bodhisattva had finished this speech, he fell prostrate on the ground. Thus three times he begged, ending and beginning again.
[Provisionally speak the expedient means] Speaking the Dharma within the dream of ignorance, hence it is called provisional.

“Then the World-Honored One said to Universal Eye Bodhisattva: Excellent! Excellent! Good man, you have been able, for the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about the progressive stages of cultivation, the contemplation and the maintenance, and even to ask about the provisional, various expedient means. Listen attentively now; I shall speak it for you. At that time Universal Eye Bodhisattva, receiving the instruction with joy, and all the assembly, listened in silence.”

Then the World-Honored One said to Universal Eye Bodhisattva: Excellent! Excellent! Good man, you have been able, for the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about the progressive stages of cultivation, how to contemplate, how to maintain, and even to ask about the provisional, various expedient means. Now still your minds and listen attentively; I shall preach it for you. At that time Universal Eye Bodhisattva, receiving the instruction with joy, and all the assembly, listened in silence.

Below, the World-Honored One answers Universal Eye Bodhisattva’s question of “the progressive stages of cultivation, how to contemplate, how to maintain.” The progressive stages of cultivation are: calm, insight, and practice. Calm is to have the power of leaving thoughts; this is the basis of contemplative practice (contemplation and practice). Insight is to contemplate in accord with principle and awaken (to know the illusory). Practice is, arising from the awakening, to practice and remove the habits (to be free of the illusory). The sutra below says: “One should correctly recollect (attained by contemplation), and be far from all illusions (done by practice).” Insight answers the question of “how to contemplate”; practice answers the question of “how to maintain.”

[Contemplative practice] contemplate and practice: contemplate in accord with principle and awaken (to know the illusory); arising from the awakening, practice and remove the habits (to be free of the illusory).

“Good man! Those newly-learned bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, seeking the Tathagata’s pure mind of complete enlightenment, should correctly recollect and be far from all illusions. First, relying on the Tathagata’s practice of samatha, firmly uphold the precepts, and settle the assembly.”

Good man! Those newly-learned bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, seeking the Tathagata’s pure mind of complete enlightenment, should correctly recollect and be far from all illusions. For this, first, relying on the Tathagata’s practice of samatha (cultivating calm), firmly uphold the precepts, and settle the assembly.

[Śamatha] In Chinese it is translated as “stillness” — the stilling of wandering thoughts. This is the practice that comes before contemplation, and has two stages: bringing the ten thousand thoughts back to one, and bringing the one back to nothing. [Dwelling peacefully with the assembly] Living in harmony with disciples and the congregation.

This passage: the World-Honored One reveals the practice that precedes contemplation — cultivating stillness. Cultivating stillness not only develops the power of leaving thought behind, but also, from concentration, gives rise to wisdom. These two are the foundations that contemplation must have. Precepts are the root of practice, so one must certainly firmly uphold the precepts. Dwelling peacefully with the assembly means creating a good environment for cultivating stillness.

[Seated quietly in a still room, I constantly reflect thus: this present body of mine is a union of the four great elements.
