Hair, down, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and the dregs of the body all return to earth; spittle, phlegm, pus, blood, body fluids, saliva, tears, and vital essence, together with urine and excrement, all return to water; warmth returns to fire; movement returns to wind. When the four great elements have each dispersed, where will this delusive body still be? I then know that this body is ultimately without substance — being a composite form, it is truly like an illusion.]

Seated quietly in a still room, I constantly reflect thus: my present body is a union of the four great elements of earth, fire, water, and wind. Hair, down, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and the dregs of the body all return to the earth element; spittle, phlegm, pus, blood, body fluids, saliva, tears, and vital essence, together with urine and excrement, all return to the water element; warmth returns to the fire element; movement returns to the wind element. If the four great elements each disperse, where will this present delusive body be? One then knows that this body ultimately has no eternal substance; being a composite form, it is truly like an illusion. (This means: the physical body is a union of the four elements — once dispersed, it is gone — and so this physical body is illusory.)
[Seated quietly] Sitting in serene stillness.
This is the contemplation: the physical body is illusory.

The key to practice is first to see through the physical body and to let it go. The lifespan of the body is short — a few decades at most, a hundred years at most — and it ends in death. Practitioners of course know the body is a borrowed dwelling, yet because of the influence of habitual tendencies they find it hard to let go, and consciously or unconsciously always take it as “I.” Therefore one must, through study and practice, genuinely let it go. If one truly lets it go, then even should one wish to give rise to delusion, there is nothing to be deluded about. For within delusion there must be an “I,” and this “I” takes the physical body as its basis and so has a name, a standing, a past, a future, and so on. Because there is this “I,” there arise “mine,” “others,” “theirs,” and the world in which “I” dwell. If this “I” is gone, the mind is naturally unmoved. If false thoughts arise, it is certain that this “I” is again being grasped; if one wakes up, delusion is extinguished — when the skin is gone, to what can the hair cling? Therefore one must ceaselessly and repeatedly work at “awareness the moment a thought arises, and that which is aware immediately vanishes”: when a thought arises, see why it arises; in just what way is it grasping at “I”? Why can it not be let go? Think it through deeply and thoroughly. Do this again and again until the physical body is truly let go.

Therefore, to see through and let go, first of all one sees through and lets go of the physical body — like felling a poisonous tree, cutting straight at its root. For the work of seeing through and letting go of the body, the “nine cemetery contemplations” in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta are excellent contemplations. (See the article
The Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta Commentary

Ordinary people take the physical body as their starting point, and so create karma and receive retribution. Practitioners should take the dharma body as their starting point, and end birth-and-death and escape the cycle.

[Falsely composed of the four conditions, there arise the six sense faculties. The six faculties and the four elements, formed within and without, falsely give rise to a breath of conditions that gathers within, so that there seems to be a conditioned form which is falsely named “mind.” Good man! This delusive mind — were there no six objects — could not exist. When the four elements are resolved, no objects can be obtained; then these conditions and objects each return to dispersion, and ultimately there is no conditioned mind to be seen.]

The four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind are falsely combined, and so there falsely arise the six sense faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). With the six faculties and four elements formed within and without, there falsely arises a breath of conditions that gathers within, so that there seems to be a conditioned form, which people falsely call the mind. Good man! This delusive mind (also called the illusory mind, the conditioned and deliberate mind), were there no six objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects), could not exist. Once the four elements are resolved and no six objects can be obtained, this conditioned form and the six objects each return to dispersion, and there is ultimately no conditioned mind to be seen. (This means: the mind arises because the six faculties contact the six objects; when the four elements are resolved, the body no longer exists, and so there are no six faculties; without six faculties to contact the six objects, there is no shadow of the six objects — that is, no mind. Therefore this delusive mind is truly like an illusion.)
This is the contemplation: the mind is illusory.
[Falsely composed of the four conditions, there arise the six sense faculties] The four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind are falsely combined, and so the illusory six sense faculties arise.

blocks.text: 3. When the Dross Is Exhausted, Brightness Appears

inline.s: [Good man! In those beings, because the illusory body is extinguished, the illusory mind is also extinguished; because the illusory mind is extinguished, the illusory objects are also extinguished; because the illusory objects are extinguished, the extinguishing of illusion
(the contemplation that extinguishes illusion)
is also extinguished; because the extinguishing of the illusory is extinguished, what is not illusory is not extinguished — like polishing a mirror, when the dross is gone the brightness appears.]

Good man! These beings contemplate in this way: when this illusory body of theirs is extinguished, the illusory mind is extinguished; when the illusory mind is extinguished, the illusory objects are extinguished; when the illusory objects are extinguished, the contemplation that extinguishes illusion is also extinguished (“the extinguishing of illusion is also extinguished” — this is to forget the fish-trap once the fish is caught, dispelling layer by layer); when the contemplation is extinguished, there alone remains the pure, perfectly-awakened mind that is not of the same illusory nature and is unextinguished — “like polishing a mirror, when the dross is gone the brightness appears.”

The process of this contemplation is: body extinguished, then mind extinguished, then objects extinguished (the worlds of the ten directions extinguished), then contemplation extinguished, then the self-nature returns to its source. When body, mind, and objects are all extinguished, is there still any need for contemplation? (To contemplate further is to add legs to a painted snake — superfluous.) Therefore “because the illusory objects are extinguished, the extinguishing (the contemplation that extinguishes illusion) is also extinguished.” At this point one turns from confusion to awakening. If one can be like this at every moment, in every thought, one naturally ends birth-and-death and escapes the cycle — indeed, when illusion is exhausted and the real appears, the nameless dream comes to an end.

[The illusory objects are also extinguished] The illusory objects refer to the worlds of the ten directions. [Forgetting the fish-trap once the fish is caught] The trap in question is the fish basket; once the fish is caught one forgets the trap. It is a metaphor for forgetting the means of attainment once success is attained; or, having reached the goal, laying down the tools and the method. [What is not illusory is not extinguished] “What is not illusory” refers to the pure, perfectly-awakened mind. [Like polishing a mirror, when the dross is gone the brightness appears] This is a metaphor: when illusory dross is entirely extinguished, the self-nature is transformed from the state of consciousness to the state of its original nature.

To see through the realm of illusion, Master Lianchi’s composition “A Single Stroke” has the same subtle flavor as the “Song of All Things Done” of Dream of the Red Chamber, and is worth savoring carefully. (See the article
Master Lianchi’s “A Single Stroke” Verse

With regard to ending birth-and-death and escaping the cycle, the self-nature (the pure, perfectly-awakened mind) is not illusory; with regard to waking from the dream of ignorance, the self-nature is also illusory (what is called “not mind, not Buddha”), while the one who dreams the dream of ignorance (“not mind, not Buddha, not a thing”) is not illusory. (See the article
The Real Nature of All Dharmas
Q: How does one rely on awakening to give rise to practice and eliminate habitual tendencies?

Answer: As above, cultivate stillness and contemplate. For example, when a deluded thought arises, contemplate: after the body is extinguished, does this deluded thought still have any meaning? Since that is so, why not direct your energy and time toward practice rather than spend that energy and time pushing yourself into a pit of fire? In this way, as the contemplation accords with the Dharma and the power of stillness becomes effective, one naturally extinguishes this deluded thought. If one treats every deluded thought in this way and keeps it up, what will the result be? Therefore the World-Honored One says later:
“Good man! Those bodhisattvas who cultivate thus, progress gradually thus, think thus, abide thus, use skillful means thus, awaken thus, and seek this Dharma thus will not be confused or despondent.”
Master Hanshan’s Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Now contemplate this mind: apart from objects it has no substance; if one does not take the false as real, then delusion naturally dissolves — and at the very place where delusion dissolves, without seeking the real, the real is naturally restored.”
[Good man! Know that body and mind are both illusory defilement; when this defiled mark is forever extinguished, the ten directions are pure.]

Good man! Know that body and mind are both illusory defilement; if this defiled mark of body and mind is forever extinguished, then the ten directions are pure. (This means: the myriad phenomena are all false views of the mind, and the mind depends on the body for its existence. When body and mind are both extinguished, the myriad phenomena are also gone, and so the ten directions are pure.)
[Illusory defilement] The body and mind of sentient beings have no real substance, hence they are called illusory; because they are defiled by afflictions and not pure, they are called defilement.

[Good man! It is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects the five colors, appearing in accordance with each direction: the foolish, seeing the jewel, believe it truly possesses the five colors. Good man! The pure nature of perfect enlightenment, appearing in body and mind, responds in accordance with each class; and the foolish say that the pure, perfect enlightenment truly possesses such a self-mark of body and mind — so it is likewise. Because of this, they cannot be far from illusion, and so I say that body and mind are illusory defilement; through the opposing contemplation that turns away from illusory defilement one is called a bodhisattva. When the defilement is exhausted, the opposing remedy is also removed — then there is neither the defilement to be opposed nor one who is named.]

Good man! It is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects the five colors of blue, red, white, black, and yellow, each appearing according to the direction (blue appears when blue comes, red appears when red comes — so it reflects whatever color comes from each direction); the foolish imagine this jewel truly possesses these five colors. Good man! The pure nature of perfect enlightenment reflects the five aggregates of form, feeling, conception, volition, and consciousness (body and mind), and so it is likewise: whatever comes appears, and the foolish imagine that the pure nature of perfect enlightenment truly possesses such a self-mark of body and mind. For this reason (grasping illusion as real), one cannot be far from illusion; so I say body and mind are illusory defilement, and through the opposing remedy one is freed from illusory defilement (using prajñā to see that the five aggregates are all empty), hence called a bodhisattva. Once the illusory defilement is entirely removed, the opposing remedy is also gone (subject and object are both extinguished); then there is neither the antithesis of purity and defilement, nor a bodhisattva to be named (ordinary and holy both vanish, leaving alone the single luminous light of the pure nature of perfect enlightenment).
[Maṇi jewel] That is, the wish-fulfilling jewel, a jewel that grants whatever is sought.

[Good man! Because this bodhisattva and the sentient beings of the latter age have realized that the images of all illusions are extinguished, at that time they attain directionless purity, and in the boundless empty space awakening is revealed.]

Good man! Because this bodhisattva and the sentient beings of the latter age (through contemplation) have realized that the images of all illusions are entirely extinguished, at that time they attain purity in every place, and the boundless empty space is revealed through awakening.
The Song of Realizing the Way says:
“In the dream, the six destinies are clearly present; after awakening, the great thousand worlds are utterly empty.”

[Six destinies] The hell destiny, the hungry-ghost destiny, the animal destiny, the asura destiny, the human destiny, and the heavenly destiny. “Destiny” means direction; sentient beings receive retribution and all go from cause to fruit, so the six realms are also called the “six destinies.” [Great chiliocosm] That is, the great thousand-world system. One great thousand-world system is the realm of a single Buddha’s teaching. One Mount Sumeru together with the four great continents is called a small world; a thousand small worlds form a “small chiliocosm”; a thousand small chiliocosms form a “medium chiliocosm”; a thousand medium chiliocosms form a “great chiliocosm.” Because it is three times multiplied by a thousand, a great chiliocosm is also called the “three-thousand great thousand-world system.” [Mount Sumeru] In Chinese it is translated “Sublime High Mountain”; it is the center of a small world. This mountain is made of the four treasures of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; no mountain can match its height, and it is the king of mountains. [The four great continents] Around Mount Sumeru are four great continents: to the east is Pūrvavideha, to the south is Jambudvīpa (the world we inhabit is on this continent), to the west is Aparagodānīya, and to the north is Uttarakuru.

[Because awakening is perfect and luminous, the mind is revealed as pure; because the mind is pure, the object of sight is pure; because it is pure, the eye faculty is pure; because the faculty is pure, eye-consciousness is pure; because consciousness is pure, the object of hearing is pure; because it is pure, the ear faculty is pure; because the faculty is pure, ear-consciousness is pure; because consciousness is pure, the object of discernment is pure; and so on through nose, tongue, body, and mind — it is likewise.]

Because of perfect and luminous awakening, the purity of the mind is revealed. Because the mind is pure, the form-object seen by the eye (the seen object) is pure; because the seen object is pure, the eye faculty is pure; because the eye faculty is pure, eye-consciousness is pure. Because the mind is pure, the object of hearing is pure; because the object of hearing is pure, the ear faculty is pure; because the ear faculty is pure, ear-consciousness is pure. Because the mind is pure, the six objects relied upon by the six faculties are all pure; and so, too, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are all pure.

What has been said is: once one realizes that the images of all illusions are entirely extinguished, one attains purity in every place and perfect, luminous awakening. Because of perfect, luminous awakening, the mind is pure; because the mind is pure, the six faculties are pure; because the six faculties are pure, the six objects are pure; because the six objects are pure, the six consciousnesses are pure.
[Good man! Because the faculties are pure, the object of form is pure; because form is pure, the object of sound is pure; smell, taste, touch, and mental objects are likewise.]

Good man! Because the six faculties are pure, in turn the object of form is pure, the object of sound is pure, the object of smell is pure, the object of taste is pure, the object of touch is pure, and the object of mind is pure.
This means: because the six faculties are pure, the six objects are pure.
[Good man! Because the six objects are pure, the earth element is pure; because the earth element is pure, the water element is pure; the fire element and the wind element are likewise.]
Good man! Because the six objects are pure, in turn the earth element is pure, the water element is pure, the fire element is pure, and the wind element is pure.
This means: because the six objects are pure, the four elements are pure.

[Good man! Because the four elements are pure, the twelve sense-fields, the eighteen realms, and the twenty-five realms of existence are pure. Because those are pure, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unobstructed knowledges, the Buddha’s eighteen unique dharmas, and the thirty-seven factors of the path are pure; so too, down to the eighty-four thousand dhāraṇī gates, everything is pure.]

Good man! Because the four elements are pure, the twelve sense-fields (the six faculties and the six objects) are pure, the eighteen realms (the six faculties, six objects, and six consciousnesses) are pure, and the twenty-five realms of existence are pure (the three realms are pure). Because those are pure, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unobstructed knowledges, the Buddha’s eighteen unique dharmas, the thirty-seven factors of the path, and so on are each pure — so too, down to the eighty-four thousand dhāraṇī gates, everything is pure.

[Twenty-five realms of existence] Because an effect-result is born from karmic causes, the fruit is called “existence.” The fruits of the three realms (the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm) are divided into twenty-five classes, called the twenty-five realms of existence. Among them, the realm of desire has fourteen: the four evil destinies (hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras), the four continents (Pūrvavideha, Jambudvīpa, Aparagodānīya, Uttarakuru), and the six heavens of desire (the heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trayastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the heaven of delight in transformation, and the heaven of free enjoyment of others’ transformations). The realm of form has seven: the four dhyāna heavens (the first, second, third, and fourth dhyāna), together with the great Brahmā heaven, the five Pure Abodes, and the heaven of No-thought. The formless realm has four: the four stations of emptiness (the station of the infinity of space, the infinity of consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception). [The ten powers] The Tathāgata’s ten powers: first, the power of knowing what is and is not the case; second, the power of knowing the karmic retributions of the three times; third, the power of knowing all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis; fourth, the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of beings; fifth, the power of knowing the manifold understandings; sixth, the power of knowing the manifold realms; seventh, the power of knowing the path that leads everywhere; eighth, the power of knowing the unobstructed divine eye; ninth, the power of knowing past lives without outflows; tenth, the power of knowing the eternal severance of habitual tendencies. [The four fearlessnesses] Fearlessness in knowing all things, fearlessness in the exhaustion of outflows, fearlessness in speaking of what obstructs the path, and fearlessness in speaking of the path that exhausts suffering. [The four unobstructed knowledges] The unobstructed knowledge of dharmas, of meanings, of eloquence, and of joyful speech. [The eighteen unique dharmas] The eighteen qualities of merit that belong only to the Buddha; because they belong only to the Buddha and are not shared with the three vehicles, they are called the “unique dharmas.” First, no loss of body; second, no loss of speech; third, no loss of mindfulness; fourth, no manifold thought; fifth, no unsettled mind; sixth, no knowing and then abandoning; seventh, no decrease of aspiration; eighth, no decrease of vigor; ninth, no decrease of mindfulness; tenth, no decrease of wisdom; eleventh, no decrease of liberation; twelfth, no decrease of the knowledge and vision of liberation; thirteenth, all bodily actions follow wisdom; fourteenth, all verbal actions follow wisdom; fifteenth, all mental actions follow wisdom; sixteenth, wisdom knowing the past without obstruction; seventeenth, wisdom knowing the future without obstruction; eighteenth, wisdom knowing the present without obstruction. [The thirty-seven factors of the path] That is, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path — thirty-seven items in all.

[Good man! Because the nature of all reality is pure, one body is pure; because one body is pure, many bodies are pure; because many bodies are pure, so too, down to the sentient beings of the ten directions, their perfect awakening is pure.]

Good man! Because the nature of all reality is pure, one body (one’s own body) is pure; because one body is pure, many bodies are pure; because many bodies are pure, so too, down to the sentient beings of the ten directions, their perfect awakening is pure.

[Good man! Because one world is pure, many worlds are pure; because many worlds are pure, so too, reaching to the end of empty space and encompassing the three times, everything is equally pure and unmoving.]

Good man! Because one world (this world) is pure, many worlds are pure; because many worlds are pure, so too, reaching to the end of empty space and encompassing the three times (past, present, and future), everything is equally pure and unmoving.

In this way, the ten directions and the three times are all empty; confusion and awakening, ordinary and holy, are all merged and vanish — there remains only the single pure, perfect, luminous nature of awakening.

[Good man! Because empty space is thus equally unmoving, you should know that the nature of awakening is equally unmoving; because the four elements are unmoving, you should know that the nature of awakening is equally unmoving; so too, down to the eighty-four thousand dhāraṇī gates being equally unmoving, you should know that the nature of awakening is equally unmoving.]

Good man! Because empty space is thus equally unmoving, you should know that the nature of awakening is equally unmoving; because the four elements are unmoving, you should know that the nature of awakening is equally unmoving; so too, down to the eighty-four thousand dhāraṇī gates being equally unmoving, you should know that the nature of awakening is equally unmoving.

[Good man! Because the nature of awakening is all-pervading, pure, unmoving, and without boundary, you should know that the six faculties pervade the dharma realm; because the faculties pervade it, you should know that the six objects pervade the dharma realm; because the objects pervade it, you should know that the four elements pervade the dharma realm; so too, down to the dhāraṇī gates pervading the dharma realm.]

Good man! Because the nature of awakening is all-pervading, pure, unmoving, and without boundary, you should know that the six faculties pervade the dharma realm; because the faculties pervade the dharma realm, you should know that the six objects pervade the dharma realm; because the objects pervade the dharma realm, you should know that the four elements pervade the dharma realm; so too, down to the dhāraṇī gates pervading the dharma realm.
[The nature of awakening is all-pervading] The tathāgatagarbha emerges from the shell of ignorance as the dharma body, pervading the dharma realm. (For the tathāgatagarbha and the dharma body, see
The Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha

[Good man! Because that wondrous nature of awakening is all-pervading, the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are neither destroyed nor mixed; because the faculties and objects are not destroyed, so too, down to the dhāraṇī gates, they are neither destroyed nor mixed — like a hundred thousand lamps lighting a single room: their light pervades it, with neither destruction nor mutual mixing.]

Good man! Because the perfect, wondrous nature of awakening is all-pervading, the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are neither destroyed nor mixed; because the faculties and objects are not destroyed, so too, down to the dhāraṇī gates, they are neither destroyed nor mixed (the logical inference is as above); like a hundred thousand lamps lighting a single room, their light pervades it and is neither destroyed nor mixed.

[Good man! Because awakening is accomplished, you should know that the bodhisattva is not bound by dharmas, nor seeks liberation from dharmas; does not weary of birth-and-death, nor delight in nirvāṇa; does not revere the precept-holders, nor hate those who break the precepts; does not esteem long practice, nor slight the beginner. Why? Because all is awakened. It is like the eye’s vision being clear of the scene before it: its light is perfect and complete, attaining neither hatred nor love. Why? Because the essence of the light is non-dual, having neither hatred nor love.]

Good man! Because awakening is accomplished, you should know that the bodhisattva is not bound by dharmas, nor seeks liberation from dharmas; does not weary of birth-and-death, nor delight in nirvāṇa; does not revere the precept-holders, nor hate those who break the precepts; does not esteem those who have long cultivated, nor slight those who are just beginning. Why? Because all is awakened. Just as the eye’s vision is clear of the scene before it (clearly seeing the scene ahead), so the light of awakening is perfect and complete, clearly seeing the real nature of all dharmas (originally not a single thing), and so has neither hatred nor love. Why? Because the light of perfect awakening illuminates the essence of all things, which is void and tranquil, non-dual (the real nature of all dharmas), with nothing to hate and nothing to love.

This section reveals the single mind of quiescent cessation, which is equal and non-dual, thereby showing the pure, awakened mark of the self-nature. For bondage and liberation, hatred and love, and so forth — these are all dual marks. Because of false views born of ignorance, there come to be these dual marks. Now, in perfect illumination, everything is awakened, and so there are no dual marks.

blocks.text: 7. Like a Dream of Last Night

inline.s: [Good man! For this bodhisattva and the sentient beings of the latter age who, by cultivating this mind, attain accomplishment — in this there is neither cultivation nor accomplishment. Perfect awakening universally illumines, quiescent and non-dual; within it, the Buddha-worlds as numerous as hundreds of thousands of millions of asamkhyeyas, inexpressible, as many as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky, arising and ceasing in confusion. Neither grasped nor abandoned, neither bound nor liberated, one then knows that sentient beings have always been Buddhas, and that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of last night.]

Good man! For this bodhisattva and the sentient beings of the latter age who, cultivating this mind of perfect awakening, attain accomplishment — in this there is neither cultivation nor accomplishment. Perfect awakening universally illumines, quiescent and non-dual (the real nature of all dharmas); within it, the Buddha-worlds as numerous as hundreds of thousands of millions of asamkhyeyas, inexpressible, as many as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky (illusions), arising and ceasing in confusion. Therefore, neither grasping (not dwelling on a single dharma) nor abandoning (not renouncing a single dharma), neither bound nor liberated, one then knows that sentient beings have always been Buddhas, and that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of last night.

[Quiescent and non-dual] Nothing exists, hence it is called quiescent and non-dual. [Within it] Within the real state of perfect awakening, which is quiescent and non-dual. [Asamkhyeya] In Chinese it is translated “innumerable”; it means so many that no number can count them. [Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of last night] Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are both matters within the dream of ignorance; now that the dream of ignorance is over, looking back on past things is like a dream of last night.

[Good man! Because it is like a dream of last night, you should know that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa neither arise nor cease, neither come nor go; what is realized neither is gained nor lost, neither taken nor abandoned; what realizes neither acts nor rests, neither abides nor ceases; in this realization there is neither that which realizes nor that which is realized; ultimately there is no realization, nor one who realizes; the nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.]

Good man! Because everything is like a dream of last night, you should know that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa neither arise nor cease, neither come nor go; what is realized neither is gained nor lost, neither taken nor abandoned; what realizes neither acts nor rests, neither abides nor ceases; in this realization there is neither what realizes nor what is realized; ultimately there is no realization, nor one who realizes; the nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.

[Neither acts nor rests, neither abides nor ceases] Acting, resting, abiding, and ceasing are the four diseases of practice. See in detail the tenth chapter later, “One Must Abandon the Four Diseases.” [Ultimately there is no realization, nor one who realizes] Realization and the one who realizes are both matters within the dream of ignorance; hence it is said that ultimately there is none.
[Good man! Those bodhisattvas who cultivate thus, progress gradually thus, think thus, abide thus, use skillful means thus, awaken thus, and seek this Dharma thus will not be confused or despondent.]

Good man! Those bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the latter age who cultivate thus, progress gradually thus, think thus, abide thus, use skillful means thus, awaken thus, and seek this Dharma thus will not be confused or despondent.
This is the World-Honored One’s concluding reply to Bodhisattva Universal Eye’s question.
At that time, wishing to restate the principle set forth above, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

[Universal Eye, you should know: all sentient beings have body and mind both like illusion. The body’s form belongs to the four elements; the mind’s nature to the six objects goes. When the four elements, each in its nature, separate, who is there that is composed? Cultivating gradually in this way, everything becomes wholly pure.]

Universal Eye, you should know that all sentient beings have body and mind both like illusions. The body’s form is a false union of the four elements; the mind’s mark is the reflected shadow of the six objects. Once the four elements separate, which one is the body (the one composed)? Cultivating gradually in this way, one realizes that everything is pure (quiescent).

[Immovable, pervading the dharma realm; no acting, resting, abiding, or ceasing, nor any one who realizes. All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky. The three times are all equal; ultimately there is no coming or going. Bodhisattvas who first arouse the resolve, and the sentient beings of the latter age, desiring to enter the Buddha path, should cultivate in this way.]

The nature of awakening is equal and unmoving, pervading the dharma realm; there are none of the four diseases of acting, resting, abiding, and ceasing, nor any one who realizes. All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in the sky (they are all illusions). The three times are all equal, with ultimately no coming or going. Bodhisattvas who first arouse the resolve, and the sentient beings of the latter age, desiring to enter the Buddha path, should cultivate in this way.
[The three times are all equal] The three times (past, present, and future) are illusory, and so are ultimately equal.

[Then, in the midst of the assembly, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt long with hands crossed, and addressed the Buddha: Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, you have well proclaimed, for all the hosts of bodhisattvas, the Tathāgata’s great dhāraṇī of perfect, pure awakening, the dharma-practice of the causal ground, and the gradual skillful means that develop the benighted and dull among sentient beings. The Dharma assembly, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, has its illusory films cleared away and its eyes of wisdom made pure.]

Then, in the midst of the assembly, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt long with hands crossed, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, you have incisively proclaimed, for all the hosts of bodhisattvas, the Tathāgata’s great dhāraṇī of perfect, pure awakening, the dharma-practice of the causal ground, and the gradual skillful means of practice that develop the benighted and deluded among sentient beings. The Dharma assembly, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate teaching, has its illusory films removed and its eyes of wisdom made pure.
[The illusory films are cleared away] The illusory films are removed, so that one no longer falsely sees flowers in the sky.

[World-Honored One, if all sentient beings have always been Buddhas, why is there again all this ignorance? If this ignorance is innate to sentient beings, why then does the Tathāgata again say that sentient beings have always been Buddhas? If the sentient beings of the ten directions have always attained the Buddha path, and ignorance arises afterward, then when will all the Tathāgatas again give rise to all afflictions? We only ask that you not abandon your boundless, all-embracing great compassion: open the secret treasury for the bodhisattvas, and enable all sentient beings of the latter age to hear such a definitive teaching of the sūtra canon, and forever cut off doubt and regret. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground. Thus he requested three times, over and over.]

World-Honored One, if all sentient beings have always been Buddhas, why is it that there arises again all this ignorance? If this ignorance is innate to sentient beings, why does the Tathāgata again say that sentient beings have always been Buddhas? If the sentient beings of the ten directions have always attained the Buddha path, and ignorance arises afterward, then when will all the Tathāgatas again give rise to all afflictions? We only ask that the World-Honored One not abandon his limitless great compassion: open the secret treasury for the bodhisattvas, and enable all sentient beings of the latter age to hear such a definitive teaching of the sūtra canon and forever cut off doubt and regret. Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground. Thus he requested three times, over and over.
[All-embracing] Without hindrance or restriction.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha raised three questions:
First: All sentient beings have always been Buddhas; since they are Buddhas, why do they arise in ignorance and fall to the state of sentient beings?
Second: If ignorance has always existed, then since there is ignorance, how can it be said that one has become a Buddha?

Third: All sentient beings have already become Buddhas, and afterward arose in ignorance and fell to the state of sentient beings. So when we now practice, after we become Buddhas, at what time will we again arise in ignorance and fall to the state of sentient beings?
To make the following scripture easier to understand, these three questions are now explained in question-and-answer form as follows:
Q: All sentient beings have always been Buddhas; since they are Buddhas, why do they arise in ignorance and fall to the state of sentient beings?

Answer: All sentient beings originally possess the wisdom and marks of the Tathāgata, so they are said to “have always been Buddhas”; but there is still fundamental ignorance in a dormant state. Once it manifests its activity (a single thought of unawareness), one falls to the state of sentient beings. The process is: a single thought of unawareness gives rise to the three subtle marks, and the realm of objects is the support for the arising of the six coarse marks (see
The Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
Q: If ignorance has existed from the very outset, then since ignorance is present, how can it be said that one attains Buddhahood?

A: The primordial Buddha may still harbor fundamental ignorance, but that fundamental ignorance lies in a dormant state, so he still possesses the Tathagata's wisdom and auspicious marks. Possessing the Tathagata's wisdom and auspicious marks, he is of course a Buddha.

Q: All sentient beings were already Buddhas from the outset, and afterward, arousing ignorance, they fell back into being sentient beings. Now, then, when we cultivate and become Buddhas, at what time will we again arouse ignorance and fall back into being sentient beings?

A: When we cultivate now so as to become a Buddha, it is precisely to uproot fundamental ignorance. Therefore, having uprooted fundamental ignorance and become a Buddha, one will never again arouse ignorance and fall back into being a sentient being. This is like a person who, before contracting smallpox, is a healthy person; once he contracts smallpox he becomes a patient; after he recovers he is again a healthy person, and, possessing lifelong immunity, he will never contract smallpox again. So the World-Honored One taught: “Good man! As when smelting a gold mine, the gold does not come to be because of the smelting; once it has become gold, it will not again become ore.

The Tathagata's perfect enlightenment is likewise so.” (Translation: Good man! As when smelting a gold mine, the gold does not come to be because of the smelting; once it has been smelted into pure gold, it will not again become a gold mine.
The Tathagata's perfect enlightenment is likewise thus (it will not reverse).)

[Fundamental ignorance] The self-nature, from the very beginningless time, in a single thought of unawareness, sinks into a long night of delusion and does not comprehend the truth; it can give rise to all the manifold afflictions and delusions. This is fundamental ignorance, also called beginningless ignorance. Both the ignorance of sentient beings and the intrinsic thusness they possess are beginningless. The Mahayana Sutra on the Meaning of the Six Paramitas says: “As the raging flame blown by the wind may be tamed, as the waves of the sea may also be stilled, yet the deluded mind alone is most difficult to subdue. Why? Because beginningless ignorance has bewitched the nature of the mind.”

Then the World-Honored One addressed Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying: “Excellent! Excellent! Good man! You are able, on behalf of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age, to ask about the Tathagata's profound and secret, ultimately-appropriate means. This is the supreme instruction for all bodhisattvas, the definitive Mahayana. It can cause the bodhisattvas of the ten directions who study, and all sentient beings of the last age, to attain decisive faith and forever cut off doubt and regret. Listen attentively now; I shall speak it for you.” At that time Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and the entire assembly, in silence, listened.

At that time the World-Honored One said to Bodhisattva Vajragarbha: “Excellent! Excellent! Good man! You are able, on behalf of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age, to ask about the Tathagata's profound and secret, ultimately-appropriate means. This is the supreme instruction for all bodhisattvas, the definitive Mahayana. It can cause the bodhisattvas of the ten directions who study, and all sentient beings of the last age, to attain decisive faith and forever cut off doubt and regret. Fix your minds now and listen attentively; I will explain it for you.” At that time Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, receiving the teaching with joy, and the whole assembly, in silence, listened.

“Good man! In all worlds, beginning and end, arising and ceasing, before and after, existence and nonexistence, gathering and scattering, starting and stopping, thought after thought succeeding and revolving, all the manifold grasping and rejecting — these are all samsara. While still within samsara, to discriminate perfect enlightenment, that very nature of perfect enlightenment would itself be subject to flowing and turning. To be freed from samsara in this way is impossible.”

Good man! All the matters of beginning and end, arising and ceasing, before and after, existence and nonexistence, gathering and scattering, starting and stopping in all worlds, thought after thought succeeding and revolving, all the manifold grasping and rejecting, are the deluded views of samsara. While still within samsara, if one uses a mind of arising and ceasing to discriminate the realm of perfect enlightenment, then that nature of perfect enlightenment itself becomes a dharma of birth and death. To escape samsara in this manner is impossible.

This rebukes the questioner for using the mind of arising and ceasing to challenge the realm of perfect enlightenment. This is the general refutation; what follows explains it in detail by way of analogies.

“For example, when the eyes move, the still water can be made to seem to sway; again, with a fixed gaze, the whirling point of fire appears as a wheel of flame; the clouds move, and the moon seems to travel; a boat advances, and the shore seems to recede. It is likewise so.”

For instance, when one constantly moves one's eyes while watching still water, one also feels that the water is heaving; again, watching a spinning firebrand without blinking, one takes it for a wheel of flame; the white clouds move, making it appear that the moon is traveling on; a boat sails forward, making one think that it is the shore that is moving. All are this principle (viewing the still with what moves, the still becomes moving; viewing the true with the deluded, the true becomes delusion).

“Good man! While the various turning has not yet ceased, to cause that object to settle first is not attainable. How much more so, then, with a defiled mind revolving through birth and death that has never been purified, observing the Buddha's perfect enlightenment — how could it not turn again? Therefore you have given rise to three doubts.”

Good man! While the observer's turning has not yet ceased, to cause the object viewed to remain still is still impossible. How much more so, then, when a defiled mind revolving through birth and death has never been purified, coming to observe the Buddha's realm of perfect enlightenment — how could it not produce deluded views? Therefore you have given rise to these three doubts.

This is to say that, viewing the Tathagata's realm of perfect enlightenment with a mind of arising and ceasing, everything seen is delusion (one cannot see the truth); and from this deluded view the three questions you raised are produced.

“Good man! It is like a phantom film in the eye, which makes one see flowers in empty space as delusion. When the phantom film is removed, one cannot say: This film has been destroyed, when will it give rise to all the films again? Why? Because the two dharmas of film and flower are not dependent on one another. It is also like the flowers in empty space: when they vanish in the sky, one cannot say: When will the sky give rise to these flowers again? Why? Because the sky originally has no flowers, so there is no arising or ceasing. Birth and death and nirvāṇa are alike subject to arising and ceasing; the wondrous enlightened, perfect illumination is free from flowers and film.”

Good man! It is like a phantom film in the eye, which makes one see flowers in empty space as delusion. When the phantom film is removed, one cannot say: This film has been destroyed, when will it give rise to all the films again? Why? Because these two dharmas of the phantom film and the flowers in empty space do not exist in a relationship of mutual dependence. It is also like the flowers in empty space: when they vanish in the sky, one cannot say: When will the sky give rise to these flowers again? Why? Because the sky originally has no flowers, so there is no arising or ceasing. Birth and death and nirvāṇa are alike subject to the arising and ceasing of these flowers in empty space; while the wondrous enlightened, perfect illumination is free from both the flowers in empty space and the phantom film.

[Mutual dependence] The meaning of mutual dependence is that where there is low there is high, where there is left there is right, where there is birth there is extinction. [The two dharmas of film and flower are not mutually dependent] This is because the phantom film and the flowers in empty space are both illusions; originally they do not exist in a state of mutual dependence of being and nonbeing. The Heart Sutra says: “These dharmas are all empty of characteristics: not arising, not ceasing, not defiled, not pure, not increased, not decreased.” [The sky originally has no flowers, so there is no arising and ceasing] The sky originally has no flowers, so the appearing and disappearing of the flowers in empty space are not due to the flowers themselves arising and ceasing, but to the deluded view of the observer.

“Good man! You should know that empty space is neither temporarily existing nor temporarily nonexisting. How much more so the Tathagata's perfect enlightenment, which, being accordant, is the equal nature of empty space.”

Good man! You should know that empty space is neither temporarily existing nor temporarily nonexisting. How much more so the Tathagata's perfect enlightenment, which, being accordant, is the equal nature of empty space.

“Good man! As when smelting a gold mine, the gold does not come to be because of the smelting; once it has become gold, it will not again become ore. Throughout endless time, the nature of gold is not destroyed. One should not say that it was not originally achieved. The Tathagata's perfect enlightenment is likewise so.”

Good man! As when smelting a gold mine, the gold does not come to be because of the smelting; once it has been smelted into pure gold, it will not again become ore. Throughout endless time, the nature of gold will not be destroyed. One should not say that the gold was not originally achieved. The Tathagata's perfect enlightenment is likewise so (it does not reverse).
[One should not say that it was not originally achieved] One should not say that the gold originally did not exist and only came to be through smelting.

“Good man! In the wondrous perfect enlightened mind of all Tathagatas, there is originally no bodhi and no nirvāṇa, no becoming Buddha and no not-becoming-Buddha, no deluded samsara and no non-samsara.”
Good man! In the wondrous perfect enlightened mind of all Tathagatas, there is originally no bodhi and no nirvāṇa, no becoming Buddha and no not-becoming-Buddha, no samsara and no non-samsara.

“Good man! The realm realized by the sravakas, in which body, mind, and speech are all extinguished, still cannot reach the nirvāṇa manifested through their own realization. How much less could one, with a thinking mind, fathom the Tathagata's realm of perfect enlightenment? It is like taking the light of a firefly to burn Mount Sumeru: it can never kindle it. With a samsaric mind giving rise to samsaric views, to enter the Tathagata's great sea of still extinction is never attainable! Therefore I say: all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age must first sever the root of beginningless samsara.”

Good man! Even the realm realized by the sravakas, in which body, mind, and speech are all extinguished, still cannot reach the nirvāṇa manifested through their own realization. How much less, then, could one fathom the Tathagata's realm of perfect enlightenment with a thinking mind? It is like taking the light of a firefly to burn Mount Sumeru: it can never kindle it. With a samsaric mind giving rise to samsaric views, to vainly try to enter the Tathagata's great sea of still extinction is never attainable! Therefore I say: all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age must first sever the root of beginningless samsara before they can discuss this matter.

“Good man! Constructive thinking, arising from the mind that holds to existence, is all the deluded energy of the six objects; it is not the real mind-substance, and has already been likened to flowers in empty space. To use this thinking to discriminate the Buddha's realm is like flowers in empty space, which again bind empty fruit, turning and multiplying deluded appearances, with nothing that is valid.”

Good man! Constructive thinking arises from the mind that holds to existence; all of this is the deluded energy of the six sense objects. They are not the real mind-substance, but are illusions like the flowers in empty space. To use this constructive thinking to challenge the Tathagata's realm of perfect enlightenment is like deludedly seeing flowers in empty space and then, again, binding empty fruit, turning out a whole series of deluded appearances, none of which is valid.
“Good man! The vain, floating mind, replete with clever views, cannot accomplish the appropriate means of perfect enlightenment. Discrimination of this sort is not a proper question.”

Good man! The vain, floating mind, replete with clever views, cannot accomplish the appropriate means of perfect enlightenment. To challenge [it] with discrimination of this sort is not a proper question.
[Replete with clever views] To dwell on clever arguments.
At that time the World-Honored One, wishing to restate the meaning explained above, spoke in verse:

“Vajragarbha, know this: the Tathagata's nature of still extinction has never had beginning or end. If with a samsaric mind one thinks of it, thinking immediately turns back; one only reaches the confines of samsara, and cannot enter the Buddha's sea.”

Vajragarbha, you should know that in the Tathagata's nature of still extinction, there is no beginning and no end. If with a samsaric mind one thinks of the Tathagata's nature of still extinction, one produces illusion upon illusion, and thus only turns about within samsara, never able to enter the Buddha's sea.

[No beginning or end] There is no temporal notion of “initial” and “later.” In the sentence “initially one is a Buddha, later one arouses ignorance and falls back into being a sentient being,” initial and later are temporal notions, and these are matters within the dream of ignorance. The Buddha's sea, on the other hand, is the realm that has departed the dream of ignorance.

“As when smelting a gold mine, the gold does not come to be because of the smelting; though it is originally gold, it is finally achieved through smelting. Once it becomes a true gold substance, it will not again become ore. Birth and death, and nirvāṇa, the ordinary man and all Buddhas, are alike the appearance of flowers in empty space. Thinking is itself like a phantom transformation; how much more so the challenging of what is vain. If one can understand this mind, then one may seek perfect enlightenment.”

As when smelting a gold mine, the gold does not come to be because of the smelting; though it is originally gold, it is finally achieved into pure gold through smelting. Once it becomes pure gold, it will never again become ore. Birth and death, and nirvāṇa, the ordinary man and all Buddhas, are alike the appearance of flowers in empty space (illusory). Your thinking is like a phantom transformation; how much more so the questions you raise, which are all vain conjecture. If one can understand this discriminating mind, then one may seek perfect enlightenment.

Then, in the midst of the assembly, Bodhisattva Maitreya rose from his seat, paid homage at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and, kneeling long with hands pressed together, said to the Buddha: “Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, you have broadly opened the secret treasury for bodhisattvas, causing the whole assembly to deeply realize samsara and to distinguish the false from the true; you are able to bestow upon all sentient beings of the last age the fearless eye of the path, to give rise to decisive faith in great nirvāṇa, so that they no longer follow the revolving realm and give rise to views of cyclic return.”

Then, in the midst of the assembly, Bodhisattva Maitreya rose from his seat, paid homage at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and, kneeling long with hands pressed together, respectfully said to the Buddha: “Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, you have broadly opened the secret treasury for bodhisattvas, causing the whole assembly to deeply realize samsara and to distinguish the false from the true; you are able to bestow upon all sentient beings of the last age the fearless eye of the path and to give rise to decisive faith in great nirvāṇa, so that they no longer follow the realm of cyclic revolving and give rise to deluded views of cyclic return.”

“World-Honored One, if bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age wish to roam in the Tathagata's great sea of still extinction, how should they sever the root of samsara? In all that is samsaric, how many kinds of nature are there? By how many grades do the bodhisattvas' practice of the Buddha's bodhi differ? Returning to the toils of the world, how many kinds of teaching means should they set up to rescue sentient beings? I only wish you will not abandon the great compassion that saves the world, so that all bodhisattvas in practice and all sentient beings of the last age may have their wisdom-eye clarified and their mirror-of-mind illuminated, and fully realize the Tathagata's unsurpassed knowledge and vision.” Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself, touching the ground with his five limbs. In this manner he made the request three times, ending and beginning again.

“World-Honored One, if bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age wish to roam in the Tathagata's great sea of still extinction, how should they sever the root of samsara? In all that is samsaric, how many kinds of nature are there? By how many grades do the practice of the Buddha's bodhi differ? Returning to the world, how many kinds of teaching means should the bodhisattvas set up to rescue sentient beings? I only wish the World-Honored One will not abandon the great compassion that saves the world, so that all bodhisattvas in practice and all sentient beings of the last age may have their wisdom-eye clarified and their mirror-of-mind illuminated, and fully realize the Tathagata's unsurpassed knowledge and vision.” After Maitreya had spoken this, he prostrated himself, touching the ground with his five limbs. In this manner he made the request three times, ending and beginning again.

Then the World-Honored One addressed Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: “Excellent! Excellent! Good man! You are able, on behalf of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age, to ask about the Tathagata's profound, secret, and subtle meaning, causing the bodhisattvas' wisdom-eye to be purified and causing all sentient beings of the last age to forever sever samsara, to awaken to true reality within the mind, and to possess the patient endurance of non-arising. Listen attentively now; I shall speak it for you.” At that time Bodhisattva Maitreya, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and the whole assembly, in silence, listened.

At that time the World-Honored One said to Bodhisattva Maitreya: “Excellent! Excellent! Good man! You are able, on behalf of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the last age, to ask about the Tathagata's profound, secret, and subtle meaning, causing the bodhisattvas' wisdom-eye to be purified and causing all sentient beings of the last age to forever sever samsara, to awaken to true reality within the mind, and to possess the patient endurance of non-arising. Fix your minds and listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.” At that time Bodhisattva Maitreya, receiving the teaching with joy, and the whole assembly, in silence, listened.

[Patient endurance of non-arising] This is the patient endurance of the non-arising dharmas, in which true wisdom abides in the principle that “all dharmas have never arisen, and hence are also unceasing,” and no longer retreats. The Great Prajñā Sutra says: “Thus the irreversible Bodhisattva Mahasattva, contemplating all dharmas as empty in their own characteristics, has already entered the right nature of the bodhisattva that is free from birth; indeed he does not see even a single dharma as attainable. Because they are unattainable, there is no making. Because there is no making, in the end there is no arising. Because in the end there is no arising, it is called the patient endurance of non-arising dharmas. Having attained this patient endurance of non-arising dharmas, he is called an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahasattva.”

“Good man! All sentient beings, from the beginningless time, because of manifold affection and craving, have samsara. All the various natures in all the worlds — oviparous, viviparous, moisture-born, and miraculously born — all take their very life through sexual desire. You should know that in samsara, craving is the root. Because of the various desires, the nature of craving is stimulated and developed; and so they cause birth and death to continue.”

Good man! All sentient beings, from the beginningless time, because of manifold affection and craving, have samsara. All the various kinds of beings in all the worlds — oviparous, viviparous, moisture-born, and miraculously born — all take sexual desire as the primary cause of their life. Therefore, craving is the root of samsara. With, in addition, the manifold desires that stimulate and develop this nature of craving, they cause birth and death to continue and so have samsara.

[The four modes of birth] Viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and miraculously born. Viviparous birth is the life that takes form within the mother's womb before being born, as with human beings; oviparous birth is the life that takes form within the eggshell before being born, as with birds; moisture-born is the life that takes form relying on moisture, as with insects; miraculously born is the life that has nothing to rely on, but is suddenly born by karmic power alone, as with the devas, the hells, and the human beings at the beginning of an age.

“Desire is born of craving; life is possessed through desire. Sentient beings love life and still rely on the root of desire. Craving and desire are the cause; love of life is the fruit. Because of the realms of desire, the manifold favorable and adverse conditions arise. When circumstances oppose the mind of craving, hatred and jealousy arise, and various karma is created; therefore one is again born in hells and among hungry ghosts. If one knows that desire is to be detested, and loves the path of detesting [desire] and taking up practice, abandoning evil and delighting in good, one is again born among gods and humans. Again, because one knows that all craving is to be detested, one abandons craving and delights in renunciation; yet this still nourishes the root of craving, and manifests the superior karmic fruit of conditioned existence. All these, because they are samsaric, do not accomplish the holy path. Therefore, sentient beings who wish to escape birth and death and avoid all samsara must first cut off greed and desire and remove the thirst of craving.”

The desires are born of craving (all the desires issue from craving); life and nature are possessed through desire (this speaks of the situation at the moment consciousness takes rebirth). Sentient beings suffer from a life of craving-thirst and still rely on greed and desire as their root. Craving and desire are the cause; love of life is the fruit. Because of the realms of desire, the manifold favorable and adverse conditions arise. When circumstances oppose the mind of craving, hatred and jealousy arise, and various karma is created; therefore one is reborn in hells and among hungry ghosts. If one knows that desire is to be detested, and loves the path of detesting [craving] and taking up practice, abandoning evil and delighting in good, one is born in the heavens or among humans. Because one knows that all craving is to be detested, one abandons greed and craving and delights in giving; yet this still nourishes the root of craving, and manifests the superior karmic fruit of conditioned existence. All these, having craving as their root, are planting the causes of samsara, and therefore do not accomplish the holy path. Therefore, sentient beings who wish to escape birth and death and avoid all samsara should first cut off greed and desire and remove the thirst of craving.

[Craving and desire is the cause; love of life is the fruit] What sentient beings covet throughout their lives is the form of male and female. And after death, when the life is relinquished, before receiving the next retribution, there is still the intermediate body. This body sees nothing else but seeks the realms of desire; so from thousands of miles away it sees the place where a man and a woman unite. If one has, from past lives, the bond of craving, one quickly rushes there. Taking the thought of male and female as one's own, with extreme thirst of craving, one rides the love-fluid and flows into the mother's womb. Guarding this semen and blood, holding the thought without letting it go, one is formed into a fetus: this is the origin of receiving life. Therefore the one who sustains its birth has craving-desire as its cause; the body that receives its retribution has love of life as its fruit. [Loving the path of detesting craving] To detest craving and [take up] the path of practice (to detest greed and craving and take up cultivation). [Conditioned] Dharmas produced through causes and conditions. [Superior] To strengthen its upward momentum.

“Good man! When bodhisattvas manifest transformation in the world, craving is not their root; but by compassion they cause those beings to abandon craving, and by means of the various desires they enter birth and death. If all sentient beings of the last age can abandon the various desires and remove hatred and craving, forever severing samsara, and diligently seek the Tathagata's realm of perfect enlightenment, then with a pure mind they will attain awakening.”

Good man! When bodhisattvas manifest transformation in the world, craving is not their root; rather, by compassion they cause sentient beings to abandon craving so as to attain liberation, and thus, by means of the various desires, they enter birth and death to save and transform sentient beings. If all sentient beings of the last age can abandon the various desires and likewise remove hatred and craving, forever sever samsara, and diligently seek the Tathagata's realm of perfect enlightenment, then with a pure mind they will attain awakening.

[Compassion] Giving joy (bestowing happiness) is called loving-kindness; removing suffering is called compassion. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: “Great loving-kindness gives joy to all sentient beings; great compassion removes the suffering of all sentient beings.”

blocks.text: 3. The Distinctions of the Five Natures

inline.s: The five natures within samsara: (1) the nature of the ordinary person; (2) the nature of the two vehicles; (3) the nature of the bodhisattva; (4) the indeterminate nature; (5) the nature of the adherents of other paths.

“Good man! By their fundamental greed and desire, all sentient beings give expression to ignorance and reveal the five natures as unequal in their distinctions, appearing shallow or deep according to two kinds of hindrances. What are the two hindrances? The first is the hindrance of principle, which obstructs right knowledge and vision; the second is the hindrance of affairs, which continues the various births and deaths.”

Good man! By their fundamental greed and desire, all sentient beings give expression to ignorance, and so reveal the five natures as unequal in their distinctions, and, according to the thickness or thinness of the two hindrances (the hindrance of principle and the hindrance of affairs), they reveal the shallow or deep nature of their practice. What are the two hindrances? The first is the hindrance of principle, which obstructs right knowledge and vision; the second is the hindrance of affairs, which causes birth and death to continue.

[The two hindrances] The hindrance of principle and the hindrance of affairs. Wrong views can obstruct right knowledge and vision and hinder great bodhi; this is called the “hindrance of principle.” The afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion cause birth and death to continue and hinder great nirvāṇa; this is called the “hindrance of affairs.”
“What are the five natures?”
What are the five natures?
“Good man! If these two hindrances have not been severed and extinguished, one is called one who has not yet become a Buddha.”
Good man! If these two hindrances have not been severed and extinguished, one is called one who has not yet become a Buddha. (This is the nature of the ordinary person.)

“If sentient beings forever abandon greed and desire, first remove the hindrance of affairs, but have not severed the hindrance of principle, then they can only awaken and enter [the stage of] sravaka or pratyekabuddha, and cannot manifest and abide in the bodhisattva's realm.”

If sentient beings forever abandon greed and desire and sever the hindrance of affairs, but have not severed the hindrance of principle, they can only awaken and enter the realm of sravaka or pratyekabuddha, and cannot manifest and abide in the bodhisattva's realm. (This is the nature of the two vehicles.)

[The two vehicles] The vehicle of the sravaka and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha. Those who cultivate the Four Noble Truths and awaken are called the sravaka vehicle, whose highest fruition is the arhat; those who cultivate the twelve links of dependent origination and awaken are called the pratyekabuddha vehicle, whose highest fruition is the pratyekabuddha. [The Four Noble Truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of accumulation, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path (briefly, suffering, accumulation, cessation, path), where “truth” means ultimate reality. The truth of suffering is the truth explaining that life is full of suffering; in the truth of accumulation, “accumulation” means gathering, and it is the truth explaining how the suffering of life comes to be; the truth of cessation is the truth explaining that the realm of nirvāṇa alone is the definitive cessation of suffering; the truth of the path is the truth explaining how one must cultivate in order to realize nirvāṇa. These Four Noble Truths exhaust the twofold causality within and beyond the world: accumulation is the cause and suffering the fruit, which is the causality of the deluded realm; the path is the cause and cessation the fruit, which is the causality of the awakened realm. [The twelve links of dependent origination] This explains the process of the flow of birth and death for sentient beings. The twelve links are: ignorance (the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, which are the root of birth and death); compositional action (the making of various karma); consciousness (the karmic consciousness entering the womb); name-and-form (having only the form of the embryo, with the six faculties not yet complete); the six sense fields (the fetus grown into a human form with the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind); contact (born as a human and touching the external world); feeling (on contact with the external world, giving rise to feelings of pleasure and pain); craving (on encountering objects, giving rise to desire); grasping (pursuing and acting); becoming (becoming the karmic cause that can attract future retribution); birth (again receiving the future five aggregates); and aging-and-death (the future body again gradually growing old and dying). These twelve links, taking the arousal of delusion, the making of karma, the receiving of birth, and aging and death — all the causality of the three times of past, present, and future — revolve round and again, continuing without end. Among them, ignorance and compositional action are the karmic causes made in the past life; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense fields, contact, and feeling are the fruits experienced in the present life; craving, grasping, and becoming are the karmic causes made in the present life; and birth through to aging-and-death are the fruits experienced in the future life.

“Good man! If all sentient beings of the last age wish to sail upon the Tathagata's great sea of perfect enlightenment, they should first make a vow and diligently sever the two hindrances. Once the two hindrances are subdued, they can awaken to and enter the bodhisattva's realm. If the hindrances of both affairs and principle have been forever severed and extinguished, then they enter the Tathagata's subtle, wondrous perfect enlightenment and completely fulfill bodhi and great nirvāṇa.”

Good man! If all sentient beings of the last age wish to sail upon the Tathagata's great sea of perfect enlightenment, they should first make a vow and diligently sever the two hindrances. Once the two hindrances are subdued, they can awaken to and enter the bodhisattva's realm. If the two hindrances have already been forever severed and extinguished, they then enter the Tathagata's subtle, wondrous perfect enlightenment and completely fulfill bodhi and great nirvāṇa. (This is the nature of the bodhisattva.)

“Good man! All sentient beings can realize perfect enlightenment. When they encounter a good spiritual friend and, following the causal-ground practice he teaches, cultivate, then at that time there is sudden and gradual. If what they encounter is the Tathagata's right path of practice of unsurpassed bodhi, then, regardless of whether the faculties are great or small, they all achieve the buddha-fruit.”

Good man! All sentient beings can realize perfect enlightenment. When they encounter a good spiritual friend and, following the causal-ground practice he teaches, cultivate, then at that time there is sudden and gradual. If what the good spiritual friend reveals is the Tathagata's right path of practice of unsurpassed bodhi, then, regardless of whether the faculties are great or small, they all achieve the buddha-fruit. (This is the indeterminate nature.)
From this we can see how vitally important it is to find a true good spiritual friend to lead the way!

“If sentient beings, though seeking good friends, meet with those of wrong views and do not attain right awakening, they are then called of the nature of followers of other paths. The error of the false teacher is not the fault of the sentient beings.”

If sentient beings, though seeking good friends, meet instead with those of wrong views, and therefore do not attain right awakening, they are then called of the nature of followers of other paths. This is the fault of the false teacher, not the fault of the sentient beings who practice with him. (This is the nature of those of other paths.)
Though the fault lies with the false teacher, the evil fruit is one's own to swallow. False teachers who attach themselves to the Buddha commit crimes that fill the heavens!
“This is called the distinctions of the five natures of sentient beings.”
What is said above is precisely the distinctions of the five natures of sentient beings.

blocks.text: 4. Entering the World to Rescue Sentient Beings

inline.s: “Good man! Bodhisattvas, solely by means of great compassion and appropriate means, enter the various worlds to develop those not yet awakened. Even to manifest all kinds of forms and appearances, to be in adverse and favorable circumstances, to work together with them, and to transform them so that they become Buddhas — all this relies on their beginningless pure vow-power.”

Good man! Bodhisattvas, solely by means of great compassion and appropriate means, return to the mundane world to develop the sentient beings not yet awakened. Even to manifest all kinds of forms and appearances, to dwell amid adverse and favorable circumstances, to work together with them, and to transform them so that they become Buddhas — all this relies on their beginningless pure vow-power.

[All this relies on the beginningless pure vow-power] When bodhisattvas enter the world to save and transform sentient beings, they must work together with them. If, without relying on their beginningless pure vow-power, they rashly work together with them, then amid the defilement of the five desires and six sense objects, there is no one who does not fall.

“If all sentient beings of the last age, toward great perfect enlightenment, arouse the superior mind, they should make the bodhisattva's pure great vow and say: ‘May I now abide in the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, seeking good spiritual friends, and never encounter adherents of other paths or those of the two vehicles.’ Practicing in accord with this vow, one gradually severs the various hindrances. When the hindrances are exhausted and the vow fulfilled, one ascends the clean Dharma-palace of liberation, realizes great perfect enlightenment, and enters the realm of marvelous adornment.”

If all sentient beings of the last age, toward great perfect enlightenment, arouse the superior mind (resolving to become Buddhas), they should make the bodhisattva's pure great vow, saying: ‘May I now abide in the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, seeking good spiritual friends, and by no means encounter adherents of other paths or those of the two vehicles who masquerade as good spiritual friends.’ Then, practicing in accord with this pure great vow, one gradually severs the various hindrances. When the hindrances are exhausted and the vow fulfilled, one ascends the clean Dharma-palace of liberation, realizes great perfect enlightenment, and enters the realm of marvelous adornment (perfectly realizing the buddha-fruit).
[The realm of marvelous adornment] The ocean of the Buddha's fruition.

“Maitreya, you should know that all sentient beings, not attaining the great liberation, all because of greed and desire, fall into birth and death. If they can sever hatred and craving, together with greed, hatred, and delusion, then, unhindered by the distinctions of the five natures, they will all attain the Buddha's path.”

Maitreya, you should know that the reason all sentient beings do not attain the great liberation is all because of greed and desire, and so they fall into birth and death. If they can sever hatred and craving, and greed, hatred, and delusion as well, then, unconstrained by the differences of the five natures, they will all perfectly realize the buddha-fruit.
Therefore, in practice, severing hatred and craving together with greed, hatred, and delusion is of the utmost importance!

“When the two hindrances are forever consumed and extinguished, seeking the teacher one attains right awakening; following the bodhisattva's vow, one relies on great nirvāṇa. All the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, by their great compassionate vows, manifest and enter birth and death. Those now practicing, and sentient beings of the last age, diligently severing all the views of craving, then return to great perfect enlightenment.”

When the two hindrances are forever consumed and extinguished, seeking the teacher one attains right awakening; following the bodhisattva's pure great vow, one relies on great nirvāṇa. All the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, by their pure, great compassionate vows, manifest in the world and enter birth and death to save and transform sentient beings. Those now practicing, and sentient beings of the last age, diligently severing all the views of craving, then return to great perfect enlightenment.
The views of craving are the root of hatred-and-craving and of greed, hatred, and delusion.
The Buddha said: “Diligently sever all the views of craving, and you will return to great perfect enlightenment.” From this we can know how important it is to sever the views of craving!

blocks.text: 6. The Differences of What Is Realized

inline.s: Then, in the midst of the assembly, Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom rose from his seat, paid homage at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and, kneeling long with hands pressed together, said to the Buddha: “Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, for our sakes you have broadly spoken of such inconceivable matters, things we have never before seen, never before heard. Now we, receiving the Buddha's skillful guidance, are at ease in body and mind and have obtained great benefit.”

Then, in the midst of the assembly, Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom rose from his seat, paid homage at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and, kneeling long with hands pressed together, respectfully said to the Buddha: “Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, for our sakes you have broadly spoken of such inconceivable matters — things we have never before seen, never before heard. Now we, receiving the Buddha's skillful guidance and instruction, are at ease in body and mind and have obtained great benefit.”

“May you, for all the Dharma-assembly gathered here, again proclaim the Dharma-King's perfect enlightened nature. All sentient beings, and the bodhisattvas, and the Tathagata, the World-Honored One — how do the realizations and attainments differ? May the sentient beings of the last age, hearing this holy teaching, accord with it and awaken, entering gradually and successively.” Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself, touching the ground with his five limbs. In this manner he made the request three times, ending and beginning again.

I pray the World-Honored One to expound afresh for all the Dharma assembly here the Tathagata’s complete perfect enlightenment.
