All living beings and all the bodhisattvas, the Tathagata, the World-Honored One — what difference is there in what they realize and what they attain? May the sentient beings of the last age, hearing this holy teaching, accord with it and awaken, and be able to enter it gradually.” When the Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom had spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground. Three times he made this request, again and again from beginning to end.
[Dharma King] The Buddha is freely sovereign over the Dharma, and so he is called the Dharma King.

“At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You are able, for the sake of all the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about the gradual sequence and the differences. Listen attentively now; I shall speak it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and the whole assembly listened in silence.”

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You are able, for the sake of all the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about the gradual sequence of practice and the differences in realization. You may now gather your mind and listen attentively; I shall expound it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Pure Wisdom, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and the whole assembly remained in silence and listened.

“Good man! The self-nature of perfect enlightenment is not a nature that exists within a nature, but arises in accordance with various natures; there is nothing taken and nothing realized. In the reality of all dharmas, there is truly no bodhisattva and no living being. Why? Because bodhisattvas and living beings are all illusions; when illusion is extinguished, there is no one who takes and no one who realizes.”

Good man! The self-nature of perfect enlightenment does not exist as a fixed nature; it appears in accordance with various conditions, and in reality there is nothing taken and nothing realized. In the reality of all dharmas, there is truly no bodhisattva and no living being. Why? Because bodhisattvas and living beings are all illusions. Once one realizes perfect enlightenment, illusion is extinguished, and so there is no one who takes and no one who realizes.

[A nature that is not a nature yet possessed of nature] The self-nature of perfect enlightenment has no substance, hence it is said to be “non-nature”; yet common beings and sages alike possess it, hence it is said to be “possessed of nature.” The principle involved is discussed in detail in
The Reality of All Dharmas

. Many of this sutra’s teachings are based on this fundamental principle of the reality of all dharmas, and at the same time they also expound this fundamental principle. To better understand the meaning of the sutra, it is recommended that you read carefully
The Reality of All Dharmas

“It is like the eye-base, which cannot see the eye itself; its nature is inherently equal. Without something to make it equal, living beings are deluded and inverted, unable to extinguish all illusion. Within the vain working of what is about to be extinguished and not yet extinguished, differences appear. If one attains the Tathagata’s accord with quiescent extinction, there is really no quiescent extinction and no one who is extinguished.”

It is like the eye, which cannot see itself; the perfect-enlightenment self-nature of buddhas and living beings is originally equal. The reason it is not equal is because living beings are deluded and inverted, unable to eliminate all illusion. Within the vain working where illusion is about to be quenched but not yet quenched, differences appear. If one attains the realm of the Tathagata’s accord with quiescent extinction, then there is truly no such thing as quiescent extinction, and no person who attains it.

[As with the eye-base that cannot see the eye] It is like having eyes, which, though they see all things, cannot see themselves. Therefore, for the eye itself, there is no duality of a seer and a seen. This is a metaphor that the perfect-enlightenment self-nature has no duality of one who realizes and that which is realized.

Below, according to the degree of completeness in according with the nature of awareness, five kinds of differences in realization are set forth; these are the milestones upon the bodhi path. These five differences are: first, ordinary beings’ accordance with the nature of awareness; second, those who have not yet entered the grounds, their accordance with the nature of awareness; third, those who have entered the grounds, their accordance with the nature of awareness; fourth, the Tathagata’s accordance with the nature of awareness; fifth, the accordance with the nature of awareness itself.

blocks.text: 1. Ordinary Beings’ Accordance with the Nature of Awareness

inline.s: “Good man! All living beings, from beginningless time, because of the delusory thought of self and of one who loves the self, have never known that it arises and ceases in every thought; therefore they give rise to aversion and love and cling to the five desires. If they meet a good friend who teaches them to awaken to the pure perfect-enlightened nature and reveals its arising and ceasing, they then know that in this life the nature itself is ever toiling and anxious. If there is further one whose toiling and anxiety are forever cut off, he attains the purity of the dharma-realm. Yet that very pure understanding becomes an obstruction to himself, and so he is not free within perfect enlightenment. This is called ordinary beings’ accordance with the nature of awareness.”

Good man! All living beings, from beginningless time, because they deludedly cling to the five aggregates of body and mind as “self” and are attached to that “self,” have never known that this “self” is an illusion arising and ceasing in every thought; therefore they give rise to aversion and love (aversion to what opposes the “self,” and love for what conforms to it), and for the delight of this “self” they cling to the five desires. If one meets a good friend who teaches one to awaken to one’s pure perfect-enlightened nature (to see one’s own nature), and reveals that the “self” arising and ceasing in every thought is an illusion, then one knows that in this life one is toiling and troubling oneself (there is originally nothing amiss in the world; it is the mediocre who trouble themselves). If there is yet another whose toiling and anxiety are forever cut off, he attains the purity of the dharma-realm. Then that very pure understanding (clinging to the pure realm as something rare and excellent) becomes an obstruction to his own advance; so within perfect enlightenment he is not free. This is called ordinary beings’ accordance with the nature of awareness.

[The five desires] Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearances; sound refers to pleasing tones; smell refers to fragrant scents; taste refers to delicious flavors; touch refers to agreeable sensations. These five can give rise to a mind of craving, and so they are called the five desires. [Toiling and anxiety forever cut off, one attains the purity of the dharma-realm] When toiling and anxiety are forever cut off, the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion no longer operate; hence it is said one attains the purity of the dharma-realm.

blocks.text: 2. The Accordance with the Nature of Awareness of Those Not Yet Entering the Grounds

inline.s: “Good man! All bodhisattvas regard understanding as an obstruction. Though they sever this obstruction of understanding, they still abide in seeing-awakening; and this seeing-awakening, as an obstruction, becomes an obstruction, and so they are not free. This is called the accordance with the nature of awareness of bodhisattvas not yet entering the grounds.”

Good man! All bodhisattvas know that the pure understanding of the purity of the dharma-realm is an obstruction to advance, and so they sever this pure understanding. Yet though they have cut off this obstruction of understanding, they still abide in seeing-awakening, and this seeing-awakening in turn becomes an obstruction to further advance (hence it is called the obstruction of awakening); so within perfect enlightenment they are not free. This is called the accordance with the nature of awareness of bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the grounds.

[Seeing-awakening] The wisdom that can sever the obstruction of understanding is called seeing-awakening. [Not yet entering the grounds] Not yet entering the ten grounds. [The ten grounds] In the fifty-two stages of the bodhisattva’s practice, the fifth set of ten is called the ten grounds; in these ten grounds the buddha-realm gradually opens up, all-seed wisdom is accomplished, and they already belong to the holy stage, hence they are also called the “ten sages.” [All-seed wisdom] The wisdom that penetrates the general and particular marks of all dharmas and, in teaching the path, severs delusion.

blocks.text: 3. The Accordance with the Nature of Awareness of Those Who Have Entered the Grounds

inline.s: “Good man! What has illumination and what has awakening are both called obstructions. Therefore the bodhisattva is constantly aware yet abides not; the illuminated and the one who illuminates are simultaneously quiescent and extinguished. It is like a person who cuts off his own head: because the head is already cut off, there is no one who cuts. Thus one uses an obstructing mind to extinguish all obstructions; once the obstructions are cut off and extinguished, there is no one who extinguishes. The scriptural teachings are like a finger pointing to the moon; if one then sees the moon, one knows that what the finger points at is by no means the moon. All the various discourses the Tathagatas use to reveal and instruct the bodhisattvas are likewise. This is called the accordance with the nature of awareness of bodhisattvas who have entered the grounds.”

Good man! What has illumination and what has awakening are both obstructions. Therefore the bodhisattva is constantly aware yet does not abide; the object illuminated (the pure understanding) and the wisdom that illuminates (the seeing-awakening) are simultaneously quiescent and extinguished. It is like a person cutting off his own head: because the head is already cut off, there is no one who cuts. Therefore, with a mind that removes obstruction, one quiesces the various obstructions; when the various obstructions have been cut off and extinguished, there is no one who extinguishes (the mind of extinguishing obstruction is also extinguished). They realize that all the scriptural teachings (the sutra teachings) are like the finger pointing to the moon; if one has already seen the moon, one knows that what points to the moon is by no means the moon. All the varied discourses that all the Tathagatas use to reveal and instruct the bodhisattvas are likewise — they are fingers pointing to the ultimate truth, not the ultimate truth itself. (Therefore those who have entered the grounds no longer cling to the “finger pointing at the moon.”) This is called the accordance with the nature of awareness of bodhisattvas who have entered the grounds.

[What has illumination and what has awakening] Illumination is the object illuminated, which is the pure understanding; awakening is the wisdom that severs the obstruction of understanding, which is the seeing-awakening.

blocks.text: 4. The Tathagata’s Accordance with the Nature of Awareness

inline.s: “Good man! All obstructions are the ultimate awareness. Gaining thought and losing thought are alike liberation. Accomplishing dharmas and destroying dharmas are alike called nirvāṇa. Wisdom and ignorance are together prajñā. The dharmas accomplished by bodhisattvas and by sectarians are alike bodhi. Ignorance and thusness are a state without difference. All precepts, concentration, and wisdom, together with lust, anger, and delusion, are all pure practices. Living beings and lands share the same dharma-nature. Hell and the heavenly palaces are all the Pure Land. Those endowed with the nature and those devoid of it alike accomplish the buddha-way. All afflictions are ultimately liberated. The ocean-wisdom of the dharma-realm illumines all marks like empty space. This is called the Tathagata’s accordance with the nature of awareness.”

Good man! All obstructions are the ultimate awareness. Gaining thought and losing thought are both liberation. Accomplishing dharmas and destroying dharmas are both called nirvāṇa. Wisdom and ignorance are both prajñā. The dharmas accomplished by bodhisattvas and by sectarians are alike bodhi. Ignorance and thusness are a state of no difference. All the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, together with lust, anger, and delusion, are all pure practices. Living beings and lands share the same dharma-nature. Hell and the heavenly palaces are all the Pure Land. Those endowed with the nature and those devoid of it alike accomplish the buddha-way. All afflictions are ultimately liberated. The ocean-wisdom of the dharma-realm illumines all marks like empty space (originally there is not a single thing). This is called the Tathagata’s accordance with the nature of awareness.

[Gaining thought and losing thought] Being able to sever and being able to establish is gaining thought; being unable to sever and unable to establish is losing thought. [Accomplishing dharmas and destroying dharmas] Cultivating in accordance with the teachings, and being diligent, is accomplishing dharmas; acting against the teachings, or being lazy and remiss, is destroying dharmas. [Pure practices] Pure conduct. [Dharma-nature] The substance of all dharmas (the reality of all dharmas). [Those endowed with the nature and those devoid of it] Possessing the nature of liberation and transcendence is called endowed with the nature; while possessing no nature of liberation and transcendence, delighting only in birth and death and not seeking transcendence, is called devoid of the nature. The devoid-of-nature refers to the “icchantika.” [Icchantika] One who has severed all roots of good and cannot become a buddha. [The ocean-wisdom of the dharma-realm] The great wisdom that contemplates the equality of the dharma-realm, deep and vast as the sea, hence called the ocean-wisdom of the dharma-realm.

blocks.text: 5. Accordance with the Nature of Awareness

inline.s: “Good man! As for bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, when in all times they do not give rise to deluded thoughts, and toward all the deluded minds they do not extinguish them either; abiding in the realm of delusion they add no understanding, and in that non-understanding they do not discriminate the real. Those living beings who hear this dharma-gate, believe, understand, receive and uphold it, and do not give rise to fear or dread — this is called accordance with the nature of awareness.”

Good man! If among the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age there are those who, “in all times not giving rise to deluded thoughts, not extinguishing all the deluded minds either, abiding in the realm of deluded thought without adding understanding, and in that non-understanding not discriminating the real,” accord naturally with the Way, then on hearing this dharma-gate of perfect enlightenment they believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, and do not give rise to fear or dread. This is called accordance with the nature of awareness.

[In all times not giving rise to deluded thoughts; toward all deluded minds not extinguishing them either] The mind has two states: the true mind and the deluded mind. No-thought is the true mind; having thought is the deluded mind. The thoughts arising from the deluded mind are of two kinds: first, evil thoughts and involuntary thoughts, called deluded thoughts; second, correct and self-mastered thoughts, called right thoughts. “In all times not giving rise to deluded thoughts; toward all deluded minds not extinguishing them either” means: at all times one should not have deluded thoughts, but should maintain right thoughts. The Diamond Sutra says: “One should not give rise to a mind that abides in form, nor a mind that abides in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to a mind that abides in nothing.” To give rise to a mind abiding in form, or a mind abiding in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas — this is a deluded thought; to give rise to a mind that abides in nothing — this is a right thought. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “The bodhisattva does not exhaust the conditioned (does not remove the conditioned), and does not abide in the unconditioned (nor does he cling to the unconditioned).” [Abiding in the realm of delusion without adding understanding; in that non-understanding not discriminating the real] The realm of delusion all arises from the mind; it is originally one’s own mind, originally the one reality. What need is there for understanding? The Surangama Sutra says: “The mind that takes its own mind makes what is not an illusion into an illusion.” In that place of non-understanding, able only to know and yet be still, that is true knowing, and so one does not discriminate the real.

“Good man! You should know that such living beings have already made offerings to a hundred thousand million billion Ganges-sands of buddhas and great bodhisattvas, and planted many roots of virtue. The Buddha says such a person is named one who accomplishes all-seed wisdom.”

Good man! You should know that such living beings have already made offerings to a hundred thousand million billion Ganges-sands of buddhas and great bodhisattvas, and planted many roots of virtue. The Buddha says such a person will accomplish all-seed wisdom (the Buddha gives them the prophecy that they will perfectly realize the buddha-fruit).

[The three wisdoms] All-wisdom, way-seed wisdom, and all-seed wisdom. All-wisdom is the wisdom by which the sravakas and the pratyekabuddhas know the general mark of all dharmas; the general mark is the mark of emptiness. Way-seed wisdom is the wisdom by which bodhisattvas understand the various methods of practice. All-seed wisdom is the wisdom by which the Buddha penetrates the general and particular marks of all dharmas and, in teaching the path, severs delusion. In other words, all-wisdom is the wisdom contemplating emptiness; way-seed wisdom is the wisdom contemplating existence; and all-seed wisdom contemplates both emptiness and existence — knowing emptiness on the one hand and knowing existence on the other — that is, the unity of the first two wisdoms. [The general mark and the particular mark] The general mark is the mark common to all dharmas (the mark of emptiness); the particular mark is the individual mark of each dharma.

“Pure Wisdom, know: the nature of perfect bodhi has nothing taken and nothing realized, no bodhisattva, no living being. In the time of awakening and of not-yet-awakening, the gradual sequence has differences. Living beings are obstructed by understanding; bodhisattvas have not left awakening. Entering the grounds, forever quiescent extinction, abiding in no mark at all. Great awareness wholly complete is called universal accordance.”

Pure Wisdom, you should know: the nature of perfect bodhi has neither a taker nor a realizer, and no bodhisattva or living being. It is only in the state of about-to-awaken and not-yet-awaken that one takes there to be a gradual sequence and differences. Living beings are obstructed by understanding (having the obstruction of pure understanding, referring to ordinary beings’ accordance with the nature of awareness); bodhisattvas have not left awakening (still having the seeing-awakening, referring to those who have not yet entered the grounds); the pure understanding and the seeing-awakening of those who have entered the grounds are both quiescent and extinguished (referring to those who have entered the grounds); abiding in no mark at all (referring to the Tathagata’s accordance with the nature of awareness). Great awareness wholly complete is called universal accordance (referring to the accordance with the nature of awareness itself).

“Living beings of the last age, whose minds give rise to no vain delusion — the Buddha says such persons are in this very life bodhisattvas. Having made offerings to Ganges-sands of buddhas, their merit is already complete.”

Among the living beings of the last age, one whose mind gives rise to no vain delusion — the Buddha says such a person is in this very life a bodhisattva; they have made offerings to as many buddhas as the sands of the Ganges, and their merit is already complete.
“Though there are many expedient means, they are all called the wisdom of accordance.”
What has been spoken above, though it has many expedient means, is all called the wisdom of accordance.

[The three great wondrous gates] Shamatha (stillness), samapatti (equal holding), and dhyana (still contemplation). [Shamatha] Rendered into Chinese as “stillness,” that is, to still one’s thoughts and be aware of the present manifestation of one’s own mind, like a mirror reflecting things. [Samapatti] Rendered into Chinese as “equal holding.” Being free from both dullness and agitation is called “equal”; fixing the mind on a single object is called “holding”; one contemplates the illusory marks and realizes their illusoriness. [Dhyana] Rendered into Chinese as “still contemplation” (stillness and contemplation: stillness is concentration, contemplation is wisdom), also “thought cultivation,” and so on; that is, to be still and quiet the thoughts while contemplating the middle-way principle of “neither empty nor existent, both empty and existent, falling into neither extreme, perfectly fused and unobstructed.”

“Then the Bodhisattva Majestic Power of Freedom, within the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circled to the right three times, knelt long with hands clasped, and said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, you have extensively discriminated for us such accordance with the nature of awareness, causing all the bodhisattvas’ minds of awareness to be luminous, and, receiving the Buddha’s perfect voice, they gain the excellent benefit without depending on practice.”

Then, the Bodhisattva Majestic Power of Freedom, within the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circled to the right three times, knelt long with hands clasped, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, you have extensively discriminated and set forth these five kinds of accordance with the nature of awareness, causing all the bodhisattvas’ minds of awareness to be luminous, and, receiving the Buddha’s perfect voice, they gain the excellent benefit without depending on practice.
[Perfect voice] The Buddha’s voice is perfect and wonderful; with a single voice he speaks the Dharma, and beings of each type understand it according to their kind.

“World-Honored One, it is like a great city with four gates outside: those who come from each direction do not come by a single road. All the bodhisattvas’ adorning of the buddha-land and attainment of bodhi likewise have not a single expedient means alone. I only pray the World-Honored One to expound extensively for us all the expedient means and the gradual sequences, and how many kinds in all there are of practitioners. May the bodhisattvas of this assembly and the mahayana-seeking sentient beings of the last age quickly attain awakening and sport in the Tathagata’s great sea of quiescent extinction.” Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground. Three times he made this request, again and again from beginning to end.

World-Honored One, it is like a great city with four gates — east, south, west, and north — outside; those who come from each direction do not come by a single road. All the bodhisattvas’ adorning of the buddha-land and attainment of bodhi are likewise: there is not a single expedient means alone. I only pray the World-Honored One to expound extensively for us all the expedient means and the gradual sequences, and how many kinds in all there are of practitioners. May the bodhisattvas of this assembly and the mahayana-seeking sentient beings of the last age quickly attain awakening and sport in the Tathagata’s great sea of quiescent extinction. The Bodhisattva Majestic Power of Freedom, having spoken these words, prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground. Three times he made this request, again and again from beginning to end.
[I only pray] “Only” means alone. There is no other wish; it is exclusively for this matter.

“At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Majestic Power of Freedom: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You are able, for the sake of all the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about such expedient means. Listen attentively now; I shall speak it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Majestic Power of Freedom, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and the whole assembly listened in silence.”

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Majestic Power of Freedom: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You are able, for the sake of all the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about such expedient means. You may now gather your mind and listen attentively; I shall expound it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Majestic Power of Freedom, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and the whole assembly remained silent and listened.

“Good man! The supreme wonderful awareness pervades the ten directions and gives rise to the Tathagatas and all dharmas, which are one substance and equal. Among all the practices, there is truly no duality. As to the expedient means of accordance, their number is unlimited. Gathering them all together by the way they return, in accordance with the differences of the natures, there should be three kinds.”

Good man! The supreme perfect-enlightened wonderful mind pervades the ten directions and gives rise to the Tathagatas and all dharmas; they are one substance and equal. As to the various methods of practice, there is truly no duality (every dharma is a gate to realization). If one speaks of the expedient means of accordance, their number is unlimited. Gathering them all together, dividing according to the sharpness or dullness of the faculties and the depth of study and practice, there should be three kinds.
[The ten directions] East, south, west, north, southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, up, and down.
As to the various methods of practice, in substance and in nature there is originally no difference (truly no duality); as to function, there are various differences (their number is unlimited).

“Good man! If bodhisattvas awaken to pure perfect enlightenment, and with the pure aware mind take stillness as practice, then by clearing all thoughts they become aware of the agitation of consciousness. Still wisdom arises, and the guest-dust of body and mind is from then on forever extinguished; then they can internally bring forth stillness and ease. Because of stillness, the minds of all the Tathagatas in the worlds of the ten directions appear within it, like images in a mirror. This expedient means is called shamatha.”

Good man! If bodhisattvas awaken to pure perfect enlightenment (see their own nature), and with the pure aware mind (cultivate in accordance with the nature) observe the still substance of the mind and still their deluded thoughts (take stillness as practice), then by clearing the deluded thoughts (the deluded pondering subsides), they become aware of the agitation of consciousness (they then see the subtle marks of arising and ceasing in the alaya consciousness). Persisting in this, still wisdom arises, and the afflictions of body and mind are from then on forever extinguished; then they can internally bring forth stillness and ease. Because of stillness, the minds of all the Tathagatas in the worlds of the ten directions appear within it, like images in a mirror. This method of practice is called shamatha.

[Take stillness as practice] Taking stillness is to still deluded thoughts in order to purify the present working of the streams of consciousness. [Guest-dust] This refers to afflictions, also called guest-dust afflictions. Afflictions are not inherently possessed by the mind-nature; they arise from being deluded about the principle, hence they are called “guests.” Because they defile the mind-nature, they are called “dust.”

“Good man! If bodhisattvas awaken to pure perfect enlightenment, and with the pure aware mind know that the nature of mind and the faculties and their objects all exist through illusion, then they set up various illusions in order to remove the illusory, and transform various illusions to open the illusory beings. Because of setting up illusion, they can internally bring forth great compassion and ease.”

Good man! If bodhisattvas awaken to pure perfect enlightenment (see their own nature), and with the pure aware mind (cultivate in accordance with the nature) know that the nature of mind and the faculties and their objects all exist through illusion, then they set up illusion-wisdom to contemplate the illusory realm, purifying the present working of the streams of consciousness to remove illusory delusion (purging the fundamental ignorance). (Once ignorance is broken, there is an inconceivable function.) So they transform various illusions and manifest the bodies of the ten realms, in order to reveal and save extensively the illusory beings (living beings). This is because of setting up illusion-wisdom, and so they can internally bring forth great compassion and ease.

This passage explains that after bodhisattvas see their nature (awaken to pure perfect enlightenment), with the pure aware mind they know that the nature of the mind and the faculties and their objects all exist through illusion; so they set up the illusion-contemplation to remove the various illusions, and with various illusory bodies save extensively the illusory beings (transforming various illusions to open the illusory beings).

“All bodhisattvas from this point begin to practice and gradually advance. That which contemplates illusion is not the same as the illusory; yet being not the same as the illusory, the contemplation too is all illusion, so the illusory marks are forever extinguished. The perfect wondrous practice of these bodhisattvas is like a sprout growing in the soil. This expedient means is called samapatti.”

All bodhisattvas from this point begin to practice and gradually advance (dispelling layer by layer: first dispelling the contemplated object, then the contemplating wisdom, until subject and object both vanish and the illusory marks are forever extinguished). That which contemplates illusion (the true wisdom apart from thought) is therefore not the same as the contemplated illusory realm (taking the contemplative as true wisdom and the contemplated as the illusory realm, so one dispels the contemplated realm, keeping only the contemplating wisdom). Although the contemplating wisdom is not the same as the contemplated realm, since both are illusory they must be further dispelled. When subject and object are both extinguished, illusory marks are forever extinguished. The perfect wondrous practice of these bodhisattvas is like a seed in the soil (the buddha-seed) gradually growing into a sprout and a crop. This method of practice is called samapatti.
[That which contemplates illusion is not the same as the illusory] The true wisdom (the one who contemplates illusion) remains alone, and so is not the same as the contemplated illusory realm.

“Good man! If bodhisattvas awaken to pure perfect enlightenment, and with the pure aware mind do not take hold of illusion or the various still marks, understand that body and mind are all hindrances, and without knowledge-awareness and brightness do not rely on the various hindrances; they forever transcend the realm of hindrance and non-hindrance. The world they enjoy, and body and mind, though their marks are within the realm of dust, are like the sound within a vessel: the sound comes forth beyond it. Afflictions and nirvāṇa do not obstruct each other.”

Good man! If bodhisattvas awaken to pure perfect enlightenment (see their own nature), and with the pure aware mind (cultivate in accordance with their nature) do not take hold of illusion or the various still marks, and know that body and mind are all hindrances; without knowledge-awareness brightness (apart from thought), they do not rely on the various hindrances of body and mind, and forever transcend the realm of hindrance and non-hindrance. Though the marks of the world they enjoy and of body and mind are within the realm of dust, the dharma-body far surpasses the realm of dust (as the sound of a bell or drum lies far beyond the bell and drum themselves); afflictions and nirvāṇa each do not obstruct the other.

[Knowledge-awareness brightness] The brightness of knowledge-awareness. The Surangama Sutra says: “When knowing and seeing establish a knowing, that is the root of ignorance; when knowing and seeing do not see, that is nirvāṇa.” Knowledge-awareness brightness is the established knowing, which is the root of ignorance. [A sound within a vessel] “Vessel” refers to a musical instrument, the bell or drum; “sound” is a loud, resonant note. [Like the sound within a vessel, the sound comes forth beyond it] Like the sound of a bell or drum, which lies far beyond the bell and drum themselves.

“Then they can internally bring forth quiescent-extinction ease, the wonderful awareness in accordance. The realm of quiescent extinction is beyond the reach of one’s own and others’ body and mind; the lifespans of living beings are all floating thoughts. This expedient means is called dhyana.”

Then they can internally bring forth quiescent-extinction ease, the wonderful awareness in accordance. This realm of quiescent extinction is beyond the reach of one’s own and others’ body and mind; the lifespans of living beings are all floating thoughts. This method of practice is called dhyana.

“Good man! These three dharma-gates are all close accordance with perfect enlightenment. The Tathagatas of the ten directions become buddhas because of these. The various expedient means of the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, all that are alike and all that are different, all rely on these three kinds of work; if one perfectly realizes them, one attains perfect enlightenment.”

Good man! These three great dharma-gates are all methods of practice that closely accord with perfect enlightenment. The Tathagatas of the ten directions all become buddhas through practicing these gates. The bodhisattvas of the ten directions, with their various expedient means, whether alike or different (practicing one of the three gates, or two, or all three, and so on — see the “twenty-five wheels” of the next chapter), in substance all rely on these three great gates; if one perfectly realizes them, one attains perfect enlightenment.

[The various expedient means of the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, all alike and all different, all rely on these three kinds of work] The bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions have various methods of practice; among them there are those that are alike (same) and those that are different (different), but in substance they all rely on these three great dharma-gates.

“Good man! Suppose a person cultivates the holy path and teaches living beings to accomplish the fruits of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of arhats and pratyekabuddhas; this is not equal to a person who hears this unimpeded dharma-gate of perfect enlightenment and, in a single instant, accords with it in practice.”

Good man! Suppose a person cultivates the holy path and teaches living beings to accomplish the fruits of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of arhats and pratyekabuddhas; it is not equal to a person who hears this unimpeded dharma-gate of perfect enlightenment and, in a single instant, accords with it in practice.

“O Majestic, you should know: the mind of supreme great awareness, in its original limit, has no two marks. According with the various expedient means, their number is indeed unlimited. The Tathagata, in his overall instruction, sets forth three kinds: stillness, that is shamatha, like a mirror reflecting the various images; illusion-like, that is samapatti, like a sprout gradually growing; and dhyana alone, quiescent extinction, like the sound within a vessel.”

O Majestic, you should know: the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment, in its original limit, has no two marks. According with the various expedient means, there is an unlimited number. The Tathagata, in his overall instruction, sets forth three great wondrous gates: taking stillness, shamatha, like a mirror reflecting the various images (faithfully manifesting them); the illusion-contemplation, samapatti, like a sprout gradually growing (when illusion is exhausted, truth appears); and dhyana alone, still contemplation, like the sound within a vessel (far surpassing the various hindrances).

“These three wonderful dharma-gates are all the accordance of awareness. The Tathagatas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas attain the Way because of them. Because the three are perfectly realized, it is called ultimate nirvāṇa.”

These three wonderful dharma-gates are all the accordance of perfect enlightenment. The Tathagatas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas attain the Way because of them. Because the three are perfectly realized, it is called ultimate nirvāṇa.

[The twenty-five wheels] This is the various combinations and arrangements of the three great wondrous gates (shamatha, samapatti, and dhyana): taking one of the three, or two, or all three, plus differences in their order of sequence — altogether twenty-five kinds.

“Then the Bodhisattva Distinguishing Sound, within the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circled to the right three times, knelt long with hands clasped, and said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, such dharma-gates are exceedingly rare. World-Honored One, as to these expedient means, of all the bodhisattvas within the gate of perfect enlightenment, how many kinds of practice are there? I pray that, for the sake of the assembly and the sentient beings of the last age, you reveal them by expedient means, causing them to awaken to the reality of all dharmas.” Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground. Three times he made this request, again and again from beginning to end.

Then, the Bodhisattva Distinguishing Sound, within the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circled to the right three times, knelt long with hands clasped, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, such three great dharma-gates are exceedingly rare. World-Honored One, as to these methods of practice, of all the bodhisattvas within the gate of perfect enlightenment, how many modes of practice are there? I pray that, for the sake of the assembly and the sentient beings of the last age, you reveal them by expedient means, causing them to awaken to the reality of all dharmas. The Bodhisattva Distinguishing Sound, having spoken these words, prostrated himself with his five limbs on the ground. Three times he made this request, again and again from beginning to end.

“At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Distinguishing Sound: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You are able, for the sake of the great assembly and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about such practice. Listen attentively now; I shall speak it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Distinguishing Sound, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and the whole assembly listened in silence.”

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Distinguishing Sound: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You are able, for the sake of all the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about the practice of these three great wondrous gates. You may now gather your mind and listen attentively; I shall expound it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Distinguishing Sound, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and the whole assembly remained silent and listened.

“Good man! The perfect enlightenment of all the Tathagatas is pure and pristine; originally there is no practice and no one who practices. All the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, relying on not-yet-awareness, practice through an illusory power; at that time there are twenty-five kinds of pure concentration wheels:”

Good man! The perfect enlightenment of all the Tathagatas is pure and pristine; originally there is no practice and no one who practices. All the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, relying on not-yet-awareness, practice through an illusory power; at that time there are twenty-five kinds of pure types:

“If bodhisattvas take only extreme stillness, and because of the power of stillness forever sever afflictions and accomplish the ultimate, without rising from the seat enter nirvāṇa — these bodhisattvas are said to practice shamatha alone.”

If bodhisattvas take only extreme stillness, and because of the power of stillness forever sever afflictions and accomplish the ultimate, without rising from the seat enter nirvāṇa — the method of these bodhisattvas is called practicing shamatha alone.

“If bodhisattvas contemplate only the illusion-like, and because of the power of the Buddha transform the world’s various operations, fully practicing the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva, and in the dharani do not lose the still thought and the various still wisdoms — these bodhisattvas are said to practice samapatti alone.”

If bodhisattvas contemplate only the illusion-like, and because of the power of the Buddha transform the world’s various operations, fully carrying out the bodhisattva’s various pure and wondrous conducts, and in the dharani (the total-holding) do not lose the still thought and the various still wisdoms — the method of these bodhisattvas is called practicing samapatti alone.

“If bodhisattvas only extinguish the various illusions, not taking up any operation, alone severing afflictions, and when afflictions are completely severed then realize the reality of all dharmas — these bodhisattvas are said to practice dhyana alone.”

If bodhisattvas merely extinguish the illusions, without adopting the function of it, and alone sever the afflictions; when the afflictions are exhausted, they realize the true mark. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called cultivating dhyana alone.

[If bodhisattvas first take up utmost stillness, and with the mind of still wisdom contemplate all the illusions, then within this they rouse the bodhisattva practices. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samatha and afterward cultivating samapatti.]

If bodhisattvas first take up utmost stillness, and with the mind of still wisdom contemplate all the illusions, then within this they rouse the bodhisattva practices. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating samatha and afterward cultivating samapatti.

[If bodhisattvas, by means of still wisdom, realize the nature of utmost stillness, then they sever the afflictions and forever transcend birth and death. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samatha and afterward cultivating dhyana.]

If bodhisattvas, by means of still wisdom, use the power of this still wisdom to perfectly realize the substance of utmost stillness, then they sever the afflictions and forever transcend birth and death. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating samatha and afterward cultivating dhyana.

[If bodhisattvas, with the still, quiescent wisdom, again manifest the power of illusion and various transformations to cross over sentient beings, and afterward sever the afflictions and enter still extinction. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samatha, in the middle cultivating samapatti, and afterward cultivating dhyana.]

If bodhisattvas, with the still, quiescent wisdom, again manifest the power of illusion and various transformations to cross over sentient beings, and afterward sever the afflictions and enter still extinction. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating samatha, in the middle cultivating samapatti, and afterward cultivating dhyana.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of utmost stillness, sever the afflictions, and afterward rouse the pure, wondrous practices of the bodhisattva to cross over sentient beings. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samatha, in the middle cultivating dhyana, and afterward cultivating samapatti.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of utmost stillness, sever the afflictions, and afterward rouse the pure, wondrous practices of the bodhisattva to cross over sentient beings. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating samatha, in the middle cultivating dhyana, and afterward cultivating samapatti.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of utmost stillness, sever the afflictions in mind, and again cross over sentient beings and establish worlds. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samatha, and cultivating samapatti and dhyana together.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of utmost stillness, sever the afflictions in mind, and cross over sentient beings and establish worlds. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating samatha, and cultivating samapatti and dhyana together (at the same time).

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of utmost stillness, supply and bring forth transformation, and afterward sever the afflictions. These bodhisattvas are called cultivating samatha and samapatti together, and afterward cultivating dhyana.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of utmost stillness, supply and bring forth transformation, and then sever the afflictions. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called cultivating samatha and samapatti together, and afterward cultivating dhyana.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of utmost stillness, use it to sustain still extinction, and afterward rouse functioning to transform worlds. These bodhisattvas are called cultivating samatha and dhyana together, and afterward cultivating samapatti.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of utmost stillness, use it to sustain still extinction, and afterward rouse functioning to transform worlds. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called cultivating samatha and dhyana together, and afterward cultivating samapatti.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation, accord with various things and take up utmost stillness. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samapatti and afterward cultivating samatha.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation, accord with various things and take up utmost stillness. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating samapatti and afterward cultivating samatha.
[If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation, take up various realms and adopt still extinction. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samapatti and afterward cultivating dhyana.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation, manifest various realms and adopt still extinction. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating samapatti and afterward cultivating dhyana.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation, perform Buddha-work, dwell in stillness, and sever the afflictions. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samapatti, in the middle cultivating samatha, and afterward cultivating dhyana.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation, perform Buddha-work, dwell in stillness, and sever the afflictions. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called cultivating samapatti, in the middle cultivating samatha, and afterward cultivating dhyana.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation and unobstructed functioning, because they sever the afflictions, dwell in utmost stillness, these bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samapatti, in the middle cultivating dhyana, and afterward cultivating samatha.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation and unobstructed functioning, because they sever the afflictions, dwell in utmost stillness, the practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating samapatti, in the middle cultivating dhyana, and afterward cultivating samatha.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation and expedient functioning, follow both utmost stillness and still extinction. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating samapatti, and cultivating samatha and dhyana together.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation and expedient functioning, practice in accord with both utmost stillness and still extinction. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating samapatti, and cultivating samatha and dhyana together.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation and various functioning, sustain utmost stillness and afterward sever the afflictions. These bodhisattvas are called cultivating samapatti and samatha together, and afterward cultivating dhyana.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation and various functioning, sustain utmost stillness and afterward sever the afflictions. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called cultivating samapatti and samatha together, and afterward cultivating dhyana.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation, sustain still extinction, and afterward dwell in purity, in unconditioned present-watching. These bodhisattvas are called cultivating samapatti and dhyana together, and afterward cultivating samatha.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of transformation, sustain still extinction, and afterward dwell in purity, in unconditioned present-watching. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called cultivating samapatti and dhyana together, and afterward cultivating samatha.
[If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction, rouse utmost stillness and dwell in purity. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating dhyana and afterward cultivating samatha.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction, rouse utmost stillness and dwell in purity. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating dhyana and afterward cultivating samatha.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction, rouse functioning, and in every realm follow the still functioning. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating dhyana and afterward cultivating samapatti.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction, rouse functioning, and in every realm follow the still functioning. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating dhyana and afterward cultivating samapatti.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction and various self-natures, dwell in present-watching and rouse transformation. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating dhyana, in the middle cultivating samatha, and afterward cultivating samapatti.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction and various self-natures, dwell in present-watching and rouse transformation. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating dhyana, in the middle cultivating samatha, and afterward cultivating samapatti.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction and the unconditioned self-nature, rouse functioning, and for pure realms return to present-watching. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating dhyana, in the middle cultivating samapatti, and afterward cultivating samatha.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction and the unconditioned self-nature, rouse functioning, and for pure realms return to present-watching. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating dhyana, in the middle cultivating samapatti, and afterward cultivating samatha.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction and various pure qualities, dwell in present-watching and rouse transformation. These bodhisattvas are called first cultivating dhyana, and cultivating samatha and samapatti together.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction and various pure qualities, dwell in present-watching and rouse transformation. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called first cultivating dhyana, and cultivating samatha and samapatti together.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction, sustain utmost stillness and rouse transformation. These bodhisattvas are called cultivating dhyana and samatha together, and afterward cultivating samapatti.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction, sustain utmost stillness and rouse transformation. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called cultivating dhyana and samatha together, and afterward cultivating samapatti.

[If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction, sustain transformation and rouse utmost stillness, with pure, bright realm-wisdom. These bodhisattvas are called cultivating dhyana and samapatti together, and afterward cultivating samatha.]

If bodhisattvas, with the power of still extinction, sustain transformation and rouse utmost stillness, with pure, bright realm-wisdom. The practice of these bodhisattvas is called cultivating dhyana and samapatti together, and afterward cultivating samatha.

[If bodhisattvas, with the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, perfectly unite all things, and in regard to the various natures and marks, never depart from the enlightenment-nature. These bodhisattvas are called perfectly cultivating the three self-natures, following them in purity.]

If bodhisattvas, with the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, perfectly unite all things, and in regard to the various natures and marks, do not depart from the enlightenment-nature. These bodhisattvas are called perfectly cultivating the three self-natures, following them in purity.
[Perfectly uniting all things] The three contemplations (samatha, samapatti, dhyana) are one mind; in a single thought they are all complete.

[Good man! This is called the twenty-five wheels of the bodhisattva. All bodhisattvas cultivate exactly thus. If bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age rely on these wheels, they should uphold pure conduct, be still and think, and seek with sorrow to repent. After twenty-one days, in regard to the twenty-five wheels set markers on each, and with utmost sincerity seek with sorrow; at random draw one. According to the drawing, then you know whether it is sudden or gradual. If there is even a single thought of doubt or regret, then it will not be accomplished.]

Good man! This is called the twenty-five wheels of the bodhisattva. All bodhisattvas cultivate in accordance with this. If bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age rely on these twenty-five wheels, they should uphold pure conduct, be still and think, and seek with sorrow to repent. After twenty-one days, in regard to the twenty-five wheels set markers on each, and with utmost sincerity seek with sorrow; at random draw one. According to the drawing you unfold, then you know whether it is sudden or gradual. If there is even a single thought of doubt or regret, then it will not be accomplished.
["Drawing a lot"] That is what is commonly called drawing lots (
niān jiū
). In advance make a mark on paper and roll it into a paper scroll or ball; then pick one, open it, and act according to what is marked on it.

[Discriminating Sound, you should know: all the bodhisattvas, the unobstructed pure enlightenment, all arise from meditative concentration. Thereupon samatha, samapatti, and dhyana: these three dharmas, cultivated progressively, have twenty-five kinds.]

Discriminating Sound, you should know: the unobstructed pure enlightenment of all bodhisattvas all arises from meditative concentration. These are samatha, samapatti, and dhyana. The progressive practice of these three dharmas has twenty-five kinds in total.

[The Tathagatas of the ten directions, the practitioners of the three times, none fail through this dharma to attain bodhi. Only those who suddenly awaken, and who do not follow the teaching, are exempt. All the bodhisattvas, and the sentient beings of the last age, should always uphold this wheel, and diligently practice in accord with it. Relying on the Buddha's great compassionate power, before long they realize nirvāṇa.]

The Tathagatas of the ten directions, the practitioners of the three times, all follow this dharma and attain bodhi. Only those who suddenly awaken are not required to rely on this gradual method. All the bodhisattvas, and the sentient beings of the last age, should always uphold this wheel and diligently practice in accord with it. Relying on the Buddha's great compassionate power, before long they realize nirvāṇa.

[The four marks] The mark of self (realization), the mark of person (awakening), the mark of sentient beings (understanding), and the mark of a life span (awareness). These are the four barriers on the path of returning from delusion to truth, and they must be eradicated one by one.

[Then, in the midst of the assembly, the Bodhisattva Purifier of Karmic Obstacles rose from his seat, touched his head to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt long with hands folded, and said to the Buddha: Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, you have broadly explained such an inconceivable matter for us, the course of practice on the causal ground of all Tathagatas. You caused the great assembly to attain what it never had before, to behold the Tamer passing through the realm of hard toil for eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all the functionings appearing as in a single thought. We bodhisattvas deeply congratulate ourselves.]

Then, in the midst of the assembly, the Bodhisattva Purifier of Karmic Obstacles rose from his seat, touched his head to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt long with hands folded, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, you have broadly explained such an inconceivable matter for us, the course of practice on the causal ground of all Tathagatas (the Tamer), that is, the twenty-five wheels set forth in the previous chapter. You caused the great assembly to attain what it never had before, as if with their own eyes they beheld the realm of hard toil through which the Buddhas passed for eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and all the functionings appearing within a single thought. We bodhisattvas deeply congratulate ourselves.
[Tamer] That is, the Taming Man, one of the Buddha's ten titles. The Buddha is the great man who can tame all the sentient beings that can be saved.

[World-Honored One, if the nature of this enlightened mind is originally pure, why is it defiled, causing all sentient beings to be confused and unable to enter? I only wish the Tathagata would broadly, for our sake, awaken us to the dharma-nature, causing this great assembly and the sentient beings of the last age to have an eye for the future. Having spoken these words, he prostrated his whole body on the ground. He made this request three times, ending and beginning again.]

World-Honored One, if the nature of this enlightened mind is originally pure, why is it defiled, causing all sentient beings to be confused and unable to realize and enter? I only wish the Tathagata would broadly reveal and cause us to enter the dharma-nature, making for this great assembly and the sentient beings of the last age an eye for the future Way. Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Purifier of Karmic Obstacles prostrated his whole body on the ground. He made this request three times, ending and beginning again.

[Dharma-nature] It is the essential nature (substance) of all dharmas, another name for the true mark of all dharmas. The Sutra on the Dharma King Spoken by the Buddha for the King of the Light of the Most Supreme Good says: All dharmas are empty and void of nature, impermanent and destined to destruction. It is like a person who, in a night-dream, sees fine gardens, mountains and rivers with crowds of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and towers all lovely and delightful; when he wakes up, he sees nothing at all. The Great Jewel Heap Sutra says: Neither coming nor going, neither born; the Buddha can expound this dharma. Though he speaks of the empty nature of all dharmas, the World-Hero (the Buddha) yet causes them to cultivate the Way. The Lantern of the Moon Samādhi Sutra says: The nature of all dharmas is forever still; the ignorant common man, lacking wisdom, cannot comprehend it. If a person can dwell the mind in still concentration, then that person always has the Buddha. In the Flower Garland Sutra

the chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru it says: Dharma-nature is originally empty and still, neither grasped nor seen. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: Sentient beings and lands share the same dharma-nature. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says: Dharma-nature is as previously explained: each dharma is empty, and together they are one emptiness; that is dharma-nature. [World-Hero] A name for the Buddha. [Way-eye] The eye that can see the right Way. The Surangama Sutra says: Arouse the luminous, wondrous mind and open my Way-eye. This sutra says: You have been able to ask the Tathagata about such practice, and can give the sentient beings of the last age the fearless Way-eye, causing them to attain the holy Way.

[Then the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Purifier of Karmic Obstacles: Good! Good! Good man. You are able, for the sake of the great assembly and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about such an expedient. Listen well now, and I shall speak it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Purifier of Karmic Obstacles, delighting in the instruction, and the great assembly, listened in silence.]

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Purifier of Karmic Obstacles: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You are able, for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about such an expedient. Now gather your minds and listen carefully; I shall proclaim it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Purifier of Karmic Obstacles, delighting in the instruction, and the great assembly, listened in silence.

[Good man! From the beginningless time, all sentient beings in delusion cling to self, person, sentient beings, and a life span, and take these four inversions to be real substance. From this there arise the two realms of hatred and love. Upon this deluded substance they again cling to delusion; the two delusions depend on each other, giving rise to the path of deluded karma. Because there is deluded karma, they deludedly see transmigration. Those who weary of transmigration deludedly see nirvāṇa. For this reason they cannot enter the pure enlightenment; it is not that enlightenment rejects those who can enter; those who can enter do not enter by enlightenment. Therefore both the arising of thought and the stilling of thought all go to confusion.]

Good man! From beginningless time, all sentient beings in delusion cling to self, person, sentient beings, and a life span, and take these four marks (the four inversions) to be real substance. From this there arise the two realms of hatred and love. Upon this deluded substance of the four marks they again cling to delusion; the two delusions depend on each other, giving rise to the path of deluded karma. Because there is deluded karma, they deludedly see transmigration. Those who weary of transmigration deludedly see nirvāṇa. Because of this deluded clinging, they cannot enter the pure enlightenment; it is not that the pure enlightenment-nature rejects them and keeps them out. Those who do enter are not made able to enter by the enlightenment-nature; rather, they enter by eradicating the four marks. Therefore, sentient beings who do not understand this cause, whether in the arising of thought or in the stilling of thought, all go to confusion.

[The four inversions] These are the four marks of self, person, sentient beings, and a life span. Originally there are no such four marks; they are falsely reckoned to exist, hence they are called inversions.

[Why? Because there is the beginningless, primal origination of ignorance, which becomes one's own master. All sentient beings, from birth, lack the eye of wisdom; the nature of body and mind is all ignorance. It is like a person who does not cut off his own life. Therefore know that with those who love me, I follow along; with those who do not follow, there arises hatred and resentment. Because the mind of hatred and love nourishes ignorance, seeking the Way with ignorance continually does not succeed.]

Why? Because there is the beginningless, primal origination of ignorance, which becomes one's own master. Therefore all sentient beings, from birth, lack the eye of wisdom; the nature of body and mind is all ignorance. But ignorance cannot itself cut off ignorance, just as a person cannot cut off his own life. Therefore, with those who love me, I follow along with them; and for those who oppose me, hatred and resentment arise. Because the mind of hatred and love nourishes ignorance, and ignorance again gives rise to the mind of hatred and love, the two turn round and depend on each other; as ignorance thus continues, seeking the Way does not succeed.

[Primal-origination ignorance] The ignorance of the arising phase, rooted in the very first thought of unawareness; it is also called fundamental ignorance. [It is like a person who does not cut off his own life] A metaphor to show that ignorance cannot itself cut off ignorance.

[Good man! What is the mark of self? It means whatever the mind, of these sentient beings, realizes. Good man! For example, when a person's hundred bones are well regulated, he suddenly forgets his own body. When the four limbs are slack, and the care departs from proper method, and a needle or moxa is slightly applied, then he knows there is a self. Therefore, through the act of realization, the substance of self then appears. Good man! If the mind, even up to realizing the Tathagata, finally knows the pure nirvāṇa, all these are the mark of self.]

Good man! What is the mark of self? It means whatever the mind, of these sentient beings, realizes; this is the mark of self. Good man! For example, when a person's whole body is well regulated, he forgets his own body. Only when he has a sickness to be treated (the four limbs slack, the care misplaced, a needle or moxa slightly applied) does he think of this body. In the same way, sentient beings, in the course of cultivating and realizing the Way, then discover 'self.' Good man! If the mind, even up to realizing the Tathagata, finally knows that 'I' have realized the pure nirvāṇa, all these are the mark of self.
[The hundred bones (
bǎi hái

)] Refers to the various bones of a person, or the whole body. Here it means the whole body. [Needle and moxa] Puncture the acupoints with needles and burn moxa at the acupoints; here it generally refers to medical treatment. [Finally knows the pure nirvāṇa, all these are the mark of self] The phrase 'finally knows' means that in the end one knows there is a pure mark before oneself, which is still a realization held in the mind, so it is still the mark of self.

[Then the substance of self appears ... all these are the mark of self] The 'self' spoken of here differs from the 'self' of which the person who has not cultivated the Way speaks. The 'self' of the person who has not cultivated the Way is the body-mind of the five aggregates. But the cultivator of the Way, after seeing the nature, realizes concretely that the body-mind of the five aggregates is not 'self.' The 'self' spoken of here is the 'self' of a mind that has something attained (the act of realization) within cultivation. As long as even the slightest mind of attaining realization exists, that is the mark of self; it is a tiger in the road on the bodhi-path. In the Diamond Sutra, the Buddha says:

"Subhuti, what do you think? Can a stream-entrant have this thought: I have attained the fruit of stream-entry? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One. Why? Because stream-entrant is called entering the stream, yet there is nothing entered; not entering forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touch, and dharmas, this is called stream-entrant."

(Translation: The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Can a person of the first fruit have this thought: I have attained the fruit of stream-entry? Subhuti replied: No, World-Honored One. Why? Because stream-entrant is called entering the stream (entering the holy stream), precisely because he has nothing in which he enters (he is free of marks), and does not enter the six sense-objects (he can empty feeling and consciousness, and be free of the marks of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touch, and dharmas); therefore he is called a stream-entrant. If he still clung to a mark of something entered (thinking there was something attained in practice), then he would not be called a stream-entrant.) The Buddha again said:

"Subhuti, there is truly no dharma by which the Tathagata attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti, if there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then Dipamkara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Because there is truly no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, therefore Dipamkara Buddha gave me the prophecy, saying: In a future life you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
(For details see
Exegesis of the Diamond Sutra

[Good man! What is the mark of person? It means whatever the mind, of these sentient beings, awakens to and realizes. Good man! One who awakens to having a self no longer recognizes the self; the realization that is not self is likewise; having awakened and surpassed all those who realize to the extent that all are the mark of person. Good man! If the mind, even up to perfectly awakening to nirvāṇa as what I possess, holds a trace of awakening, and exhausts all the principle of realization, all these are called the mark of person.]

Good man! What is the mark of person? It means whatever the mind, of these sentient beings, awakens to and realizes; this is the mark of person. Good man! One who awakens to having the mark of self no longer recognizes the mark of self; one who awakens to the non-self likewise no longer recognizes the mark of self (in all this the realms it has realized are dissolved, hence there is no mark of self). One who awakens to having already surpassed all the realms of realization, this entirely is the mark of person. Good man! If the mind, even up to perfectly awakening to the realm of nirvāṇa as what I have realized, this is the mark of person; as long as even a trace of the mind of awakening has not perished, even if one thoroughly masters the principle it has realized, it is all called the mark of person.
[Thoroughly mastering the principle of realization (
dān
)] Completely mastering the principle it has realized.

This passage means: awakening to the fact that realization is the mark of self and not dwelling in it, one then thinks there is already no mark. But one does not realize there is still a thought of one who can awaken, which is still a mark; this is the mark of person. That is to say, as long as even a trace of the mind of awakening exists, that is the mark of person. The defect lies in the character 'awaken.' Why? Because if both mind and realm were forgotten, then there would be no such thing as awakening.

[Good man! What is the mark of sentient beings? It means whatever the mind, of these sentient beings, that its own realization and awakening cannot reach. Good man! For example, if someone says: 'I am a sentient being.' Then know that the sentient being of which that person speaks is neither self nor the other. Why not self? I am a sentient being, so it is not self. Why not the other? I am a sentient being, therefore it is not the other. Good man! But when all sentient beings understand realization and awakening as the mark of self and the mark of person, and what the mark of self and the mark of person cannot reach still holds something understood, this is called the mark of sentient beings.]

Good man! What is the mark of sentient beings? It means whatever the mind, of these sentient beings, that realization (the mark of self) and awakening (the mark of person) cannot reach, yet still has a mind that leaves realization and awakening; this is called the mark of sentient beings. Good man! For example, if someone says: 'I am a sentient being,' then one knows that the sentient being of which he speaks (this group, a metaphor for the mark of sentient beings) is neither self (a metaphor for the mark of self) nor the other (a metaphor for the mark of person). Good man! As long as sentient beings understand that realization and awakening are the mark of self and the mark of person, and what the mark of self and the mark of person cannot reach still holds something understood, this is called the mark of sentient beings.

[What its own realization and awakening cannot reach] That which realization (the mark of self) and awakening (the mark of person) cannot reach, yet still has a mind that leaves realization and awakening; this is called the mark of sentient beings.

This passage means: having understood that realization (the mark of self) and awakening (the mark of person) are both delusion, and this mindful-understanding, because it sees that there is realization and awakening that can be left behind, is called the mark of sentient beings. The defect lies in the character 'understand.'

blocks.text: 4. The Mark of a Life Span (Awareness)

inline.s: [Good man! What is the mark of a life span? It means whatever the mind, of these sentient beings, that contemplates purity and is aware of what it has understood; which all the wisdom of karma cannot itself see, like a life-root.]

Good man! What is the mark of a life span? It means whatever the mind, of these sentient beings, that contemplates purity and is aware of what it has understood as the mark of sentient beings; which all the wisdom of karma cannot itself see (as the eye cannot see the eye), like the life-root. This very 'awareness' is the mark of a life span.

Master Hanshan's Direct Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: 'The preceding mind that can understand is the mark of sentient beings. Now, as the contemplation-wisdom grows brighter and illumines this mind of understanding, it too is unobtainable; there is only the one pure enlightenment-substance, what is called awakening to the source of mind, therefore it is called ultimate awareness. When it reaches this point, realm and wisdom are both gone, and everything is left behind; it is said that with the wisdom of the immediate mind one still illumines the substance of still extinction, realm and wisdom as one. As the eye cannot see the eye, it is said all the wisdom of karma cannot itself see it. Having returned from delusion to truth and arrived at the ultimate point of the dharma-body, if one only guards the still extinction and cannot turn around and come back, this is what is called holding onto the top of the pole, sunk still in dead water. The school [of Chan] calls this the fall of the noble; in this very place of the fall one cannot transcend, therefore it is like the life-root, and is the mark of a life span. The proverb says: The man who does not move on the top of a hundred-foot pole, though he has entered, is not yet real; a step further from the top of the hundred-foot pole, and the whole great world manifests his whole body. Therefore, sitting in guard over the profound and subtle, the life-root is not cut. Previously it was said, not dwelling in birth and death, not dwelling in nirvāṇa; this very state is dwelling in the mark of nirvāṇa.'
[Sitting in guard over the profound and subtle] Stagnating in a realm that is deep and subtle.

[Good man! If the mind illuminates and sees all those who are aware, they are all dust and defilement; for awareness and what is aware do not leave the dust. Just as hot water melts ice, there is no other ice that knows the melting ice; holding a self and being aware of a self are also thus.]

Good man! If the mind rouses wisdom to illuminate and see all those who are aware (the three marks of realization, awakening, understanding), then the wisdom roused (awareness) together with realization, awakening, and understanding are all dust and defilement. This is because awareness and what is aware also do not leave the dust. Just as boiling water melts ice, all becoming one water, there is no other ice that knows the ice is melting. Holding a self (realization, awakening, understanding) and being aware of a self (the wisdom roused) are also thus, becoming one ultimate awareness, with no separate self knowing that the self is exhausted.

blocks.text: 5. One Must Understand the Four Marks

inline.s: [Good man! The sentient beings of the last age, if they do not understand the four marks, though they pass through many eons and diligently cultivate the Way, in the end cannot accomplish all the holy fruits. Therefore it is called the last age of the true Dharma. Why? Because they take all the marks of self to be nirvāṇa, and because they consider having realization and having awakening to be accomplishment. It is like a person who takes a thief as his son; the wealth and treasures of his home will in the end not be accomplished.]

Good man! The sentient beings of the last age, if they do not understand and eradicate these four marks, though they pass through many eons and diligently cultivate the Way, in the end cannot accomplish all the holy fruits. Therefore it is called the last age of the true Dharma. Why? Because they take all the marks of self (realization, awakening, understanding, awareness) to be nirvāṇa, and because they regard having realization, having awakening, having understanding, and having awareness, deludedly thinking this is accomplishment. It is like a person who takes a thief as his son; the wealth and treasures of his home are continually stolen away by this thief-son, and in the end cannot be accumulated.

[Why? Those who love me also love nirvāṇa; they suppress the root of my love, and make it the mark of nirvāṇa. Those who hate me also hate birth and death; not knowing that the root of love is true birth and death, they separately hate birth and death; this is called non-liberation.]

Why does recognizing the self obstruct the Way? This is because the self that loves also loves nirvāṇa, and suppresses the root of my love, making it the mark of nirvāṇa; this is not true nirvāṇa. The self that hates also hates birth and death, yet does not know that the root of love is true birth and death; separately hating birth and death is called non-liberation.
