[How do we know that the dharma is not liberated? Good man! The sentient beings of the last age who practice bodhi, taking their own subtle realization to be pure self, have not yet exhausted the root of the mark of self.]

How do we know that this way of practice does not attain liberation? Good man! The sentient beings of the last age who practice bodhi, taking their own subtle realization (realization, awakening, understanding, awareness) as pure nirvāṇa, have in fact not yet entirely eradicated the root of the mark of self (so-called: a mountain nine fathoms high fails by one basket of earth).
[Subtle realization] A subtle, fine realm of the Way, referring to 'realization, awakening, understanding, awareness.'

[If someone praises that dharma, he immediately gives rise to joy and wishes to save them. If someone slanders what is attained, he immediately gives rise to anger and hatred. Then one knows that the mark of self is firmly held, lurking in the realm of consciousness, sporting among the sense-organs, never interrupted.]

Suppose someone praises his practice, then he immediately gives rise to joy and desires to save them. Suppose someone slanders his attained realization, then he immediately gives rise to anger and hatred. Then one knows the mark of self is firmly held, lurking in the alaya-consciousness, sporting among the six sense-organs, never interrupted.
[Good man! Those who cultivate the Way without eliminating the mark of a self therefore cannot enter the pure and clear enlightenment.]
Good man! Those who cultivate the Way without eliminating the mark of a self therefore cannot enter the pure and clear enlightenment.

[Good man! If one knows the self is empty, there is none who destroys me. If one says that I preach the Dharma, it is because the mark of a self is not yet cut off; so also for sentient beings and for life.]

Good man! If one knows the self is empty, there is none who destroys me. Yet to hold that there is a self that preaches the Dharma and saves beings is precisely the mark of a self not yet cut off. If the mark of a self is not cut off, then the marks of a person, of sentient beings, and of a life-span are all likewise not cut off.

[Good man! In the last age, sentient beings call sickness the Dharma; therefore they are called pitiable. Though they diligently advance, they only increase their sicknesses, and therefore cannot enter the pure and clear enlightenment.]

Good man! In the last age, sentient beings call their sickness (realization, awakening, understanding, awareness) the Dharma; therefore they are called pitiable. Though they diligently and earnestly advance, they only increase their sicknesses, and therefore cannot enter the pure and clear enlightenment.

[Calling sickness the Dharma] To speak of what one has realized is precisely the mark of a self; to speak of what one has awakened to is precisely the mark of a person; to speak of what one has understood is precisely the mark of sentient beings; to speak of what one is aware of is precisely the mark of a life-span. This is taking sickness (the four marks) as the Dharma.
[Good man! In the last age, sentient beings, not understanding the four marks, regard the Tathagata's understanding and place of practice as their own cultivation, and in the end attain nothing.]

Good man! If last-age sentient beings do not understand the elimination of the four marks, and do not take the Tathagata's understanding and practice as their own in cultivating, then in the end they can never accomplish anything.

[Some sentient beings, having not attained, claim to have attained; having not realized, claim to have realized. Seeing one who advances to the better, they give rise to envy. Because these beings have not cut off self-love, therefore they cannot enter the pure and clear enlightenment.]

There are also sentient beings who, having not attained, think they have attained; having not realized, think they have realized; and seeing those who advance to the better, give rise to envy (envy arises from self-love). Because these beings have not cut off self-love, therefore they cannot enter the pure and clear enlightenment.

[Good man! Sentient beings of the last age who hope to attain the Way; let them not seek awakening, for this only increases much learning and grows the view of a self. They should only be diligent, subduing afflictions. Rousing great courage, causing the not-yet-attained to be attained and the not-yet-cut-off to be cut off; greed, hatred, love, arrogance, flattery, crookedness, and envy not arising when facing conditions; the love of self and other wholly extinguished. The Buddha says such a person gradually accomplishes. Seek the good friend, and do not fall into wrong views. If toward what is sought there arises separate hatred and love, then one cannot enter the pure and clear enlightenment sea.]

Good man! Last-age sentient beings who hope to attain the Way should not seek awakening with the mind, for seeking awakening only increases much learning and grows the view of a self. They should only be diligent and subdue afflictions (not by seeking awakening, but by subduing afflictions!). Rousing great courage, causing the not-yet-attained to be attained and the not-yet-cut-off to be cut off, so that greed, hatred, love, arrogance, flattery, crookedness, envy, and the like do not arise when facing conditions, and the love of self and other is wholly extinguished. The Buddha says such a person will certainly gradually accomplish. Still more should one gain the instruction of a good friend and not fall into wrong views. If toward what is sought separate hatred and love arise, one cannot enter the pure and clear enlightenment sea.

[Let them not seek awakening, only increasing much learning] As long as there is a mind seeking awakening, one will surely read the scriptures and treatises widely to seek the state of awakening, and cultivate while clinging to marks. Thus one only increases much learning and grows the view of a self; this is not true cultivation.

blocks.text: 6. Reciting Verses to Restate the Teaching

inline.s: [Jingye, you should know: all sentient beings, all by clinging to self-love, have from beginningless time vainly transmigrated; not yet having removed the four kinds of marks, they cannot attain bodhi.]

Jingye, you should know that all sentient beings, by clinging to self-love, have from beginningless time vainly transmigrated through birth and death; if they have not eliminated the marks of self, person, sentient beings, and life-span, they cannot attain bodhi.

[Love and hate arise in the mind; flattery and crookedness dwell in the thoughts; therefore many are confused and dim and cannot enter the city of enlightenment. If one returns to the enlightenment-land, first remove greed, hatred, and delusion; if love of the Dharma does not remain in the mind, gradually one may accomplish. My body originally is not; where do hate and love arise? Such a person seeking the good friend will never fall into wrong views. If toward what is sought another thought arises, in the end it is not accomplishment.]

Love and hate arise in the mind, and flattery and crookedness dwell in the thoughts; because of this many are confused and dim and cannot enter the city of enlightenment (nirvāṇa). To return to the source and go back to the enlightenment-land (the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment), one must first remove greed, hatred, and delusion, and also not let love of the Dharma dwell in the mind; thus gradually one may accomplish. My body originally is not; where do hate and love arise? Such a person seeking the good friend will never fall into wrong views. If toward what is sought there again arises a mind of separate love and hate, in the end one cannot accomplish.
[Love of the Dharma] For the four states of realization, awakening, understanding, and awareness, clinging to them gives rise to love; this is called love of the Dharma.

blocks.text: 10. One Must Depart from the Four Sicknesses

inline.s: [The four sicknesses] First, the sickness of making: making means giving rise to a mind that contrives. If one says: I make various practices in my fundamental mind, seeking perfect enlightenment; that enlightenment-nature is not gained by making, so it is called a sickness. Second, the sickness of relying: relying means following conditions and indulging one's nature. If one says: We now neither cut off birth and death nor seek nirvāṇa, letting everything be, seeking perfect enlightenment; that enlightenment-nature is not had by relying, so it is called a sickness. Third, the sickness of stopping: stopping means stopping the false and realizing the true. If one says: I now forever still all thoughts, serene and equal, seeking perfect enlightenment; that enlightenment-nature is not gained by stopping, so it is called a sickness. Fourth, the sickness of extinguishing: extinguishing means quiescence. If one says: I now forever extinguish all afflictions, and body and mind, faculties and objects, and all vain realms are forever still, seeking perfect enlightenment; that enlightenment-nature is not a mark of extinction, so it is called a sickness.

[At that time, the Bodhisattva Pujue, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, circled him three times to the right, knelt with palms together and said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-honored One, you have spoken swiftly of the sicknesses of Chan, causing the great assembly to gain what they never had, their minds open and free, and to attain great peace.]

At that time, the Bodhisattva Pujue, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, circled three times to the right, knelt with palms together, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-honored One, you have lucidly expounded the sicknesses of Chan, causing the great assembly to gain what they never had, their minds opened and their intentions released, all doubts dissolved, and to attain great peace.

[Swiftly speaking the sicknesses of Chan] For details see the previous chapter, Removing the Four Marks. [Peace] Stable and at ease, free and unobstructed; the character is an old variant of the character for stable.

[World-honored One, in the last age sentient beings go ever farther from the Buddha, the sages and saints hide away, and wrong teachings grow ever raging. What persons should they seek? Relying on what Dharma? Practicing what practice? Removing what sickness? How should they arouse the mind so that this crowd of the blind does not fall into wrong views? Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself, his five limbs on the ground. Thus he requested three times, ending and beginning again.]

World-honored One, in the last age sentient beings go ever farther from the Buddha, the sages and saints hide away, and wrong teachings rage. What persons should they seek? Relying on what Dharma? Practicing what practice? Removing what sickness? How should they arouse the mind so that this crowd of the blind does not fall into wrong views? The Bodhisattva Pujue, having spoken these words, prostrated himself, his five limbs on the ground. Thus he requested three times, ending and beginning again.
[The crowd of the blind] The last-age sentient beings, born without the eye of wisdom, cannot distinguish right from wrong; therefore they are called the crowd of the blind.

[At that time, the World-honored One said to the Bodhisattva Pujue: Well! Well! Good man! You are able to ask the Tathagata about such practice and to give all last-age sentient beings the fearless eye of the Way, causing them to accomplish the holy Way. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Pujue, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and with the great assembly listened in silence.]

At that time, the World-honored One said to the Bodhisattva Pujue: Well! Well! Good man! You are able to ask the Tathagata about this way of practice and to give all last-age sentient beings the fearless eye of the Way, causing them to accomplish the holy Way. Now concentrate and listen attentively; I shall speak for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Pujue, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and with the great assembly listened in silence.

[Good man! Last-age sentient beings, about to rouse the great mind and seek the good friend, who wish to cultivate, should seek one of right knowledge and insight. A mind that does not dwell in marks and does not cling to the states of sravakas and pratyekabuddhas; though manifesting worldly toil, the mind is ever pure; though showing various faults, he praises the pure conduct and does not cause sentient beings to enter what is not in accord with the rules of discipline. Seeking such a person, one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

Good man! Last-age sentient beings, about to rouse the great mind and seek the good friend, who wish to cultivate, should seek the one of right knowledge and insight. Such a person's mind does not dwell in marks and does not cling to the two-vehicle states of sravakas and pratyekabuddhas; though he manifests affliction, his mind is ever pure; though he shows various faults, he praises the pure conduct and does not cause sentient beings to enter what is contrary to the rules of discipline. Seeking such a person, one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
[Worldly toil] The mind's toil in the dusty realm is another name for affliction.

[In the last age, sentient beings who see such a person should make offerings to him, not sparing body or life. That good friend, in the four demeanors, always manifests purity, even to the point of showing various faults, with a mind without arrogance; how much less would he seize wealth, wife, and kin? If a good man does not give rise to evil thoughts toward that good friend, then he can ultimately accomplish right enlightenment, and the flower of the mind opens and shines, illuminating the lands of the ten directions.]

In the last age, sentient beings who see such a person should make offerings to him, not sparing body, wealth, or life. Such a good friend, in the four demeanors, always manifests purity, even to the point of showing various faults, yet with a mind without arrogance; how much less would he seize another's wealth, wife, and relatives? If a good man does not give rise to evil thoughts toward that good friend, then he can ultimately accomplish right enlightenment, and the flower of the mind opens and shines, universally illuminating the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.

[The four demeanors] These are the rules monks and nuns must observe, namely to be careful in the daily activities of life so as to maintain solemnity and dignity: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Walk like the wind, stand like a pine, sit like a bell, lie like a bow. [Bo, pronounced b
o

)] Seizing. [The flower of the mind] Comparing the purity of the fundamental mind to a flower, it is called the flower of the mind. The Avatamsaka Sutra says: Again, like the full moon appearing in empty space, causing the minds of those who can be transformed to bloom (fully open).
[Good man! That good friend's realized wondrous Dharma should be free of the four sicknesses. What are the four sicknesses?]
Good man! The wondrous Dharma of perfect enlightenment realized by that good friend should be free of the four sicknesses. What are they?

[First, the sickness of making. If there is a person who says: I make various practices in my fundamental mind, seeking perfect enlightenment; that enlightenment-nature is not obtained by making, therefore it is called a sickness.]

First, the sickness of making. If one says: I make various practices in my fundamental mind, seeking perfect enlightenment. Since the wondrous enlightenment-nature is originally complete in itself and does not depend on contrivance, if one now seeks it through a practice that contrives, how could it be attained? Therefore it is called a sickness.

[Second, the sickness of relying. If there is a person who says: We now neither cut off birth and death nor seek nirvāṇa, with no thought of arising or ceasing in nirvāṇa and birth and death, letting everything be, following the nature of all dharmas, seeking perfect enlightenment; that enlightenment-nature is not had by relying, therefore it is called a sickness.]

Second, the sickness of relying. If one says: We now neither cut off birth and death nor seek nirvāṇa, with no thought of arising or ceasing in nirvāṇa and birth and death, letting everything be, following the nature of all dharmas, seeking perfect enlightenment. Since the wondrous enlightenment-nature is not had by relying, therefore it is called a sickness.

The sickness of relying is for those of wild view who, on the pretext that there is no birth and death to cut off and no nirvāṇa to realize, idle and indulge their nature, letting loose body and mind, claiming there is no thing and no obstruction and that they have attained great liberation. If one follows such persons, one falls into wildness; therefore indulging the nature is called a sickness.

[Third, the sickness of stopping. If there is a person who says: I now, in my own mind, forever still all thoughts, attaining all natures, serene and equal, seeking perfect enlightenment; that enlightenment-nature is not united with by stopping, therefore it is called a sickness.]

Third, the sickness of stopping. If one says: I now, in my own mind, forever still all thoughts, attaining all natures, serene and equal, seeking perfect enlightenment. Since the wondrous enlightenment-nature cannot be united with by stopping, therefore it is called a sickness.

[Fourth, the sickness of extinguishing. If there is a person who says: I now forever cut off all afflictions, and body and mind are ultimately empty, how much more the faculties, objects, and vain realms? All forever still, seeking perfect enlightenment; that enlightenment-nature is not a mark of quiescence, therefore it is called a sickness.]

Fourth, the sickness of extinguishing. If one says: I now forever cut off all afflictions, and body and mind are ultimately empty, how much more the faculties, objects, and vain realms? All forever still, seeking perfect enlightenment. Since the wondrous enlightenment-nature is not a mark of arid quiescence, therefore it is called a sickness.
[One who departs from the four sicknesses then knows purity. One who contemplates thus is called right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is called wrong contemplation.]

One who departs from the four sicknesses then knows that the self-nature of perfect enlightenment is perfectly bright and pure. One who contemplates thus is called right contemplation; otherwise, wrong contemplation.

In the first chapter the World-honored One already instructed: All Tathagatas, at the beginning of their ground of arising, rely on the perfect illumination of the pure and clear enlightenment-mark, forever cutting off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha Way. Therefore the right method of practice is: perfectly illuminate the pure and clear enlightenment-mark, and forever cut off ignorance.

[Good man! Last-age sentient beings who wish to cultivate should, to the end of life, make offerings to the good friend and serve the good teacher. When that good teacher wishes to draw near, one should cut off arrogance; if he again departs, one should cut off hatred. Seeing adverse and favorable conditions, be like empty space. Know that body and mind are ultimately equal and of one substance with all sentient beings, without distinction. Cultivating thus, one enters perfect enlightenment.]

Good man! Last-age sentient beings who wish to cultivate should, to the end of life, make offerings to the good friend and serve the good teacher. When he draws near, welcome him with an open and humble mind (cutting off arrogance); when he departs, do not harbor hatred. When one sees him manifest favorable and adverse conditions, know this tests and refines oneself, and accept it with a mind like empty space. Know that body and mind are ultimately equal and of one substance with all sentient beings. Cultivating thus, one enters perfect enlightenment.
[To the end of life] To exhaust the measure of one's body and life.

[Good man! In the last age, sentient beings cannot attain the Way because they have the seeds of all their beginningless love and hate of self and other, and are therefore not liberated. If there is a person who contemplates his enemy as his own parents, with a mind without duality, he then removes the various sicknesses. In all dharmas, the love and hate of self and other are likewise so.]

Good man! The reason last-age sentient beings cannot attain the Way is that they have the seeds of the beginningless hate and love of self and other (hatred and love toward self and toward others), and are therefore not liberated. If there is a person who contemplates his enemy as his own parents, with a mind without duality, he then removes the various sicknesses of love and hate. In all dharmas, the way of removing the love and hate of self and other is likewise this: treat everything equally, with a mind without duality.

[Contemplating the enemy as one's own parents, with a mind without duality, then removing the various sicknesses] When enemy and kin are regarded equally and the mind has no duality, then the seeds of hatred and love are cut off of themselves, and the root of the sickness that obstructs the Way is removed of itself; therefore it says one then removes the various sicknesses. Hence cultivating an equal mind is of the utmost importance, regarding everything equally (favorable and adverse, gain and loss, early and late death, enemy and kin, noble and lowly, and so on)

[Good man! Last-age sentient beings who seek perfect enlightenment should arouse the mind and say thus: Within all of empty space, I will cause all sentient beings to enter ultimate perfect enlightenment. In perfect enlightenment, there is none who takes enlightenment, apart from removing all the marks of self and other. Arousing the mind thus, one does not fall into wrong views.]

Good man! Last-age sentient beings who seek perfect enlightenment should arouse the mind and say thus: Within all of empty space, I will cause all sentient beings to be saved into ultimate perfect enlightenment (regarding enemy and kin equally). In perfect enlightenment,
with nothing taken up or clung to,

causing them to have no minds of realization, awakening, understanding, and awareness (see the previous chapter, Removing the Four Marks), and removing their four sicknesses of the mark of a self (realization), of a person (awakening), of sentient beings (understanding), and of a life-span (awareness). Arousing the mind thus, one does not fall into wrong views.
[None who takes enlightenment] Though saving sentient beings, one does not see the mark of saving beings. This is the ordinary mind that takes up and clings to nothing.

blocks.text: 6. Reciting Verses to Restate the Teaching

inline.s: [Pujue, you should know: last-age sentient beings who seek the good friend should seek right views and minds far from the two vehicles. In the Dharma remove the four sicknesses, namely making, stopping, relying, and extinguishing. When near, be without arrogance; when far, be without hatred. Seeing various states, the mind should give rise to wonder, as if the Buddha appeared in the world.]

Pujue, you should know that last-age sentient beings who seek the good friend should seek one who has right views and a mind far from the two vehicles. In cultivation one must dispel the four sicknesses of making, stopping, relying, and extinguishing. When the good friend draws near, be without arrogance; when he departs, do not give rise to hatred; when one sees him manifest favorable and adverse states, give rise to a mind of wonder, as if the Buddha appeared in the world to teach and transform oneself personally.

[Not violating what is contrary to the rules of discipline, the root of the precepts is forever pure. Saving all sentient beings, ultimately entering perfect enlightenment, without the marks of self, other, and person. Relying on right wisdom, one then surpasses wrong views and realizes enlightenment and great parinirvāṇa.]

And not violating nor slandering the rules of discipline, the root of the precepts is forever pure. Saving all sentient beings to enter ultimate perfect enlightenment, causing them to be free of the four marks of a self (realization), of a person (awakening), of sentient beings (understanding), and of a life-span (awareness). Relying on right wisdom, one then surpasses wrong views and realizes enlightenment and the great parinirvāṇa.

[Great parinirvāṇa] In Sanskrit, maha-parinirvāṇa: maha means great, praising the virtue of stillness; pari means entering, the meaning of the destination; nirvāṇa means extinction, the extinction of afflictions and of body and mind; va means rest. Combined, it is the great entering into extinction and rest, abbreviated great parinirvāṇa, or parinirvāṇa, or nirvāṇa.

blocks.text: 11. Dwelling in Quiet and Devoted Cultivation

inline.s: [At that time, the Bodhisattva Yuanjue, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, circled three times to the right, knelt with palms together and said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-honored One, for the sake of our kind, you have spoken widely of the various skillful means of the pure and clear enlightenment, causing the last-age sentient beings to have great benefit.]

At that time, the Bodhisattva Yuanjue, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, circled three times to the right, knelt with palms together, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-honored One, for the sake of our kind, you have spoken widely of the various skillful means of the pure and clear enlightenment, causing the last-age sentient beings to have great benefit.

[World-honored One, we have now gained awakening. If after the Buddha's passing, last-age sentient beings who have not awakened, how should they dwell in peace and cultivate this pure and clear realm of perfect enlightenment? In this perfect enlightenment, of the three pure contemplations, which should be first? We only beg the Great Compassionate One to bestow great benefit on the great assembly and the last-age sentient beings. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself, his five limbs on the ground. Thus he requested three times, ending and beginning again.]

World-honored One, we have now gained awakening. If after the Buddha's passing, last-age sentient beings who have not awakened, how should they dwell in peace and cultivate this pure and clear realm of perfect enlightenment? In this perfect enlightenment, of the three pure contemplations (samatha, samapatti, dhyana), which should be first? We only beg the World-honored One in his great compassion to bestow great benefit on the great assembly and the last-age sentient beings. The Bodhisattva Yuanjue, having spoken these words, prostrated himself, his five limbs on the ground. Thus he requested three times, ending and beginning again.

[At that time, the World-honored One said to the Bodhisattva Yuanjue: Well! Well! Good man! You are able to ask the Tathagata about such skillful means, bestowing great benefit on sentient beings. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Yuanjue, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and with the great assembly listened in silence.]

At that time, the World-honored One said to the Bodhisattva Yuanjue: Well! Well! Good man! You are able to ask the Tathagata about such skillful means, and to bestow great benefit on sentient beings. Now concentrate and listen attentively; I shall speak for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Yuanjue, receiving the teaching, rejoiced, and with the great assembly listened in silence.

[Good man! Of all sentient beings, whether the Buddha dwells in the world, or after the Buddha's passing, or at the end of the Dharma, if there are sentient beings endowed with the nature of the Great Vehicle who believe in the Buddha's secret great mind of perfect enlightenment, and wish to cultivate, if in a temple they settle the assembly, then owing to the circumstances of external affairs, they should contemplate each according to their lot, as I have already said.]

Good man! Among all sentient beings, whether the Buddha dwells in the world, or after his passing, or at the end of the Dharma, if there are beings endowed with the Great Vehicle nature who believe in the Buddha's secret great mind of perfect enlightenment and wish to cultivate, if in a monastery they settle the assembly, then because of various external circumstances, they should contemplate with right mindfulness according to their situation, cultivating by the method I have already set forth.

blocks.text: 1. Setting a Period for Devoted Cultivation

inline.s: [If besides there is no other cause or condition, then establish a practice ground and fix a period. If the long period, one hundred twenty days; the middle period, 100 days; the lower period, 80 days; and settle in a pure dwelling.]

If there is no cause or condition of other affairs, then one should establish a practice ground and set a period. If the long period, 120 days; if the middle period, one hundred days; if the lower period, eighty days. Then one arranges a pure dwelling place and makes sure that outsiders and external affairs cannot interfere.

[If the Buddha is present, then contemplate rightly. If after the Buddha's passing, set up an image, keep it in mind and gaze, produce right recollection, as in the days when the Tathagata dwelt in the world. Hang up banners and streamers, and for twenty-one days bow to the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, seeking pity and repenting; when meeting a good state, one's mind becomes light and at ease. After the twenty-one days, collect the mind entirely.]

If the Tathagata dwells in the world, one should hear the Buddha preach the Dharma and contemplate rightly. If after the Buddha's passing, one should set up a Buddha image, keep it in mind and gaze upon it, produce right recollection, as in the days when the Tathagata dwelt in the world. Hang up banners and streamers, burn incense and scatter flowers, to adorn the practice ground; after twenty-one days, bow to the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, seeking pity and repenting; when meeting a good state, one's mind becomes light and at ease. After these twenty-one days, one collects the mind entirely and cultivates by one of the twenty-five wheels described above.
[If it reaches the beginning of summer, then dwell in peace for three months. One should dwell as a pure bodhisattva, with a mind far from the sravakas, not employing a retinue.]

If it is the beginning of summer, then one dwells in peace for three months. In these three months of the summer retreat, one should hold to the conduct of a pure bodhisattva, with a mind far from the sravakas, and not employ a retinue.

[The summer retreat] According to the Buddha's rule, during the three months of summer, monks and nuns may not go out at will, in order to devote themselves to sitting meditation and the study of the Buddha Dharma.

[When the day of retreat arrives, one should say thus before the Buddha: I, the monk, the nun, the upasaka, or the upasika named so-and-so, riding the Bodhisattva vehicle, cultivate the practice of quiescence, and together enter the abiding of the pure and real mark. Taking the great perfect enlightenment as my temple, body and mind abide in peace in the wisdom of the equality of nature; because the self-nature of nirvāṇa has no affiliation. Now I respectfully announce: not relying on the sravakas, I shall dwell in peace for three months with the Tathagatas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas. For the sake of the great cause of cultivating the supreme wondrous enlightenment of the bodhisattva, I do not tie myself to a retinue.]

When the day of retreat arrives, one should say thus before the Buddha: I, the monk, the nun, the upasaka, or the upasika named so-and-so, abiding in the Bodhisattva vehicle, cultivate the practice of quiescence, and together enter the abiding of the pure and real mark. Taking the great perfect enlightenment as my temple, body and mind abide in peace in the wisdom of the equality of nature, because the self-nature of nirvāṇa has no affiliation. Now I respectfully announce: not relying on the sravakas, I shall dwell in peace for three months with the Tathagatas of the ten directions and the great bodhisattvas. For the sake of the great cause of cultivating the bodhisattva's supreme wondrous enlightenment, I do not tie myself to a retinue.

[Upasaka] In Chinese translation: pure-faith man; that is, a male lay practitioner who in lay life draws near and attends to the Triple Gem and upholds the five precepts. [Upasika] In Chinese translation: pure-faith woman; that is, a female lay practitioner who in lay life draws near and attends to the Triple Gem and upholds the five precepts. [The wisdom of the equality of nature] The wisdom obtained by turning the view of a self of the manas consciousness and realizing the principle of the equality of self and other.
[Good man! This is called the bodhisattva's manifestation of dwelling in peace. After passing the three periods, one goes wherever one wishes without obstruction.]

Good man! This is called the bodhisattva's manifestation of dwelling in peace. Having passed the periods of the three terms (120 days, or 100 days, or 80 days) of pure cultivation, one attains great freedom and great liberation (going wherever one wishes without obstruction).
[The three periods] These are the long period of 120 days, the middle period of one hundred days, and the lower period of eighty days spoken of above.
[Good man! If those last-age sentient beings who cultivate, seeking the Bodhisattva Way, enter the three periods, then all states other than those they have heard are never to be taken.]

Good man! If those last-age sentient beings who cultivate, seeking the Bodhisattva Way, enter the three periods (120 days, or 100 days, or 80 days), then all states other than those heard above are never to be taken.

[Good man! If sentient beings cultivate samatha, first take ultimate stillness, without giving rise to thought; when the stillness is extreme, then awareness arises. Thus the initial stillness, from one body to one world, is likewise so.]

Good man! If sentient beings cultivate samatha, first take ultimate stillness, without giving rise to thought; when the stillness is extreme, awareness arises. Thus the initial stillness, from one's body to one world, is likewise so.

[From one body to one world, likewise so] From one body: contemplate this present body as a union of the four great elements. When the four elements separate, where is this vain body? This mind is a shadow of the objects of the six senses. When the shadow of conditions scatters, no mind remains. When body and mind detach, this is the stillness of one body. When the one body is still, the very substance is awareness, the awareness of one body. Since the one body is so, all things are likewise so; since the sentient world is so, the material world is likewise so. This is leaving the world without, inner and outer equal, still and unmoving, body, mind, and world fused into one awareness; hence it says: to one world, likewise so. [The material world] The world of material things is the collective term for mountains, rivers, the earth, houses, and all utensils and articles.

[Good man! If awareness extends and fills one world, then in that world if one sentient being gives rise to a single thought, one knows it all; so too for hundreds and thousands of worlds. Other than the states heard, they are never to be taken.]

Good man! If awareness extends and fills one world, then in that world if one sentient being gives rise to a single thought, one knows it all; so too for hundreds and thousands of worlds. All states other than those heard above are never to be taken.

[Good man! If sentient beings cultivate samapatti, first recollect the Tathagatas of the ten directions and all the bodhisattvas of the ten directions' worlds, and by various gates gradually cultivate the diligent and bitter samādhi, broadly making great vows, and self-cultivating to become a seed. Other than the states heard, they are never to be taken.]

Good man! If sentient beings cultivate samapatti, first recollect the Tathagatas of the ten directions and all the bodhisattvas of the ten directions' worlds, and by various gates gradually cultivate the diligent and bitter samādhi, broadly making great vows, and accumulating practice into nature (self-cultivating to become a seed). All states other than those heard above are never to be taken.

[Good man! If sentient beings cultivate dhyana, first take the gate of counting, clearly knowing in the mind the thoughts of arising, dwelling, and ceasing, their boundaries and number, and so universally, in the four demeanors, distinguishing the counted thoughts, none not clearly known. Gradually increasing, to the point of knowing a single drop of rain in hundreds and thousands of worlds, as if seeing directly the objects one uses. Other than the states heard, they are never to be taken.]

Good man! If sentient beings cultivate dhyana, first take the gate of counting, clearly knowing in the mind the thoughts of arising, dwelling, and ceasing, their boundaries and number, and so universally, in the four demeanors, distinguishing the counted thoughts, none not clearly known. Gradually increasing, to the point of knowing a single drop of rain in hundreds and thousands of worlds, as if seeing directly the objects one uses. All states other than those heard above are never to be taken.

[The gate of counting] Here counting means clarifying; the gate of counting means contemplating the thoughts of one's own mind, clearly knowing each thought's arising, dwelling, and ceasing, and the number and order of its divisions. The common annotation says the gate of counting is an abbreviation for the gate of counting the breath, that is, the contemplation of counting the breath. This is wrong. Counting the breath is an elementary beginner's practice for stopping, superficial beyond all else; with such a practice how could one know a single drop of rain in hundreds and thousands of worlds, as if seeing directly the objects one uses? The text later says: Dhyana is called the gate of counting. Would that not become: Dhyana is called the gate of counting the breath? [Counting the breath] Silently counting the out-breath or in-breath to make the mind single. [Divisions] Differences, boundaries.
[This is called the first expedient of the three contemplations.]
This is the first expedient of the three contemplations. (Answering the question, “Of the three pure contemplations, which is taken as the first?”)
[First expedient]The expedient for the initial attainment of the Way.

[If sentient beings universally cultivate the three contemplations and diligently practice vigor, this is called the Tathagata appearing in the world. If again sentient beings of dull faculties in the last age, with minds wishing to seek the Way, are unable to attain success, because of past karmic obstacles they should diligently repent. Constantly arousing hope, they should first cut off hatred and love, envy, sycophancy and crookedness, and the mind that seeks to surpass [others]. Of the three pure contemplations, they should practice one matter as taught. If this contemplation is not attained, then cultivate that contemplation; not letting go of the mind, they seek its realization step by step.]

If sentient beings universally cultivate the three contemplations and diligently practice vigor, this is called the Tathagata appearing in the world. If sentient beings of dull faculties in the last age, with minds wishing to seek the Way, are unable to attain success, this is due to karmic obstacles from the past, and so they should diligently add repentance. Constantly arousing hope and wishing to cut off karmic obstacles, they should first cut off hatred and love, envy, sycophancy and crookedness, as well as the arrogant mind that seeks to surpass all others. Of the three pure contemplations, they should study one gate as it suits them. If they cannot get a start in this contemplation, then take up another contemplation; not letting go of the mind, they seek its realization step by step.

[Perfect Enlightenment, you should know: all sentient beings, if they wish to seek the unsurpassed Way, should first enter the three periods. Repenting the karma without beginning, passing through twenty-one days, then engage in right reflection. The realms not heard by them can never be taken up.]

Perfect Enlightenment, you should know: all sentient beings, if they wish to seek the unsurpassed Way, should first enter the three periods (one hundred twenty days, or one hundred days, or eighty days). Repenting the karma without beginning, passing through twenty-one days, then engage in right reflection. Unless the realms are those heard above (the World-Honored One's instructions in the preceding ten chapters), none of them are to be taken up.

[Samatha is the utmost stillness, samapatti is right recollection and holding, dhyana is the gate of counting; these are called the three pure contemplations. If one can diligently cultivate them, this is called the Buddha appearing in the world. For those of dull faculties who have not yet succeeded, always diligently repent the whole karma without beginning. If all the obstacles are eliminated, the Buddha-realm appears before one.]

Samatha is the utmost stillness, samapatti is right recollection and holding, dhyana is the gate of counting; these are called the three pure contemplations. If one can diligently cultivate these three pure contemplations, this is called the Buddha appearing in the world. For those of dull faculties who have not yet succeeded, always diligently repent in mind all the karmic offenses without beginning. If all the obstacles are eliminated, the Buddha-realm appears before one.

blocks.text: 1. The Five Questions of the Bodhisattva Xianshanshou

inline.s: [Thereupon, in the midst of the assembly, the Bodhisattva Xianshanshou rose from his seat, touched his head to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt long with hands folded, and said to the Buddha: Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, you have broadly opened and awakened such an inconceivable matter for us and for sentient beings of the last age. World-Honored One, what is the name of this Mahayana teaching, and how should it be upheld? What merit do sentient beings gain by cultivating it? How should we protect the one who upholds this sutra? To what stage does circulating this teaching reach? Having spoken these words, he prostrated his whole body on the ground. He made this request three times, ending and beginning again.]

Thereupon, in the midst of the assembly, the Bodhisattva Xianshanshou rose from his seat, touched his head to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt long with hands folded, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Greatly compassionate World-Honored One, you have broadly opened and caused us to enter into such an inconceivable matter for us and for sentient beings of the last age. World-Honored One, what is the name of this Mahayana sutra, and how should it be upheld? What merit do sentient beings gain by cultivating this sutra? How should we protect the one who upholds this sutra? Circulating this teaching and cultivating it thus, will it reach what stage (that is, what fruit-position will it reach)? Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Xianshanshou prostrated his whole body on the ground. He made this request three times, ending and beginning again.

[At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Xianshanshou: Good! Good! Good man. You are able, for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about the merit and the name of this sutra-teaching. Listen well now, and I shall speak it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Xianshanshou, delighting in receiving the instruction, and the great assembly, listened in silence.]

At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Bodhisattva Xianshanshou: Excellent! Excellent! Good man. You are able, for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about the merit and the name of this sutra-teaching. Now gather your minds and listen carefully; I shall proclaim it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Xianshanshou, delighting in receiving the instruction, and the great assembly, listened in silence.

[Good man! This sutra was spoken by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is guarded by the Tathagatas of the three times, is relied upon by the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, and is the pure eye of the twelve categories of scriptures. The name of this sutra is the Great, Vast, Perfect Enlightenment Dharani; it is also called the Ultimate Meaning of the Sutras; it is also called the King of Secret Samādhi; it is also called the Determined Realm of the Tathagata; it is also called the Distinctions of the Self-Nature of the Tathagata-Store. You should uphold it.]

Good man! This sutra was spoken by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is guarded by the Tathagatas of the three times, is relied upon by the bodhisattvas of the ten directions, and is the pure eye of the twelve categories of scriptures. The name of this sutra is the Great, Vast, Perfect Enlightenment Dharani; it is also called the Ultimate Meaning of the Sutras; it is also called the King of Secret Samādhi; it is also called the Determined Realm of the Tathagata; it is also called the Distinctions of the Self-Nature of the Tathagata-Store. You should uphold it as such.

[Good man! This sutra alone reveals the Tathagata's realm; only the Buddha-Tathagata can fully proclaim it. If the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age cultivate according to this, advancing gradually, they will reach the Buddha-ground.]

Good man! This sutra alone reveals the Tathagata's realm; only the Buddhas and Tathagatas can proclaim it penetratingly. If the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age cultivate according to this, advancing gradually, they can reach the Buddha-ground. (Answering the Bodhisattva Xianshanshou's earlier question, “To what stage does it reach?”)

blocks.text: 4. Both Sudden and Gradual Are Included

inline.s: [Good man! This sutra is called the Sudden Teaching of the Great Vehicle; sentient beings of sudden faculties awaken from it. It also includes all the groups of beings who cultivate gradually. It is like the great ocean, which does not refuse small streams. Even to mosquitos and asuras, those who drink its water all become filled.]

Good man! This sutra is called the Sudden Teaching of the Great Vehicle; sentient beings of sudden faculties awaken according to it. This sutra also includes the various types of beings who cultivate gradually. It is like the great ocean, which does not abandon the small rivers. Even to mosquitoes (a metaphor for the very small) and asuras (a metaphor for the very great), those who drink its water all become filled in their bellies.
[All the groups of beings]Sentient beings of various faculties.
[Good man! Suppose someone used only the seven treasures to fill the entire trichiliocosm as a gift; it would not equal someone hearing the name of this sutra and the meaning of a single phrase.]

Good man! Suppose someone used only the seven treasures to fill the entire trichiliocosm and used them as gifts; it would not equal someone hearing the name of this sutra and the principle of a single phrase of its text.
This paragraph and the following answer the question, “What merit do sentient beings gain by cultivating it?”

[Good man! Suppose someone taught hundreds of thousands of sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to attain the fruit of arhatship; it would not equal someone proclaiming this sutra and explaining half a verse.]

Good man! Suppose someone taught hundreds of thousands of sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to attain the fruit of arhatship; it would not equal someone proclaiming this sutra and clarifying half a verse.

[Good man! If again someone hears the name of this sutra and has faith without confusion, you should know that this person has planted blessings and wisdom not merely before one Buddha or two Buddhas, but thus even down to having planted wholesome roots before all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and so is able to hear this sutra-teaching.]

Good man! If again someone hears the name of this sutra and has faith without confusion, you should know that this person has planted blessings and wisdom not merely before one Buddha or two Buddhas, nor merely before three Buddhas or four Buddhas, but thus even down to having planted wholesome roots before Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, indeed before all the Buddhas, and so is able to hear this sutra-teaching and have faith without confusion.
[You good men should protect these practitioners of the last age, and not let evil demons and the various heretics disturb their body and mind and cause them to retreat.]

You good men should protect these practitioners of the last age (those who have heard the name of this sutra and have faith without confusion), and by no means let evil demons and the various heretics disturb their body and mind and cause them to retreat.

[At that time, in the assembly there were the Fire-Headed Vajra, the Crushing Vajra, the Nilamba Vajra, and other eighty thousand vajras with their retinues, who rose from their seats, touched their heads to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, if in the last age there are sentient beings able to uphold this Determined Great Vehicle, we shall guard them as we guard our own eyes. Even at the places of the bodhimanda where they cultivate, we vajras will ourselves lead our followers to guard them morning and evening, causing them not to retreat. Their homes will be forever free of disasters and hindrances; epidemics will be eradicated; treasure and wealth will be abundant, never lacking.]

At that time, in the assembly there were the Fire-Headed Vajra, the Crushing Vajra, the Nilamba Vajra, and other eighty thousand vajras with their retinues, who rose from their seats, touched their heads to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and respectfully said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, if in the last age there are sentient beings able to uphold this sutra of the Determined Great Vehicle, we shall guard them strictly, as we protect the pupils of our own eyes. Even at the places of the bodhimanda where they cultivate, we vajras will ourselves lead our followers to guard them day and night, causing them not to retreat. Their homes will be forever free of disasters and hindrances; epidemics will be eradicated; treasure and wealth will be abundant, always rich.

[At that time, the Great Brahma king, the twenty-eight heaven-kings, and the king of Mount Sumeru, the state-protecting heaven-kings, and others rose from their seats, touched their heads to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, we too shall guard these upholders of the sutra, always causing them to be at peace and their minds not to retreat.]

At that time, the Great Brahma king, the twenty-eight heaven-kings, and the king of Mount Sumeru, the state-protecting heaven-kings, and others rose from their seats, touched their heads to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and respectfully said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, we too shall guard these upholders of the sutra (the ones who uphold this sutra), always causing them to be at peace and their minds not to retreat.

[At that time, there was a powerful ghost king named Jipantu, with a hundred thousand ghost kings, who rose from their seats, touched their heads to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, we too shall guard these upholders of the sutra, attending them morning and evening, causing them not to retreat. If, within one yojana of the place where they dwell, any ghost or spirit invades their realm, we shall grind it to dust as fine as motes.]

At that time, there was a powerful ghost king named Jipantu, with a hundred thousand ghost kings, who rose from their seats, touched their heads to the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and respectfully said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, we too shall guard these upholders of the sutra, attending them morning and evening, causing them not to retreat. If, within one yojana of the place where they dwell, any ghost or spirit invades their realm, we shall grind them to dust as fine as motes.
[Yojana]A unit of distance in India. There are three sizes: a great yojana is about eighty li; a middle yojana about sixty li; a small yojana about forty li.

[When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, the devas, dragons, ghosts, and spirits, the eight classes and their retinues, and the various heaven-kings, Brahma kings, and the whole assembly, having heard what the Buddha said, all rejoiced greatly, believed, received, and practiced it.]

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, the devas, dragons, ghosts, and spirits, the eight classes and their retinues, and the various heaven-kings, Brahma kings, and the whole assembly, having heard what the Buddha said, all rejoiced greatly, believed, received, and practiced it.

[Devas and dragons]The deva assembly and the dragon assembly are two of the eight classes. [Eight classes]The deva assembly, the dragon assembly, the yakshas (rendered “brave ghosts” in Chinese), the gandharvas (rendered “fragrant spirits” in Chinese), the asuras (rendered “non-gods” in Chinese), the garudas (rendered “golden-winged birds” in Chinese), the kimnaras (rendered “non-humans” in Chinese), and the mahoragas (rendered “great python spirits” or “great-bellied earth-dragons” in Chinese). Because the eyes of human beings cannot see them, they are also called “the eight classes of the unseen assembly.” And because among the eight classes the devas and dragons are the most excellent, they are also called “the eight classes of devas and dragons,” or “the eight classes of dragon-spirits.”
